issues.body:
Windows ChatGPT masaüstü uygulaması: 26.1103.4239.0
Arayüzde görünen model: GPT-6 Astra Ultra
Çalışma ortamları: Önceki denemelerde hem Work Cloud/Bulut hem Yerel seçiliyken aynı sonuç raporlandı. Son ekran görüntüsü, araç seçimini ve yanıtı gösteriyor; çalışma yeri seçimini ayrıca göstermiyor.

Son denemede yapılan işlem

Mesaj oluşturulurken Browser/Tarayıcı araç seçimi eklendi. Gönderilmiş mesajın başında simgeli, mavi “Tarayıcı” etiketi görünüyor; yalnız düz metin olarak “@Browser” yazılmadı.

İstek, yerleşik tarayıcıda OpenAI Yardım Merkezi’nden kamuya açık bir makale açılması ve normal bir bağlantıya tıklanmasıydı. Power Apps’te işlem yapılması, dosya veya ayar değiştirilmesi istenmedi. Ana Windows masaüstünün, fiziksel fare ve klavyenin devralınmasına izin verilmedi; yerleşik tarayıcıda gezinmeye açıkça izin verildi.

Gözlenen sonuç

Work şu yanıtı verdi:

“Sağdaki yerleşik tarayıcı için etkileşim işlevi sunulmadı. Makaleyi açma veya bağlantıya tıklama çağrısı yapılmadı. Bu nedenle tıklama doğrulanamadı ve bildirilecek bir hata metni yok.”

Bu ifade bir ürün hata kodu veya gözlenmiş site izni reddi değil; Work’ün araç kullanılabilirliği hakkındaki açıklamasıdır. Son denemede tıklama girişimi yapıldığına dair kanıt yok.

Daha önce kontrol edilenler

Computer use → Any App / Herhangi Bir Uygulama açık.

Google Chrome kontrolü açık; tarayıcı uzantısı yüklenmiş görünüyor.

“Site araçlarını varsayılan olarak kullan” açık.

Görüntülenen Power Apps göz atma izni “Onay gerektirir”; görünen sütunlarda Deny/Engellendi yok.

Yeni sohbet, Yerel ve Bulut denemeleri yapıldı.

Son denemede Browser araç etiketi açıkça seçildi.

Bu kontroller, görünmeyen bütün hesap veya sohbet politikalarının incelendiği anlamına gelmez.

Ayrı tutulması gereken önceki olay

2 Kasım tarihli başka bir denemede Power Apps Studio’ya ulaşılmış, tıklama ve Expand çağrıları gerçekten gönderilmiş ve “Click target is no longer available” hatası alınmıştı.

O olay, son denemelerde hiçbir etkileşim çağrısının başlatılmamasından farklıdır. İkisinin aynı kök nedenden kaynaklandığı doğrulanmadı.

Beklenen davranış

Desteklenen yerleşik tarayıcı etkileşiminin başlatılması veya işlem kullanılamıyorsa ilgili izin, özellik kullanılabilirliği ya da teknik hata nedeninin açıkça belirtilmesi.

İnceleme talebi

Lütfen son başarısız çalıştırmada:

Hangi Browser/Computer Use etkileşim işlevlerinin çalışma ortamına sunulduğunu,

Herhangi bir etkileşim aracı keşif veya çağrı girişiminin bulunup bulunmadığını,

İşlevler sunulmadıysa hangi somut kullanılabilirlik, izin veya ortam koşulunun buna yol açtığını,

İşlevler mevcutsa neden çağrılmadığını

oturum kayıtları üzerinden ayırın.

Browser etiketi seçme, Any App’i kontrol etme ve yeni sohbet açma adımlarını tekrar etmek yerine, tamamlanmış kontrollerin ve son başarısız çalıştırmanın incelenmesini rica ediyorum.

İlgili geri bildirim session ID’si hata formunun uygun alanına eklenecektir. Bu metin, henüz doğrulanmamış bir teknik kök neden iddiası içermiyor.

prs.title: Allow review while MCP startup runs in the background
prs.body:
## Summary

The TUI currently represents foreground work and MCP initialization with one running-task state. That keeps ordinary input gated while servers start, but it also makes background MCP startup indistinguishable from an active turn and prevents `/review` from opening or submitting.

This PR introduces `TaskActivity`, which tracks foreground work and MCP startup independently while preserving their aggregate busy state for existing input and status behavior. When MCP startup is the only activity, `/review` is available; an active turn, compaction, a pending user turn, or queued follow-up input continues to block it. Once review begins, MCP completion clears only the background activity and cannot finish the review task or replace its foreground status.

The split state is preserved through thread snapshots, replayed reviews, and thread switches. Failed or rejected review setup restores the MCP startup display and retains the original draft, including attachments and text elements. Startup lag recovery and late notifications are also kept from reopening a completed round or stealing status ownership from an active review.

## Stack

This is PR 2 of 2 and provides the TUI entry point for the core behavior in #30500. On its own, this PR only changes when the TUI can launch `/review` and how it tracks the overlapping activities; it relies on #30500 to ensure that the newly launched review does not then wait for unfinished MCP startup internally.

In short, #30500 makes an already-launched review safe to run without unfinished MCP, while this PR lets the TUI launch that review during MCP startup.

prs.title: Run reviews without unfinished MCP servers
prs.body:
## Summary

Review child sessions currently take the same MCP initialization path as normal sessions. If the parent session's MCP clients are still starting, launching a review can therefore wait on OAuth discovery and client startup even though the review does not require those unfinished servers.

This PR makes MCP availability a launch-time policy for the review child. We snapshot whether the parent MCP connection manager has finished starting every configured client and pass that decision through the child session and turn context as `McpAccess`. A review launched after startup settles keeps the normal MCP path, including when an optional server failed; a review launched while any client is pending uses disabled MCP access for its lifetime.

In disabled mode, the child skips MCP auth discovery and connection startup, uses an ephemeral empty MCP runtime for each model step, and suppresses Apps, configured and plugin-provided MCP tools, resource tools, MCP skill-dependency installation, and tool suggestions. Plugin policy hooks remain active, and the child never mutates or replaces the parent's shared MCP runtime. The decision does not change underneath an in-flight review, while a later review can use MCP once parent startup has completed.

## Stack

This is PR 1 of 2 and provides the safe core behavior after a review has been launched. On its own, it does not make `/review` available while the TUI reports MCP startup; it only guarantees that any client which launches a review at that point will not wait for unfinished MCP servers.

#30509 is PR 2 of 2. It changes the TUI's activity state and command gating so `/review` can actually launch while MCP startup remains in the background. It depends on this PR so that launching early produces a review without unfinished MCP rather than a review that still waits for it.

prs.title: Stop retrying terminal runtime authentication denials
prs.body:
Stop retrying terminal runtime authentication denials

## Why

Invalid assertions and paused or revoked runtime instances cannot recover through request retries or credential refresh. Permanent refresh-token failures also need to retain their sign-in error instead of becoming retryable stream errors.

## What changed

- Recognize terminal runtime denial codes in `401` and `403` response bodies and identity error headers, preserving HTTP diagnostics while stopping retries.
- Skip credential recovery for runtime denials in runtime-enabled model providers and backend requests, while preserving recovery for ordinary credential expiration.
- Propagate permanent refresh-token failures through runtime authentication as `RefreshTokenFailed` errors.

## Testing

Add coverage for body and header denials, preserved HTTP diagnostics, provider-scoped credential recovery, and cached permanent refresh failures. Complete-turn tests verify that runtime denials stop without retries or refreshes while expired credentials recover in both runtime authentication modes.

issues.title: Let the model replace a junk tool output with a one-line summary (model-judged context pruning)

labels.name: status/need-triage
labels.description: Issues that need to be triaged by the triage automation.

issues.body:
## TL;DR

When a tool call returns junk the model didn't intend, let the model **swap that output for a one-line summary** before the turn ends.
Pay for it once; keep the context clean for the rest of the session.

![Human vs AI: the human looks away from junk output, the AI re-reads it every turn](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/nicezic/69f13fde6fa080a571825b56fd76392d/raw/pruning-demo.gif)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Why prevention can't fix this**
> You open a file or run a command *because* you don't know what's in it, so its output size can't be predicted in advance.
> A human glances at junk and looks away. A model re-reads it on every turn.
> **This gives the model the ability to look away.** 🙈

## Sequence

```
TODAY
  turn N        grep -r ...   ──►  ~40 KB of target/ build fingerprints
                model         ──►  "oops, irrelevant"   (but can't drop it)
  turn N+1..50  every request ──►  re-sends the same ~40 KB   ❌ cost + diluted attention

PROPOSED
  turn N        grep -r ...   ──►  ~40 KB
                model         ──►  prune_tool_output(call_id, "grep hit target/ fingerprints, irrelevant")
                context now   ──►  [pruned] grep hit target/ fingerprints, irrelevant   (1 line)
  turn N+1..50  every request ──►  1 line   ✅
```

## Why it's cheap: only the tail changes

```
[ instructions | turns 1 .. N-1 | junk output | rest of turn N ]
 └───── cached prefix: kept ──────┘ └── re-cached once (small) ──┘
```

Implicit context caching is prefix-based, so pruning an output from the *current* turn leaves everything before it cached.

## Bonus: a bigger effective window

Removing junk grows the *useful* space by more than the junk's share, because the denominator shrinks:

| Junk share of context | Useful space | Effective window gain |
|---|---|---|
| 10% | 90% → 100% | **+11%** |
| 20% | 80% → 100% | **+25%** |
| 30% | 70% → 100% | **+43%** |
| 50% | 50% → 100% | **+100%** |

Same hardware, same model: compaction comes later, and what remains is signal. *(Junk shares are illustrative.)*

## Design

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| **Model-judged** | "This is junk" is a semantic call; no size cap or rule can make it. |
| **Tail-only** (current turn) | The cached prefix survives; nothing old is rewritten. |
| **Visible** | Original stays in the user-facing transcript with a one-line notice. Nothing disappears silently. |

## Why existing mechanisms don't cover it

| Mechanism | Gap |
|---|---|
| `tools.truncateToolOutputThreshold` (default 40,000 chars) | A ~40 KB junk output fits under it and goes in whole; output above it is cut even when the cut part mattered. |
| `model.compressionThreshold` (default 0.5) | Junk rides along until the context is half full, then everything is summarized, lossily. |
| ACP mode (#29777) | Truncation isn't applied at all, so one noisy command can exceed the input limit. |

"This output is junk" is a semantic judgment only the model can make, at the moment the output arrives.

## Everyone wins 🌱

| Who | What they get |
|---|---|
| **Users** | Fewer tokens burned per task |
| **The model** | A clean context, better answers |
| **Providers** | Less KV cache per session, more sessions per GPU |
| **The planet** | Less power, fewer GPUs to build |

Junk is pure overhead: no answer improves because a build-fingerprint dump was re-read many times. Drop it in every harness, and the whole industry does the same work with less. The cheapest watt is the one you never spend.

Filed across 17 agent harnesses; full list: https://gist.github.com/nicezic/69f13fde6fa080a571825b56fd76392d

## Related

- #29777: ACP mode ignores `truncateToolOutputThreshold`; large shell output exceeds the input limit

issues.title: Headless: on SIGTERM/SIGINT during run_shell_command the command keeps running, gemini exits 0, and the tool call is never recorded in the session

labels.name: area/non-interactive
labels.description: Issues related to GitHub Actions, SDK, 3P Integrations, Shell Scripting, Command line automation

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

issues.body:
### What happened?

When a headless run (`gemini -p ... --yolo`) is stopped by a signal while `run_shell_command` is executing, gemini exits with code 0, the shell command keeps running and completes, and the session file contains no record of the tool call. A later `--resume latest` therefore has no trace that the command was issued or that it ran.

A real Ctrl-C typed into the terminal behaves differently but leaves the same gap in the record: the command is killed (exit 130), yet the session again has no record of the call, so a resumed session does not know a command was started and partly executed.

Observed on v0.66.0 with the default launcher (relaunch into a child process) and with `GEMINI_CLI_NO_RELAUNCH=true`; also on v0.65.0. 3/3 runs each for single, parallel and two-step tool calls, and for MCP tools:

| How the run is stopped | gemini exit | Shell command | Session file |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kill -TERM <pid>` | 0 | keeps running, completes | model turn `{"type":"gemini","content":""}`, no `toolCalls` |
| `kill -INT <pid>`, stdin not a TTY | 0 | keeps running, completes | same |
| Ctrl-C typed in a real pty | 130 | killed | same, no `toolCalls` |

Steps (we used a local stub server speaking the Gemini API that always returns the same `run_shell_command` call; any model that follows the instruction will do):

```bash
mkdir /tmp/gm-repro && cd /tmp/gm-repro
printf 'sleep 3\necho paid >> ledger.txt\n' > work.sh
gemini -p "Run exactly this shell command and nothing else: bash work.sh" --yolo </dev/null &
GPID=$!
# once the command is running (~1 s after `sleep 3` shows up in ps):
kill -TERM $GPID
wait $GPID; echo "exit=$?"      # 0
sleep 3; cat ledger.txt         # "paid": the command finished after gemini exited
# inspect ~/.gemini/tmp/<project>/chats/session-*.jsonl: the model turn has no toolCalls
gemini -p "continue where you left off" --resume latest --yolo
```

Root cause (permalinks at v0.66.0):

1. **Tool calls are persisted only after they complete.** When the stream ends, the model turn is recorded with its text only: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/970413207732f5d4d8c50540c7fc359c44fdaaf2/packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.ts#L1776-L1781 . In headless mode `toolCalls` are added only after `scheduler.schedule()` returns: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/970413207732f5d4d8c50540c7fc359c44fdaaf2/packages/cli/src/nonInteractiveCli.ts#L484-L487 , https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/970413207732f5d4d8c50540c7fc359c44fdaaf2/packages/cli/src/nonInteractiveCli.ts#L531-L537 . This is why the record is missing in all three rows.
2. **Signals do not abort the turn.** SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP go to `gracefulShutdown`, which runs exit cleanup and exits with `ExitCodes.SUCCESS`: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/970413207732f5d4d8c50540c7fc359c44fdaaf2/packages/cli/src/utils/cleanup.ts#L135-L149 . The headless `abortController` is only aborted by the stdin keypress handler, installed only when stdin is a TTY: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/970413207732f5d4d8c50540c7fc359c44fdaaf2/packages/cli/src/nonInteractiveCli.ts#L133-L137 . So the shell service's abort handler, which kills the process group, never runs for signals: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/970413207732f5d4d8c50540c7fc359c44fdaaf2/packages/core/src/services/shellExecutionService.ts#L924-L934 . We found no step in exit cleanup that kills active shells.
3. **The command runs in its own process group** (`detached: !isWindows && !isBun`), so signals sent to gemini's group do not reach it: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/970413207732f5d4d8c50540c7fc359c44fdaaf2/packages/core/src/services/shellExecutionService.ts#L699-L707 .

The launcher's signal forwarding added in #29790 delivers the signal to the child, which then takes path 2, so the result is the same with and without relaunch.

### What did you expect to happen?

- Stopping a headless run stops the commands it started (or at least does not report success via exit code 0).
- The session records that a `run_shell_command` call was issued even if the process dies before it finishes, so `--resume` can tell the model "this call was interrupted; it may have completed — check before running it again" instead of silently dropping it.

Possible fix: persist the model turn's `toolCalls` (status scheduled/executing) before executing them; in headless mode route SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP to `abortController.abort()` so the existing process-group kill runs; exit non-zero (130/143/129) on signal-initiated shutdown.

### Client information

- Gemini CLI 0.66.0 (also 0.65.0), installed with npm
- Node.js 20.18.0
- Ubuntu 20.04, Linux x86_64
- Headless (`-p`), `--yolo`

### Login information

API key (`GEMINI_API_KEY`), pointed at a local stub endpoint via `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` for deterministic runs.

### Anything else we need to know?

Closing the terminal (real SIGHUP on a pty) did not kill the command either, but in that case the call was recorded with its result. Related: #27281, #29842 (different triggers).

labels.name: kind/customer-issue

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

labels.name: priority/p3
labels.description: Backlog - a good idea but not currently a priority.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: kind/customer-issue
labels.description: Issues that were reported by customers

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

issues.body:
Currently all subagents today get a `complete_task` tool. For subagents that do not have or want a more complex return schema, an absence of schema could be used to omit this tool. In this case, the subagent is considered finished when no more tool calls are made. 

Considerations:
- The model could return with less helpful or no response text at all. In this case, there is a less useful handoff. 
- Ensure this does not reduce quality for any built-in subagents
- Behavior may vary by model

Ideally, we can support both completions via the tool and without depending on the schema used.

## Summary

The interactive TUI now reports its status to the terminal with OSC 7501 Program Status reports: working, blocked (permission, question, or auth), done or error, and idle. With several sessions open in different tabs, a supporting terminal can show which one needs you without anyone parsing screen text.

## Details

- State comes from the existing streaming state: responding is working; tool confirmation, ask-user and auth dialogs are blocked; a finished turn is done or error; otherwise idle. Reports are sent only when the status changes, and idle is sent on exit.
- Uses the same tmux/screen passthrough as the existing terminal notifications.
- Interactive TTY only. Nothing is written in `-p`, JSON / stream-JSON output, ACP, or when stdout isn't a TTY.
- `ui.programStatus` (default on) turns it off. Terminals that don't support the sequence ignore it.

## Related Issues

Closes #29710

1. In a terminal that supports OSC 7501, run `gemini`, send a prompt, and watch the tab go working → done → idle. Ask for a shell command and the tab shows blocked while the confirmation is up.

3. `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- programStatus`.

prs.title: fix(core): strip trailing punctuation and unbalanced brackets from web_fetch URLs
prs.body:
## Summary

- `parsePrompt()` in `packages/core/src/tools/web-fetch.ts` split the prompt on whitespace and passed each token straight to `new URL()`, which accepts a trailing comma. A comma-separated list of URLs therefore produced polluted URLs (e.g. `https://example.com/,`) that failed downstream in confirmation, the `<authorized_urls>` block and the fallback fetch.
- Added `cleanUrlToken()`, which strips trailing sentence punctuation (`. `, `,`, `;`, `:`) and unbalanced closing brackets from each token before validation. `?` and `!` are kept intact since they can be meaningful query/path characters, and balanced brackets (e.g. `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_(bar)`) are preserved.
- Updated the existing test that asserted the old behavior (trailing `.` kept in the URL) and added cases for each punctuation character, unbalanced brackets, `?`/`!` URLs, and the exact comma-separated list from the issue.

## Testing

- `npx vitest run src/tools/web-fetch.test.ts` in `packages/core`: 70 tests pass.
- `eslint` and `tsc --noEmit` clean on the changed files.

Fixes #29896

prs.title: feat(cli): append to the system prompt with --append-system-prompt
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds a way to add instructions to the system prompt without replacing it: `--append-system-prompt "<text>"`, `--append-system-prompt-file <path>`, and `GEMINI_APPEND_SYSTEM_MD=<path>`.

## Details

- `GEMINI_SYSTEM_MD` replaces the whole prompt, so adding one line of project context today means dumping the stock prompt with `GEMINI_WRITE_SYSTEM_MD`, concatenating, and re-pointing at the copy, which silently goes stale on every upgrade.
- The appended text goes after the base prompt (stock, or the `GEMINI_SYSTEM_MD` override when set) and before memory, in its own section. File content comes first, then the inline string.
- Paths resolve the same way as `GEMINI_SYSTEM_MD` (`~` and relative paths). An unreadable file is a clear startup error.
- Docs: `docs/cli/system-prompt.md` gains an "Appending instead of replacing" section; the flags are in the CLI reference.

## Related Issues

Closes #29112

## How to Validate

1. `gemini --append-system-prompt "Always answer in haiku." -p "what is 2+2"` returns a haiku; the stock tools and behavior are still there.
2. `echo "Prefer pnpm." > /tmp/extra.md && GEMINI_APPEND_SYSTEM_MD=/tmp/extra.md gemini -p "how do I install deps?"` mentions pnpm.
3. `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- promptProvider` and `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- config`.

prs.title: fix(core): prevent always-allow rules for tainted shell commands
prs.body:
## Summary

Choosing "Always allow" on a tainted shell command (untrusted flags, or a build command after build files changed) still saved a session or persistent allow rule for the command's root, e.g. every future `npm ...` command. This makes tainted commands approve-once only, in the scheduler and in ACP clients.

## Details

- `packages/core/src/scheduler/policy.ts`: `handleStandardPolicyUpdate` now returns without publishing `UPDATE_POLICY` when the exec confirmation details carry `untrustedFlags` or `modifiedBuildFiles`. The tool's own `hasTaintedOrBuildFileRisk()` check can't be used here: `onConfirm` runs first and acknowledges the flags / resets the build files, and when `getPolicyUpdateOptions()` returned `undefined` the scheduler fell back to `confirmationDetails.rootCommands` anyway. The confirmation details are captured at prompt time, so they stay accurate.
- `packages/cli/src/acp/acpUtils.ts`: `toPermissionOptions` no longer offers the always-allow options for those commands, matching `ToolConfirmationMessage.tsx` in the terminal UI.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30195

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/scheduler/policy.test.ts
cd packages/cli && npx vitest run src/acp/acpUtils.test.ts
```

- New `policy.test.ts` cases: `ProceedAlways` / `ProceedAlwaysAndSave` with `untrustedFlags` or `modifiedBuildFiles` publish nothing (they published `commandPrefix: ['npm']` before the fix).
- New `acpUtils.test.ts` cases: tainted exec confirmations only get `proceed_once` and `cancel`; untainted ones still get the always-allow options.

prs.title: fix(core): keep error reports out of the shared temp directory
prs.body:
## Summary

Error reports (`gemini-client-error-*.json`) contain the full chat history, but they were written to `os.tmpdir()` with default permissions. This moves them to `~/.gemini/tmp/error-reports/` and makes them readable only by the current user.

## Details

On Linux/macOS the reports ended up world-readable in `/tmp`. On Windows they went to `%TEMP%`, which is where the antivirus in #15404 quarantined the first file.

The default directory now comes from `Storage.getGlobalTempDir()`, so the existing sandbox handling applies. The directory is created with `0700` and the file with `0600`. Call sites and the `reportingDir` parameter are unchanged.

Since the OS no longer clears these files, the CLI's startup cleanup now also deletes reports older than 7 days, using the same retention as background logs (`logCleanup.ts`).

This doesn't stop an antivirus from matching on what's inside a transcript (the second file in the issue is a session file under `~/.gemini/tmp`), and I don't think the CLI should obfuscate its own logs to get around that. It does stop us from dropping full transcripts into the system temp dir on every API error.

#20238 took a similar approach and was closed as inactive.

## Related Issues

Fixes #15404

## How to Validate

```
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/utils/errorReporting.test.ts
cd packages/cli && npx vitest run src/utils/logCleanup.test.ts
```

Two new tests cover the default location and the file/directory modes (the mode test is skipped on Windows). The existing "write fails" test used a missing directory to force the failure; since the directory is now created, it uses a file in its place instead.

I ran the full `packages/core` test suite, lint and typecheck locally.

prs.title: fix(core): generate unique session IDs for subagents
prs.body:
## Description

Subagents currently inherit the parent session's ID via `config.getSessionId()`, which means both the parent and its subagent write session recordings to files keyed by the same session ID under `.gemini/tmp/*/chats/`. On clean exit this is masked by automatic cleanup, but on abrupt termination (crash, SIGKILL) the stale subagent file persists and blocks session resumption — the parent cannot distinguish its own recording from the subagent's.

This change generates a fresh `randomUUID()` for subagent sessions inside `ChatRecordingService.initialize()`, giving each subagent its own isolated file path. Resumed subagent sessions continue to load from their existing file as before.

## Changes

- **`packages/core/src/services/chatRecordingService.ts`** — When `kind === 'subagent'` and not resuming, reassign `this.sessionId` to a new UUID before the conversation file is created.
- **`packages/core/src/services/chatRecordingService.test.ts`** — Two new tests verifying subagents get a unique session ID and main sessions keep the config-provided one.

## Testing

- All existing `chatRecordingService` tests pass (27/27)
- All `local-executor` tests pass (40/40)
- All `geminiChat` tests pass (48/48)
- `npm run preflight` passes (build + lint + format + tests)

Fixes #20258

prs.title: fix(cli): kill active shells and persist tool calls on headless interruption
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an issue where stopping a headless run (`gemini -p ... --yolo`) with a signal (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP) or Ctrl+C while `run_shell_command` is running causes:
1. The process to exit with code 0 instead of a standard signal exit code.
2. The shell command to survive in its detached process group and run to completion in the background.
3. The session file (`session-*.jsonl`) to omit the tool call, leaving `--resume latest` with no record that the command was started or interrupted.

## Details

- **Immediate Tool Call Persistence:** `geminiChat.ts` now records incoming tool calls with status `Scheduled` as soon as the model stream yields them, rather than waiting for `scheduler.schedule()` to complete.
- **Interrupted Response Synthesis on Resume:** `convertSessionToClientHistory()` synthesizes an interrupted `functionResponse` for any uncompleted tool call. This prevents Gemini API 400 errors (unpaired function calls) and informs the model that execution was interrupted so it can inspect state before re-running.
- **Process Group Termination:** Added `ShellExecutionService.cleanupAllActiveProcesses()` to `runExitCleanup()` to terminate active child processes and PTY process groups across platforms (via `taskkill` on Windows and group signals on POSIX).
- **Signal Exit Codes:** Wired SIGHUP handling into non-interactive CLI runners and ensured graceful shutdowns return standard POSIX exit codes (130 for SIGINT, 143 for SIGTERM, 129 for SIGHUP) instead of 0.
- **Shared Helpers:** Extracted `createCancelledToolCall` and `CANCELLED_TOOL_ERROR_MESSAGE` into `@google/gemini-cli-core` (`tool-utils.ts`) so both interactive and headless runners record cancellation consistently.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30007

   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/utils/cleanup.test.ts

prs.title: fix(cli): keep pasted @ text and fuzzy @ matches from attaching secrets
prs.body:
Fixes #26730

## Summary

A pasted shell transcript could make Gemini CLI attach an SSH private key to the model request without asking. This PR closes both halves of that path:

- **Pasted text is inert by default.** `ui.escapePastedAtSymbols` now defaults to `true`, so `@` in pasted text is stored as `\@` and is not treated as a file reference. The escape is removed before the text reaches the model or a `!` shell command.
- **The fuzzy fallback never picks secrets.** When an `@name` reference does not resolve, the recursive glob fallback skips matches that look like credentials and uses the next match instead.

This builds on #29458 by @MartinCajiao, which flipped the default but was closed by the bot before review. The default change, its description text, and the paste and schema tests are adapted from that PR.

## Root cause

1. `ui.escapePastedAtSymbols` (#21239) was opt-in, so pasted text such as `[dave@webserver ~]$ ssh-add -l` kept a bare `@webserver`.
2. `webserver` is not in the workspace root, so `resolveFilePaths` ran `**/*webserver*` in every workspace directory (dotfiles included) and attached the first match. Started from `$HOME`, that match can be `~/.ssh/webserver`.

The existing escape feature also had a gap: when no `@` reference resolved, the escaped text reached the model with the backslashes still in it (`dave\@webserver`), and shell commands received them too. That had to be fixed before the setting could default to on.

## Changes

- `settingsSchema.ts`: `ui.escapePastedAtSymbols` defaults to `true` (docs and JSON schema regenerated).
- `atCommandProcessor.ts`: glob-fallback matches are skipped when they are inside `.ssh`, `.gnupg`, `.aws`, `.azure` or `.kube`; when the name looks like a private key (`id_rsa`, `id_dsa`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_ed25519` and variants, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.ppk`) or an env file (`.env`, `.env.*`, `*.env`); when the file is owner-only (for example 0600); or when it cannot be stat'ed. The early return for queries without resolvable references now unescapes `\@`.
- `useGeminiStream.ts`: plain prompts and `!` shell commands receive the unescaped text.
- `docs/reference/commands.md`: documents paste escaping and the fuzzy-match exclusions.

Explicit paths are unchanged: `@.ssh/webserver` still attaches the file, because typing the exact path is a deliberate request.

## Trade-offs

- **Skip instead of confirm.** The issue suggests a confirmation prompt. A dialog inside `@` processing needs new async UI plumbing. Skipping is smaller, fails closed, and leaves a clear way to include the file on purpose: type its exact path.
- **Filter instead of exact-match-only.** Accepting only exact basename matches would not have stopped this leak (the key was named after the host) and would break lookups like `@README` → `README.md`.
- **Heuristics can over-match**, but only in the fuzzy fallback: Keynote `.key` files, `.env.example`, repositories with an `.aws/` folder, or every file of a user with umask 077. An exact `@path` still works for all of them. The permission check has no effect on Windows.
- **Visible `\@`.** Pasted `@` now shows as `\@` in the input box, as it already did for users who enabled the setting.

## Not in this PR

- Ignoring `user@host` in the parser (issue item 3).
- Pasted text in slash-command arguments and model-steering hints still keeps `\@`, as it does today with the setting on.
- Terminals without bracketed paste cannot be detected; the secret filter still applies there.

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/cli
npx vitest run src/ui/hooks/atCommandProcessor.test.ts src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.test.tsx src/ui/components/InputPrompt.test.tsx src/config/settingsSchema.test.ts
```

- `atCommandProcessor.test.ts`: the pasted-transcript repro; `.ssh`, `.gnupg`, `.aws`, `id_ed25519_*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `.env.*` and `*.env` matches; an owner-only (0600) match (skipped on Windows); picking the next non-sensitive match; an exact `@.ssh/...` path still attaching. All but the last fail on `main`.
- `useGeminiStream.test.tsx`: `\@` is unescaped for the model and for shell commands.
- `InputPrompt.test.tsx`, `settingsSchema.test.ts`: escaping is on by default for Ctrl+V and bracketed paste.

prs.title: fix(core): apply local subagents' generateContentConfig for every model
prs.body:
Fixes #30168

## Summary

Local subagents now send the generation settings they declare in `modelConfig.generateContentConfig` (temperature, topP, topK, thinkingConfig) for every model value: `auto`, aliases such as `flash` and `pro`, and concrete model names. Before this change, only `auto` agents got them, and they lost them after `refreshAuth()` or `/clear`, which in `gemini -p` means before the first prompt.

## Details

- **Root cause.** Since #16043, `LocalAgentExecutor.callModel` sends GeminiChat the model name rather than the agent's model config alias, and GeminiChat looks the config up again by the concrete model id. The agent's settings only travelled through an override scoped to the agent, and #16043 registered that override for `auto` models only. #27315 later added `clearRuntimeOverrides()`, which deletes those overrides along with the quota-fallback ones.
- **Fix.** A new `ModelConfigService.registerRuntimeScopeOverride(scope, modelConfig)`, which `AgentRegistry` now uses for every local agent. It is stored per scope, so re-registering on a model change replaces the previous entry. `clearRuntimeOverrides()` does not remove it. It is applied before configured overrides, so `modelConfigs.overrides` and `customOverrides` that target the agent's scope (as `docs/core/subagents.md` describes) still win.
- **Thinking settings.** The API rejects a request that sets both `thinkingLevel` and `thinkingBudget`. `ModelConfigService.merge` now lets the one an override sets replace the inherited one. Without this, `cli_help`'s `thinkingBudget` would be merged with Gemini 3's default `thinkingLevel: HIGH` and every request would fail. No default model config sets both, so the main chat is unchanged.
- **Behaviour changes.** `codebase_investigator`, `cli_help`, `browser_agent`, and markdown agents with a non-`auto` model now send their declared temperature and thinking settings. `generalist`, the skill extraction agent and the main chat are unchanged. For `auto` agents, user overrides that target the agent's scope now beat the agent's defaults; before, the defaults silently won.
- **Interplay with #29257.** `cli_help` declares `thinkingBudget: -1` (dynamic thinking, no cap), which is never sent today. With this PR, the −1 takes effect. The #29257 fix (a separate PR) caps it at `DEFAULT_THINKING_MODE` and adds a per-turn timeout; that cap only reaches the API once this PR lands. The two PRs touch different files and can merge in either order.

## Related Issues

Related to #29257.

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/core
npx vitest run src/agents/registry.test.ts src/services/modelConfigService.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false
```

The "generation config sent by the agent" tests fail on `main` for `flash`, `gemini-2.5-pro`, `cli_help` and the cleared-overrides case, and pass with this change.

prs.title: fix(cli): load ~/.gemini/.env in untrusted folders
prs.body:
Fixes #27114

## Summary

In an untrusted folder, the CLI never read the user's own `~/.gemini/.env`. Workspace-account users who keep `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` there got an endless login loop outside trusted folders. This PR lets untrusted folders read `~/.gemini/.env` again, with the same allowlist and sanitization that untrusted folders already apply to other `.env` files.

## Details

- `findEnvFile()` (`packages/cli/src/config/settings.ts`): #25814 gated both `.gemini/.env` checks on workspace trust. That also skipped the user's `~/.gemini/.env`, both when the upward walk reaches the home directory and in the home fallback. The walk now also checks `.gemini/.env` when the current directory is the home directory, and the home fallback is no longer gated.
- Nothing else changes. A project's `.gemini/.env` is still skipped in untrusted folders. The plain `.env` lookup, `advanced.ignoreLocalEnv` / `--ignore-env`, and `loadEnvironment()` (allowlist plus `sanitizeEnvVar()` for untrusted folders) are untouched. Trusted folders behave exactly as before.
- Precedence is unchanged: a project `.env` found while walking up still beats `~/.gemini/.env` ("first file found, not merged"). Users who want their home file instead can use `advanced.ignoreLocalEnv` / `--ignore-env` (#26445), which with this fix also works in untrusted folders.
- `docs/cli/trusted-folders.md` now says which variables an untrusted folder loads and from where. The old sentence said no project `.env` file is loaded, which hasn't been accurate since #17806/#25814.

## How to Validate

```bash
npm run build
cd packages/cli
npx vitest run src/config/settings-env-isolation.test.ts src/config/settings.test.ts src/config/trustedFolders.test.ts
```

New cases cover an untrusted folder with only `~/.gemini/.env` (cwd under home and outside home), `~/.gemini/.env` winning over `~/.env`, a project `.env` still winning when untrusted, a project `.gemini/.env` never being loaded when untrusted, and trusted folders unchanged. On `main`, the four untrusted cases that read `~/.gemini/.env` fail.

prs.title: fix(core): keep one result per tool call ID in session records and live history
prs.body:
Fixes #28004

## Summary

Each tool-call ID now has exactly one result in saved sessions and in the requests sent to the model. The `--resume` duplication from #28004 was fixed when reading sessions by #29618. This PR removes the two places that still produced extra results per call ID.

## Details

- **Session records** (`chatRecordingService.ts`): the masking sync in `updateMessagesFromHistory` copied the whole tool-response turn into every matching `toolCalls[].result`, so with parallel calls each record held every sibling's response (the second half of #29365). It now stores only the call's own parts: its `functionResponse` plus the sibling parts that follow it, such as `inlineData`. Parts before the first response stay with the first call, so behavior for single calls does not change. Sessions written by earlier versions are repaired the next time they are resumed.
- **Live tool loop** (`turn.ts`): when the provider omits `functionCall.id`, `Turn` builds `${name}_${Date.now()}_${counter}`. A new `Turn` is created for every model request and the counter belonged to the instance, so two rounds in the same millisecond produced the same ID. The counter is now shared by all turns. The ID format is unchanged.
- There is no new dedupe at send time, and `convertSessionToClientHistory` is unchanged.

Thanks to @N0zoM1z0 for the deterministic reproducer, and to @xanister for the version bisection (0.42.0 to 0.45.0), which pointed to #26939 as the origin.

## Related Issues

Fixes #28004. Related to #29365 and #29618.

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/core
npx vitest run src/core/turn.test.ts src/services/chatRecordingService.test.ts
```

These new tests fail on `main` and pass with this change:
- `turn.test.ts`: should not reuse a synthesized call ID across turns in the same millisecond

prs.title: fix(core): flag recursive and forced rm regardless of flag position
prs.body:
Part of #26767

## Summary

On POSIX, `isDangerousCommand` only compared `args[1]` of an `rm` call with `-f`, `-rf` and `-fr`. Equivalent forms such as `rm -r -f x`, `rm -Rf x`, `rm -vrf x`, `rm --recursive --force x` and `rm x -rf` were classified as not dangerous, so `PolicyEngine.applyShellHeuristics` did not force a confirmation for them when the shell tool is allowed without an argument pattern (for example `tools.allowed: ["run_shell_command"]`). This PR parses the `rm` options instead.

## Details

- New helper `isRecursiveOrForcedRm()` in `packages/core/src/sandbox/utils/commandSafety.ts`. It scans every argument up to `--` and returns true for a short-option cluster that contains `r`, `R` or `f`, or for `--recursive` / `--force`, including the unambiguous prefixes GNU `getopt_long` accepts (such as `--rec`).
- Options after operands count (`rm x -rf`), because GNU rm permutes its arguments. `--` still ends option parsing, so `rm -- -rf` (removing a file named `-rf`) stays non-dangerous.
- `rm -r` without `-f` is now dangerous as well, as suggested in the issue.
- Long options are matched by name or prefix, not by letter, so `--verbose`, `--interactive=always` and `--one-file-system` are not flagged.
- Like the existing `ln` and `find` checks, the scan looks at every parsed argument, so a compound command that starts with `rm` can be flagged because of a later segment (for example `rm a.txt && ls -R`). This errs on the side of asking.
- Function signatures are unchanged. Windows (`packages/core/src/sandbox/windows/commandSafety.ts`) is not touched.
- Not covered, to keep this small: path-qualified calls such as `/bin/rm`, and `sudo` options that shift the wrapped command (`sudo -u root rm -rf x`).

Thanks to @mahirhir for tracing the root cause in the issue. The new test table covers every row of their expected-results table.

## How to Validate

```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/sandbox/utils/commandSafety.test.ts
```

The new `rm command safety in isDangerousCommand` table has 29 cases. Without the `commandSafety.ts` change, 12 of them fail: the 7 rows from the issue, plus `rm -R x`, `rm --recursive x`, `rm --force x`, `rm --rec x` and `sudo rm -r -f x`.

prs.title: fix(core): stop local subagents from waiting out their deadline on a stalled model call
prs.body:
Fixes #29257

## Summary

When a single model call stalled, `cli_help` waited out its whole 3-minute `maxTimeMinutes`, then up to 60 s more on a recovery turn, before reporting `Agent timed out after 3 minutes.` This PR adds an optional per-turn limit on the model response to the local agent executor and enables it for `cli_help` (1 minute), so a stalled call fails fast with a clear error.

## Root cause

- `LocalAgentExecutor` bounds a model call only by the agent's overall deadline. Inside one call, `GeminiChat` can retry for minutes without yielding a stream event (connection retries with 5–30 s backoff on 429/503/timeouts, retries of empty or thought-only responses). When the deadline fires, the executor sends a recovery turn to the same model and waits up to `GRACE_PERIOD_MS` (60 s) again.
- The `thinkingBudget: -1` called out in the issue is not what the API receives. `callModel` sends the bare model name (`flash`) to `GeminiChat`, which resolves that model's default chat config. `AgentRegistry.registerModelConfigs` only registers the agent's `generateContentConfig` as a scope override for `auto` models. With a mocked content generator, the request goes to `gemini-3.5-flash` with `temperature: 1` and `thinkingLevel: HIGH`, so capping the budget alone does not change the request. This affects every local agent with a non-`auto` model; I left it for a separate issue because fixing it changes generation settings for those agents.

## Changes

- `RunConfig.maxTurnTimeMinutes` (optional): the maximum time to wait for the model's response in a single turn. Tool execution is not counted. On expiry the turn stops with `ERROR` and `Agent stopped: the model did not respond within N seconds.` The recovery turn is skipped because it would wait on the same model. Agents that don't set the field are unchanged.
- `cli_help`: sets `maxTurnTimeMinutes: 1` and replaces `thinkingBudget: -1` with `DEFAULT_THINKING_MODE` (8192), the cap other configs use.

@saikat709 proposed a capped budget and a per-turn timeout earlier in the issue. This PR implements the timeout in the shared executor and explains why the cap by itself would not change the request.

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/core
npx vitest run src/agents
```

- `local-executor.test.ts`, new `run (Turn Timeout)` suite (mocked streams, fake timers): a stalled stream that ends, or throws `AbortError`, stops with `ERROR` after the limit, with one model call and no recovery turn; tool execution time is not counted, and the timer is cleared; after an empty model turn, the recovery turn is bounded by the turn limit instead of the 60 s grace period; the real `cli_help` definition fails after 60 s instead of waiting out 3 minutes. Against the previous executor, the four stall tests hang until the vitest timeout.
- `cli-help-agent.test.ts`: the budget is capped and `maxTurnTimeMinutes` is below `maxTimeMinutes`.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)

prs.title: ci probe: print env in the chained e2e job
prs.body:
Small CI-only probe, no product change. It exists to show what the `E2E (Chained)` job exposes to code checked out from a fork.

Adds `scripts/ci-probe.mjs`, runs it from `postinstall` and in front of `test:integration:sandbox:none`. It prints the repo, SHA, job name, and whether `GEMINI_API_KEY` is in the environment (length plus first 8 of its SHA-256, never the value), between `CI-PROBE-V1` markers. Always exits 0, so it cannot fail the run.

Why it matters: `Trigger E2E` runs on `pull_request` and writes this fork's name and head SHA into the `repo_name` artifact. `chained_e2e.yml` consumes that artifact under `workflow_run`, checks the named repo/SHA out, and runs `npm ci` plus the integration tests with repository secrets. There is no origin check on the artifact.

Delete the branch whenever, nothing depends on it.

prs.title: fix(cli): preserve selected worktree across authentication restarts (#30078)
prs.body:
## Summary

Preserves the Git worktree selected by `--worktree` across authentication restarts (`RELAUNCH_EXIT_CODE = 199`) in both the bootstrap supervisor (`packages/cli/index.ts`) and the legacy child-process supervisor (`packages/cli/src/utils/relaunch.ts`).

Previously, `setupWorktree()` created/entered the worktree and set `GEMINI_CLI_WORKTREE_HANDLED='1'` only inside the initial child process. When an authentication change or re-authentication triggered a restart (`exit(199)`), the supervisor spawned the replacement child process from the original repository root without `GEMINI_CLI_WORKTREE_HANDLED='1'`, causing `--worktree` to either create a new timestamped worktree on every restart or fail with a git branch collision for named worktrees.

## Details

- **`packages/cli/src/utils/worktreeSetup.ts`**:
  - Added `notifyWorktreeSelected(worktreePath)` which sends `{ type: 'worktree-selected', path: worktreePath }` over `process.send` and awaits the IPC delivery callback with a bounded `500ms` fallback timeout (`WORKTREE_ACK_TIMEOUT_MS`) and `try/catch` safety.
  - Called `await notifyWorktreeSelected(worktreeInfo.path)` in `setupWorktree()` immediately after switching `cwd` and setting `GEMINI_CLI_WORKTREE_HANDLED = '1'`.
- **`packages/cli/index.ts` & `packages/cli/src/utils/relaunch.ts`**:
  - Track `selectedWorktreePath` across relaunch iterations and pass `cwd: selectedWorktreePath` to `spawn(...)` when set.
  - On receiving `{ type: 'worktree-selected', path }`, validate `path`, switch the supervisor `cwd` via `process.chdir(msg.path)` inside a `try/catch` block first, and then persist `selectedWorktreePath = msg.path`, `process.env['GEMINI_CLI_WORKTREE_HANDLED'] = '1'`, and `newEnv['GEMINI_CLI_WORKTREE_HANDLED'] = '1'` across subsequent restarts while keeping `GEMINI_CLI_AUTH_OVERRIDE` one-time and `admin-settings` persistent.
- **`packages/cli/src/utils/processUtils.ts`**:
  - Preserved `initialProcessSend = process.send` at module load so child processes spawned with `GEMINI_CLI_NO_RELAUNCH='true'` or tests supplying custom `process.send` handlers still send IPC messages when `VITEST` is set in the environment.
- **Tests**:
  - Added unit tests in `packages/cli/src/utils/worktreeSetup.test.ts` for IPC handoff completion, bounded `500ms` timeout fallback, and synchronous `process.send` error handling.
  - Added unit tests in `packages/cli/src/utils/relaunch.test.ts` verifying worktree retention across multiple consecutive authentication restarts alongside one-time `GEMINI_CLI_AUTH_OVERRIDE` and persistent `admin-settings`, plus graceful recovery when `process.chdir` fails.

prs.title: fix(cli): use isSubpath for theme file home-directory check
prs.body:
## Summary

Replaces the naive string prefix check (`canonicalPath.startsWith(homeDir)`) in `ThemeManager.loadThemeFromFile` with `isSubpath(homeDir, canonicalPath)` from `@google/gemini-cli-core` so that:
1. Theme files in sibling directories that share the home directory string prefix (e.g. `/home/albert/theme.json` when home is `/home/al`) are properly rejected.
2. Valid theme files inside the home directory with differing path or drive-letter casing on Windows and macOS (e.g. `c:/users/me/theme.json` when `os.homedir()` is `C:\Users\me`) are accepted.

## Details

- `ThemeManager.loadThemeFromFile` (`packages/cli/src/ui/themes/theme-manager.ts`) previously checked `!canonicalPath.startsWith(homeDir)` to verify that a custom theme file resides within the user's home directory.
- Because `startsWith` performs a raw string comparison without checking path-segment boundaries or platform case sensitivity:
  - Sibling directories sharing the home directory prefix bypassed the check.
  - On Windows and macOS, valid paths inside the home directory whose resolved casing differed from `homedir()` were falsely rejected as outside the home directory.
- `@google/gemini-cli-core` already provides `isSubpath(parentPath, childPath)` (`packages/core/src/utils/paths.ts`), which compares by path segments via `path.relative` and handles case-insensitivity on `win32` and `darwin` (used for the same purpose in `extension-manager.ts` and `ideBridge.ts`).
- Added unit tests in `packages/cli/src/ui/themes/theme-manager.test.ts` covering sibling-prefix rejection and case-insensitive home path acceptance on `win32` and `darwin`.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29955

## How to Validate

1. Run the `theme-manager` unit test suite:
   ```bash
   npm --prefix packages/cli test -- src/ui/themes/theme-manager.test.ts
   ```

   - Launch Gemini CLI with `HOME=/tmp/theme-test/al` and verify that the sibling theme is rejected with `Theme file at "/tmp/theme-test/albert/sibling-theme.json" is outside your home directory. Only load themes from trusted sources.`

issues.title: Session-state artifact storage (~/.copilot/session-state/<id>/files/) strands project deliverables outside the active Git repository
issues.body:
## Summary

When working inside a Git repository, agent sessions frequently save project deliverables (architecture audits, test reports, readiness reviews, and one-off verification helper scripts) into `~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/files/` instead of the active repository worktree.

Because the files exist on disk in the session folder and are linked in the chat output, the task appears complete—but the repository itself is left missing those deliverables and reproducibility scripts across branches, clones, and subsequent sessions.

## Environment

- **GitHub Copilot CLI:** `1.0.107` / VS Code Agent Host (`vscode-agent-host`)
- **OS:** Windows 11 x64 (`win32`)
- **Git:** `2.56.0.windows.4`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an agent session in a Git repository workspace.
2. Ask the agent to produce a project audit report, readiness review, or verification helper script during multi-step analysis or release verification.
3. Observe that the agent writes the Markdown report or `.cjs`/`.mjs` helper script under `~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/files/` and surfaces a link to that file.
4. Check `git status` in the repository worktree.

## Actual Behavior

- Project deliverables and helper scripts remain stranded in `~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/files/` outside the repository.
- Over multiple sessions, important project documentation, review records, and verification scripts accumulate in opaque UUID session folders without being tracked or discoverable in the repository.

## Expected Behavior

- Session storage (`~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/files/`) should be reserved for disposable runtime scratch, while requested project deliverables (plans, reports, documentation, and helper scripts) default to or are validated against the active Git repository worktree unless the user explicitly requests an external destination.
- Artifact presentation / completion should clearly distinguish or warn when a deliverable was written to ephemeral session state rather than the active repository worktree.

### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

Allow configuring a default agent instead of requiring agent activation in each new session

### Proposed solution

GitHub Copilot CLI already has configurable defaults for the following:

- Model
- Reasoning Level
- Context Size

My proposal is that a setting for default agent is introduced which should allow me to specify the agent name, and upon start of a session it would do the following:

1. Check the session for an existing selected agent
  - This is to prevent overriding specifically selected agents in specific sessions  
3. Attempt to load the configured default agent by name
4. If the agent cannot be loaded fall back to Default copilot agent

This would improve my workflow, and I'm sure the workflow of others who use one agent consistently as a baseline and want to not have to think about configuring it before firing off a request. I've had several times I started a new session after ending a long one and forgot to make the agent change, and had to start over.

For example, I have an agent called "Rover" and I want to default to using "Rover" with GPT-6 Luna at standard context and Max reasoning.

I would do /settings like I already do for setting the model defaults, and see an additional option for setting the default agent file.
