issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Summary

On Linux/Docker (2026.10.8, single Gateway) the SQLite snapshot reclaimer logs `Skipped SQLite snapshot reclamation: Unrecognized snapshot artifact` on every maintenance tick and has never reclaimed a single artifact. First observed 2026-10-28, still firing now: **572 occurrences, 304 in the last 24 h, ~14/hour**. It keeps firing even when the only files present are the live database and its own sidecar files — there are no snapshot artifacts left to misidentify.

### Environment

- version 2026.10.8, Docker, Linux (Synology NAS)
- state directory contents at time of report:
```
157,724,672  openclaw.sqlite
 10,431,872  openclaw.sqlite-wal
     32,768  openclaw.sqlite-shm
     20,480  openclaw-quarantine.sqlite
        219  openclaw.sqlite.cron-authority.lock
          0  *.bak
```

### Evidence

Every skip carries an **empty structured payload** — no artifact name, no path, no reason:

```json
{"0":"{\"subsystem\":\"infra/sqlite-snapshot\"}","1":{},"2":"Skipped SQLite snapshot reclamation: Unrecognized snapshot artifact"}
```

Before manual cleanup, two doctor-created snapshots had sat unreclaimed for roughly two weeks:

```
openclaw.sqlite                          151M
openclaw.sqlite.doctor-cron-...4eaa.bak  107M   (Oct 16)
openclaw.sqlite.doctor-cron-...4fa7.bak  101M   (Oct 13)
openclaw.sqlite-wal                       10M
```

After archiving and removing both `.bak` files by hand, the warning rate did not change. That rules out "an unknown file is present" as the trigger: the matcher appears to reject the live set it is supposed to recognise.

### Expected

- The reclaimer recognises its own artifacts — including the live database and the sidecar files it must not touch — and reclaims genuinely stale snapshots without operator intervention.
- When a skip occurs, the structured payload names the rejected artifact and the reason. An empty object makes the message undiagnosable from logs.

### Impact

- Silent, unbounded growth of orphaned snapshots: 217 MB accumulated here on the same volume as the session database.
- ~14 WARN/hour of indistinguishable noise. In the same window the log also holds 1,905 `slow SQLite` WARN lines, so real failures are effectively invisible.

### Related

#188586 (main-thread session-sqlite maintenance/reclamation commits blocking the event loop).

issues.title: [Bug]: backup git create fails with "Could not determine whether backup files are SQLite databases" — fixed 10s header-probe timeout vs ~90s measured on a 600k-file state dir (2026.11.1)
issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Description

`openclaw backup git create --all` (scheduled daily via a `command` automation) fails on a state dir of ordinary size, with a message that points at file readability rather than at the real cause:

```
Error: Could not determine whether backup files are SQLite databases.
Check that the backup worker can run and the source files are readable, then retry the backup.
```

Exit code 1. Two consecutive nightly runs failed this way; the Git backup repository last received a commit two days before.

The real cause is a **fixed 10 s timeout on a whole-tree header probe**, which cannot finish on a state dir with a few hundred thousand files. The run does not time out gracefully; it is misreported as "files are not readable".

### Steps to reproduce

1. Release `2026.11.1` (4ffdd20), macOS 26.5.1 arm64, Node v26.12.1, APFS.
2. State dir with ~600k files (here: `~/.openclaw` walk = 601,169 paths: `agents/` 174k, `workspace/` 103k, `tmp/` 194k after cleanup, plus `npm/`, `extensions/`, logs).
3. Run `openclaw backup git create --repository <repo> --all`.
4. Observe the error above after a few minutes; no commit is created.

### Measured evidence

Running the shipped worker directly on the same path list shows the probe itself takes ~90 s, i.e. 9× the built-in 10 s budget:

```
$ find ~/.openclaw \( -type f -o -type l \) | grep -v '\.sqlite' > paths.txt
$ wc -l < paths.txt
601169
$ time node dist/infra/sqlite-header-probe.worker.js < paths.json > out.json
2.52s user 28.67s system 34% cpu 1:29.89 total   # exit 0, 601169 answers, 17 true
```

So the worker is healthy and every path is readable; it simply cannot process the whole inventory within 10 s. The same probe is also part of what makes the command slow overall.

### Where

`dist/backup-sqlite-snapshot-D38jOyo9.mjs`:

```js
function probeSqliteDatabaseHeaders(pathnames) {
  const paths = [...new Set(pathnames)];
  if (paths.length === 0) return new Map();
  try {
    const result = childProcess.spawnSync(process.execPath, resolveRuntimeWorkerArgv(...), {
      input: JSON.stringify(paths),
      encoding: "utf8",
      maxBuffer: 67108864,
      timeout: 1e4,          // <-- fixed 10 s for the entire inventory
    });
    ...
  } catch (cause) {
    throw new Error("Could not determine whether backup files are SQLite databases. ...", { cause });
  }
}
```

and the caller passes every candidate plus every visited directory in one batch:

```js
const probePaths = [...candidates.map((entry) => entry.path), ...visitedDirectories]
  .map(stripSqliteSidecarSuffix)
  .filter((pathname) => !pathname.endsWith(".sqlite"));
for (const [pathname, sqlite] of probeSqliteDatabaseHeaders(probePaths)) answers.set(pathname, sqlite);
```

The worker itself (`dist/infra/sqlite-header-probe.worker.js`) is fine: it `lstat`s each path, opens the first 16 bytes, and tolerates `ENOENT`/`ELOOP`.

### Expected behavior

Either the backup completes, or it fails with a message that names the actual cause (probe timeout / oversized inventory) instead of telling the operator that the source files are not readable.

### Suggested fix

- Chunk the probe (e.g. 5k–20k paths per spawn) and/or scale the timeout with batch size instead of a fixed `1e4`.
- Propagate `cause` into the user-facing message (timeout vs. spawn failure vs. unreadable file), so `ETIMEDOUT` is not reported as a permissions problem.
- Optional: skip the header probe for subtrees the inventory already excludes from backup (package content, volatile capture dirs) — they are being stat'ed today for nothing.

### Impact

On any long-lived install, the only automated SQLite-layer backup silently stops producing commits, while the automation status just shows `error: command exited with code 1`. Diagnosing it requires reading dist internals, because the documented remedy ("check that the source files are readable") is wrong for this failure mode.

issues.body:
## Summary

A provider error that is recognized as a rate-limit failure before compaction wraps it can become unclassified afterward. In a controlled reproduction, this prevents compaction from trying an eligible configured fallback.

This is separate from #194759, which concerns the incorrect `guard_blocked` diagnostic label.

## Reproduction

Tested source: f6d1e4c9c56d5d51a5fd1b7bbb912620559654c1.

Using the existing compaction safeguard integration-test harness:
- Run budget-triggered compaction in safeguard mode.
- Leave `compaction.model` unset.
- Configure a fallback on another provider.
- Have the primary summarization stream return an error.
- Have the fallback return a valid summary.

Two otherwise identical cases:

1. `Provider API error (429): too many requests`
   - Fallback is requested.
   - Compaction succeeds and saves the fallback summary.

2. `Provider API error (429): daily token quota exhausted`
   - Only the primary is requested.
   - Compaction fails without trying the fallback.

The second result contains `failure.code = summarization_failed`
and the provider error text in `failure.rawError`, but no
`failure.status` or `failure.reason`.

## Additional evidence

Both unwrapped error messages classify as `rate_limit`.

After adding:
`Summarization failed for 2 messages: Summarization failed: `

the quota-worded error becomes unclassified, while the
“too many requests” error remains recognized.

The paired integration test produced one passing control and one failing regression case.

## Expected behavior

Compaction should preserve or normalize the underlying provider failure so that a recognized HTTP 429 remains eligible for configured model fallback after summary-error wrapping.

Fallback eligibility should not depend on whether the provider's message happens to contain “too many requests”.

## Scope and limitations

This reproduction uses simulated provider responses through the real summary generator, safeguard, and compaction/fallback code. It does not exhaust a live provider quota.

It proves a current recovery edge case, not the cause of the historical incident described in #194759. Other quota-error wordings can still be recognized correctly.

The existing diagnostic-label issue should remain separate.

issues.body:
## Environment
- OpenClaw self-hosted gateway, systemd user service, Node.js v24 (24.19.0 on 2026.9.8, 24.22.1 on 2026.10.6), Linux x64
- Single-user deployment, active Discord channels, ~50 cron jobs (many spawning isolated agent sessions), browser automation in regular use
- ExecStart carries --max-old-space-size=4972 (host has ~10 GiB RAM + 4 GiB swap)

## Symptom
Gateway process RSS grows continuously from a ~2.1-2.5 GiB post-restart baseline until a restart is required. On repeated controlled restarts:

- 2026.9.8: RSS re-crossed 2.7 GiB within ~8h of restart; reached ~3.2 GiB within ~24h. Same shape on the prior install.
- 2026.10.6 (after full reinstall + upgrade): RSS ~2.1 GiB at restart → ~3.0 GiB at +12h → ~3.23-3.40 GiB at +17h. Sawtooth pattern: oscillates a few hundred MB, but the ceiling rises steadily.

The growth is NOT in the JS heap. Verified via the gateway's own diagnostics and /proc during live peaks: main heap stays ~1.4 GiB (well under the 4972 MiB cap), worker heaps total ~1.0-1.3 GiB, heap is stable across the growth period. The delta is off-heap: external/ArrayBuffers, which per the gateway's own memory-pressure log message are "not capped."

## Impact
The RSS growth ratchets the host swap band upward (swap never returns to baseline without a restart), and over ~3 days of uptime drives the box toward swap exhaustion. We experienced one hard wedge at ~4 days uptime (gateway unresponsive, in-flight replies lost, ~7.5h before manual recovery). Recovery is a gateway restart; recurrence is within hours.

## The monitoring blind spot (secondary bug)
The gateway's own "memory pressure: level=warning reason=rss_threshold" log fires reliably on the 2.52 GiB threshold in the heap-visible component on some builds — but on 2026.10.6 it produced ZERO rss_threshold lines across an entire day in which raw process RSS exceeded that threshold by ~0.7-0.9 GiB continuously (verified: journal grep count 0, /proc/<pid>/status VmRSS 3.2-3.4 GiB at the same timestamps). The internal monitor appears to measure a subset (heap + known structures) rather than process RSS, so it reports "no pressure" while the OS-level footprint is 30%+ past its own alarm line. Anyone relying on the gateway's self-reported memory health will miss this leak class entirely.

## Repro
We have not found a minimal repro. The deployment is long-lived (multi-week continuous uptime except for maintenance), high-turnover (isolated agent sessions created and destroyed by cron every hour), and uses browser automation. Recurrence is deterministic across restarts and survives a full reinstall (2026.9.8 → 2026.10.6) and a Node minor bump (24.19.0 → 24.22.1), which suggests it is not a one-batch leak but a steady-state accumulation — candidates: session-transcript worker lifecycle, archive/cache buffers in external memory, or per-turn allocations that never GC because nothing references them from the JS heap.

## Evidence available
- Redacted excerpts from the gateway's diagnostics export (heap ~1.4 GiB vs process RSS ~3.2 GiB at peak, worker/heap breakdown) — the full bundle contains deployment-identifying details so we will share sanitized sections on request, or run any instrumentation you specify on a live instance
- Hourly RSS/swap sample log across the growth curves (2.1 → 3.4 GiB over multiple restart cycles)
- Gateway journal excerpts (memory-pressure lines, worker startup states)
- Timeline documentation across three restart cycles

Happy to run any additional instrumentation on a live instance.

## Ask
1. Is off-heap/external memory growth a known issue on this usage profile? Any flags/mitigations to cap or force reclamation (e.g. periodic worker recycling, an external-buffer pressure trigger)?
2. Should the internal rss_threshold check measure process RSS (VmRSS) rather than the current subset? As-is it gives false "healthy" during a leak that consumes the host.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Description

On a **non-owner turn**, an owner-only core tool is still reachable through the Tool Search / `dispatch_action` path, and instead of a host-gated refusal the caller gets an **outputSchema validation error**:

```
Tool "openclaw:core:automations" returned details that do not match its declared outputSchema.
Check current state before retrying; the tool returned and side effects may already have occurred.
Validation: enabled: must have required property 'enabled';
<root>: must not have additional properties: "gated";
jobs: must have required property 'jobs'; 6 additional validation issues omitted.
```

This is the same class of defect reported in #189488 (closed as "already implemented on main by the merged refusal-provenance repair", with the note that released stable and beta builds still lack it). Filing the release-side follow-up because it still reproduces on released `2026.11.1`.

Why it matters beyond cosmetics:

- The message tells the agent the tool **may already have run**, which is the opposite of the truth (the execution body was replaced by a gate). An agent that follows the hint will re-inspect state or retry, exactly what `ownerOnlyDenied` is designed to prevent.
- A permission boundary is surfaced as a malformed tool result, so a caller cannot distinguish "you may not" from "the tool is broken". In my case this was misread for a while as an `automations` defect rather than an authorization boundary.
- Side effect: every non-owner turn that touches one of these tools burns a tool call and injects a scary "side effects may already have occurred" line into the transcript.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Release: `2026.11.1` (4ffdd20), fresh gateway, one agent whose configured owner (`gateway.owner`-equivalent) is a **different** Feishu `open_id` than the sender of the turn.
2. From that non-owner chat turn, call any owner-only core tool through Tool Search dispatch, e.g.:
   ```
   dispatch_action(id="automations", args={"action":"status"})
   ```
3. Observe: no refusal text, no `gated`-shaped success, but the outputSchema validation error above.

Control: at the same moment, CLI `openclaw cron list` / `openclaw cron add` work normally, so this is unrelated to scheduler health — it is specific to the agent-tool gate projection.

### Expected behavior

Either the tool is not projected into the catalog at all for that turn, or the call fails/returns with the refusal string that `ownerOnlyDenied` already builds:

`"<tool> needs the owner's authority, and this turn was not started by the owner. Do not retry <tool>."`

In neither case should the caller see a schema mismatch.

### Root cause (read from the shipped dist, not from source assumptions)

`dist/agent-tool-availability-DZN62JsD.mjs`:

```js
function gateAgentToolExecution(tool, message) {
  return markAgentToolExecutionUnavailable(copyAgentToolAvailability(tool, {
    ...tool,
    prepareArguments: void 0,
    prepareBeforeToolCallParams: void 0,
    finalizeBeforeToolCallParams: void 0,
    execute: async () => textResult(message, { gated: true })
  }));
}
```

The gate swaps `execute` for a `textResult(message, { gated: true })`. For tools whose declared `outputSchema` is a sealed object with no `gated` variant (owner-only core tools such as `automations`), that result is then validated against the declared schema and necessarily fails: `gated` is an additional property and the per-action required branches (`enabled`, `jobs`, …) are absent.

`dist/agent-tools-CviBz5Mk.mjs` contains the refusal text the gate was supposed to deliver:

```js
ownerOnlyDenied.has(tool.name)
  ? `${tool.name} needs the owner's authority, and this turn was not started by the owner. Do not retry ${tool.name}.`
  : ...
```

So the refusal string exists, but the gated execution path cannot deliver it to a strict-schema caller.

### Suggested fix (either is fine)

- Make the gate raise a tool-call error / host refusal instead of returning a `textResult` payload that downstream schema validation will reject; or
- Have `gateAgentToolExecution` bypass output validation for gated results (the same way the refusal-provenance repair appears to do for Code Mode catalog calls on main); or
- Give gated results a schema the validator accepts (`{ gated: true }` union) for every tool the denylist can cover.

### Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.11.1` (4ffdd20), macOS 26.5.1 arm64, Node v26.12.1
- Channel: Feishu DM, agent session `agent:<agent>:feishu:direct:<open_id>`
- Non-owner sender by design: gateway owner is account A, the turn was started by account B (two-account isolation is intentional here, not a misconfiguration)
- Also observed: `plugins`, `openclaw` (system) and gateway restart are unavailable in the same session for the same reason, and only the schema-mismatch dialect leaks through; the other owner-only tools simply disappear from the catalog.

### Related

#189488 (closed, same symptom class, fixed on main, released builds still affected)

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

`openclaw update`'s post-restart health verification can report a false-negative failure (`reason: "restart-unhealthy"`, `recovery.reason: "runtime-verification-failed"`) and leave the gateway stopped, even when the new build is completely healthy — confirmed by manually starting the exact same build immediately afterward and watching it come up clean. The captured health snapshot shows the check hit `ECONNREFUSED` with the port reported as `"status": "free"`, consistent with the verification probing before the new process had finished its normal startup sequence (observed to take ~7-15s from process start to the HTTP server listening), rather than the gateway actually being broken.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On a native (systemd-managed, git-checkout `dev` channel) install, run `openclaw update --yes --json` where the update genuinely succeeds: fetch, rebase, `pnpm install`, `pnpm build`, and `openclaw doctor` all complete with no errors, and `git rev-parse HEAD` moves to the target commit.
2. The updater proceeds to its restart/handoff step (doctor output shows `Gateway health will be checked after Doctor repair.`) and signals the live gateway to restart for the update (`[gateway] restart mode: managed update handoff owns successor`, `received SIGUSR1; restarting`).
3. Intermittently (did not reproduce on two prior same-week updates from this same host; reproduced on the third), the health check captured at that moment shows the gateway simply hasn't started listening yet:
   ```json
   // health/gateway-health.json in the diagnostics bundle
   {
     "status": "failed",
     "error": "Gateway not reachable at ws://127.0.0.1:18789 (ECONNREFUSED)..."
   }
   ```
   ```json
   // status/gateway-status.json, same capture
   "port": { "port": 18789, "status": "free", "listeners": [] },
   "health": { "healthy": false, "staleGatewayPids": [] },
   "rpc": { "connectFailure": { "kind": "unreachable" }, "ok": false }
   ```
4. The updater returns `{"status":"error","reason":"restart-unhealthy","recovery":{"serviceRestartSafe":false,"reason":"runtime-verification-failed"}}` and does not restart the service. `systemctl --user status` confirms the process exited cleanly (`status=0/SUCCESS`) and stays `inactive (dead)` — nothing brings it back up automatically.
5. Manually running `systemctl --user start openclaw-gateway` immediately afterward (no code/config changes) brings up the exact same build cleanly: `[gateway] http server listening (21 plugins...)`, `[gateway] ready`, Telegram channel polling starts normally, and it has remained stable since.

### Expected behavior

The post-restart health verification should tolerate the gateway's normal startup window (retry/poll for at least as long as a cold start is observed to take) before concluding the new build is unhealthy. At minimum, when it does give up, the failure should carry enough diagnostic detail (what was checked, how many attempts/how long it waited) for the operator to distinguish "still starting up" from "actually broken" — right now the result JSON's `steps` array is empty for this failure and the only signal is the opaque label `runtime-verification-failed`.

### Actual behavior

The gateway was left `inactive (dead)` (systemd: `status=0/SUCCESS`, i.e. it exited cleanly, it just was never restarted) for about 4 minutes until manually started. No error was surfaced anywhere except the CLI's own JSON output and the auto-generated triage bundle — there was no proactive alert that the update had left the service offline.

### OpenClaw version

Before: 2026.8.1 (`0be4cd7512582b66cda1da6e2ee095103bc78a9a`). After (the version that was actually running fine once manually started): 2026.9.1 (`fcb8eb4deb4dc0a5721e9e0ebeaca922f702a7a8`).

### Operating system

Ubuntu Linux (kernel 7.0.0-29-generic)

### Install method

Native systemd user service, git-checkout `dev` channel install (`pnpm build`), not npm global / Docker / Mac app.

### Model

N/A — this is an update-tooling/restart-verification infrastructure bug, not tied to any specific model or provider request path.

### Provider / routing chain

N/A — unrelated to model routing.

### Additional provider/model setup details

N/A

### Logs

```
Update JSON result:
{
  "status": "error",
  "mode": "git",
  "reason": "restart-unhealthy",
  "before": { "sha": "0be4cd7512582b66cda1da6e2ee095103bc78a9a", "version": "2026.8.1" },
  "after": { "sha": "fcb8eb4deb4dc0a5721e9e0ebeaca922f702a7a8", "version": "2026.9.1" },
  "postUpdate": { "plugins": { "status": "ok", "sync": { "errors": [] } } },
  "recovery": { "serviceRestartSafe": false, "reason": "runtime-verification-failed" },
  "steps": []
}

Diagnostics bundle health/gateway-health.json (captured at the moment of failure):
{
  "status": "failed",
  "capturedAt": "2026-09-05T03:16:27.724Z",
  "error": "Gateway not reachable at ws://127.0.0.1:18789 (ECONNREFUSED).\nStart it with `openclaw gateway run` or check `openclaw gateway status`.\nBind: lan"
}

Diagnostics bundle status/gateway-status.json (same capture, abbreviated):
"gateway": { "bindHost": "0.0.0.0", "bindMode": "lan", "port": 18789, "portSource": "service args" },
"health": { "healthy": false, "staleGatewayPids": [] },
"port": { "port": 18789, "status": "free", "listeners": [] },
"rpc": { "ok": false, "connectFailure": { "kind": "unreachable" } }

Gateway journal, ~3.5 minutes after the failed verification, on manual systemctl start (identical binary/commit, no changes made):
[gateway] loading configuration...
[gateway] resolving authentication...
[gateway] starting...
[gateway] starting HTTP server...
[health-monitor] started (interval: 300s, startup-grace: 60s, channel-connect-grace: 120s)
[gateway] starting channels and sidecars...
[gateway] agent model: ollama/mistral-small3.2:24b (thinking=off, fast=off)
[gateway] http server listening (21 plugins: acpx, anthropic, browser, canvas, codex, cua-computer, device-pair, file-transfer, geolocation, google, google-meet, linux-node, memory-core, ollama, openai, talk-voice, teams-meetings, telegram, workboard, xai, zoom-meetings; 3.7s)
[gateway] ready
[telegram] [ceo-info] starting provider (@NOC150_BOT)
[telegram] [diag] isolated polling ingress started spool=...
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

None captured (headless server; diagnosed via systemd/journalctl and the update's own diagnostics bundle).

### Impact and severity

- Affected: native (systemd/launchd-managed), git-checkout `dev` installs where the post-restart health check races the gateway's own startup time.
- Severity: High — full service outage (Telegram/channel bot completely unresponsive) with no automatic recovery and no operator-facing alert; the operator only knows something is wrong if they happen to check.
- Frequency: Intermittent — did not reproduce on the two most recent prior CLI-driven `openclaw update` runs on this same host; reproduced on the third, the same day a related but distinct update-tooling bug ([openclaw/openclaw#138684](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/138684)) had already caused an outage a few hours earlier.
- Consequence: ~4 minutes of complete bot downtime, resolved only because the operator was actively watching this update run (per a standing decision to switch from the unattended Control-UI "Update" button to a watched CLI run, made specifically because of #138684's outage earlier that day).

### Additional information

This may share a root cause or at least a code path with [openclaw/openclaw#138684](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/138684), filed the same day against the same update/restart-handoff machinery on the same host: in both cases, the live gateway had already torn itself down expecting the update process to safely bring up (or restore) a successor, the updater's own safety check then failed for a reason unrelated to the actual build's health, and the updater chose to leave the service stopped rather than restart it — with no automatic recovery path and minimal diagnostic detail surfaced to the operator. Whatever fixes #138684's rollback-safety logic may be worth auditing this restart-health-check path at the same time.

Workaround used to recover: `systemctl --user start openclaw-gateway` (no code or config changes needed — the build was already correct).

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect pending state without a crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

OpenClaw2026.11.1 leaves the trusted external iMessage plugin's state migration pending after successful native update repair when its channel is disabled, even though all retired sources named by its contract are absent. Doctor excludes that owner before inspecting its state-only migration contract.

### Steps to reproduce

1. In a disposable installation of OpenClaw2026.11.1 with the official `@openclaw/imessage@2026.11.1`, explicitly enable/allow the plugin but set `channels.imessage.enabled:false`.
2. The plugin manifest declares `doctorContract.stateMigrations:[{id:"imessage-retired-state"}]`. Its contract checks only `<state-dir>/imessage/reply-cache.jsonl`, `sent-echoes.jsonl`, and `catchup/*.json`. In the observed installation all three locations are absent.
3. Native update repair completes with its ledger finished/succeeded, but reports that the plugin has not confirmed saved data/settings readiness. The pending iMessage state-migration obligation remains.
4. Independently reproduce the selection behavior with the actual packaged registry export and synthetic metadata below. Run only in a disposable isolated environment; this test does not run Doctor, import plugin runtime code or open a state database.

The following fixture was executed inside a sparse filesystem namespace with the OpenClaw package read-only at `/package`, Node24.22.1 at `/node`, private `/tmp` and `/run`, and no real home, state, configuration or network mounted:

```js
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import {m as resolveRecords} from '/package/dist/doctor-contract-registry-B4NMIsug.mjs';

const plugin = {
  id:'imessage', packageName:'@openclaw/imessage', origin:'config',
  rootDir:'/tmp/public-imessage', channels:['imessage'], providers:[],
  doctorContract:{configRepair:true,
    stateMigrations:[{id:'imessage-retired-state'}]}
};
const config = {
  plugins:{enabled:true,allow:['imessage'],deny:[],
    entries:{imessage:{enabled:true}}},
  channels:{imessage:{enabled:false}}
};
const selected = cfg => resolveRecords({
  config:cfg,manifestRegistry:{plugins:[plugin]},pluginIds:['imessage']
}).map(row=>row.id);

assert.deepEqual(selected(config), []);
assert.deepEqual(selected({...config,
  channels:{imessage:{enabled:true}}}), ['imessage']);
```

Provide a supported way for Doctor to inspect/certify this trusted disabled owner's declared state-only migration without enabling its messaging runtime, or a specific actionable diagnostic if this is intentionally unsupported. Keep the channel disabled, retained inputs and ownership/trust guards intact. The documented recovery command currently points back to Doctor, which excludes this owner.

### Actual behavior

`filterPluginDoctorStateMigrationRecords` in `src/plugins/doctor-contract-registry.ts` excludes non-bundled owners that fail `isActivatedManifestOwner`. A disabled channel fails that condition even when the plugin is explicitly selected/enabled/allowlisted. The later deferred-completion flow requires completed inspection for an obligation with `requiresStateMigration:true`, so it cannot settle through this selection path.

The plugin's `defineRetiredPluginStateMigration` contract detects no work when the named retired sources are absent, but the disabled external owner never reaches that inspection. No channel activation, bridge connection or message send is needed by the declared contract.

OpenClaw2026.11.1; official `@openclaw/imessage@2026.11.1`.

### Operating system

Ubuntu26.04, x64. Actual isolated selection reproduction: Node24.22.1.

### Install method

Global npm host package; official managed npm iMessage plugin.

Not involved: deterministic Doctor metadata/owner selection before any model request.

### Provider / routing chain

Native update repair → Doctor plugin-contract selection → deferred migration completion. No messaging/provider request in the reproduction.

### Logs

```text

remaining pending plugin obligation: imessage, requiresStateMigration:true
plugin package:2026.11.1, trustedOfficialInstall:true
activation reason: channel disabled in config
three declared retired-source locations: absent

```

The fixture validates real packaged registry selection, not an end-to-end migration-ledger mutation. The completion condition and absent-source behavior are source analysis; the persistent warning and successful repair ledger were separately observed. No live database rows, credentials, user messages, host identifiers or private configuration payloads are included.

### Impact and severity

Affected observed configuration: trusted official external iMessage plugin enabled, channel intentionally disabled. Consequence: an unresolved advisory migration warning despite otherwise successful update/repair. The gateway remains healthy. The synthetic selection behavior is deterministic. No data loss or messaging failure is claimed because the channel remains disabled.

The `reported-refusal` case in `test/scripts/cross-os-release-gateway-startup.test.ts` failed at commit `942fa60f9f08eccc6e91c945912c690b44d61834` with `EADDRINUSE` while rebinding a released replacement port.

`configureReplacementGatewayPort` obtains an OS-assigned port, persists it, and closes the reservation. The test later asks `reserveTestPortListener({port: expectedPort})` to bind that exact port again. This is an unowned interval: another socket may use the released ephemeral port before the assertion. Cooperative test claims do not constrain the OS client-port allocator. The test itself mocks the Gateway process, so there is no real replacement Gateway listener retaining this port.

All seven cases pass unchanged in a focused reproduction (24ms test time, 2.43s wrapper). That passing replay is not a fix. Treat the observed collision as a test-harness flake, preserve the original failure, and replace the global availability assertion with deterministic proof that the reservation was closed while retaining the existing recovery/configuration assertions. Current main still contains the exact-port rebinding assertion.

No timeout, production port-selection policy, or release gate should be weakened.

issues.body:
### Summary

When a WhatsApp chat has disappearing messages turned on, outbound messages sent by OpenClaw should follow that chat's timer instead of being sent as permanent messages.

This is a fresh request, as suggested when #71157 was closed on 2026-10-24 for lack of further demand. This request is narrower than #71157: it asks OpenClaw to follow the timer the chat already uses, not to add a new expiration setting that OpenClaw controls.

### Problem to solve

On OpenClaw 2026.10.10 (macOS), a message sent with the `message` tool (`channel: "whatsapp"`) into a 1:1 chat that has disappearing messages turned on is delivered as a normal, non-expiring message. The recipient's phone (and the account owner's phone) shows:

> **This message won't disappear**
> The sender may be using an older version of WhatsApp.

The message stays in the chat after everything around it expires, so someone has to delete it by hand. The warning also makes it look as if the account owner's own WhatsApp is out of date.

### Proposed solution

- When sending to a chat with an active disappearing-message timer, pass that duration as Baileys' `ephemeralExpiration` (or set `contextInfo.expiration`) on the outbound message.
- Take the timer from the chat's known state. Inbound messages in such chats carry `contextInfo.expiration`, and Baileys also emits ephemeral-setting updates. Remember the latest value for each chat.
- If no timer is known for a chat, keep today's behavior.
- Apply it to every outbound path: text, quoted replies, media, polls, and tool or channel sends.
- Optional: a channel- or account-level opt-out for anyone who wants permanent agent messages.

Following the chat's own timer avoids the open questions raised on #71157: it adds no new retention policy, only matches the one the chat participants already chose.

### Alternatives considered

- Deleting messages by hand: unreliable, and the recipient still sees the warning.
- A configured fixed expiration (#71157): this works, but it can disagree with the chat's actual setting and adds a new config contract.

### Impact

- Affected: WhatsApp users whose chats with family or contacts use disappearing messages, which is common.
- Frequency: every OpenClaw outbound message into such a chat.
- Consequence: privacy mismatch (agent messages outlive the rest of the conversation), manual cleanup, and a confusing "older version" warning shown to the other person.

### Evidence

- OpenClaw 2026.10.10 (7dc3350), WhatsApp channel plugin on Baileys, macOS.
- No reference to `ephemeral`/`expiration` in the WhatsApp extension code outside `node_modules`; Baileys supports `sendMessage(jid, content, { ephemeralExpiration })`.
- Related: #71157 (closed not_planned, 2026-10-24).

issues.body:
## Summary

A swarm collector can permanently freeze a failed completion with `schemaError: "structured_output was not called"` even when the child execution succeeds and a schema-valid `structured_output` call is recorded at the terminal boundary.

The task registry then reports the task as succeeded, while repeated `agents_wait` calls return the collector as failed. Because the failed collector completion is durable/idempotent, callers can repeatedly reattach the same poisoned completion.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: 2026.8.2
- Swarm task: `collect: true`
- An `outputSchema` is supplied
- The child calls `structured_output` with schema-valid JSON near terminal completion

## Observed behavior

1. The child task reaches an authoritative successful execution outcome.
2. The child calls `structured_output` with data that validates against the requested schema.
3. Collector completion is frozen first as:
   ```json
   {
     "status": "failed",
     "schemaError": "structured_output was not called"
   }
   ```
4. The late state update is rejected because `collectorCompletion` already exists.
5. Task status remains `succeeded`, but `agents_wait` keeps returning the failed collector completion.

This produces contradictory durable state: successful execution and valid structured output, but a permanently failed collector.

## Expected behavior

When all of the following are true:

- execution has an authoritative `outcome.status === "ok"`;
- the existing collector completion failed only with the exact missing-output diagnostic;
- the existing completion has no structured payload;
- a later `structured_output` state contains schema-valid structured data;

the registry should atomically reconcile the collector completion to `status: "done"`, persist it, and clear the obsolete missing-output diagnostic.

It must **not** promote authoritative execution failures or other schema failures.

## Reproduction shape

A deterministic registry regression test can create a collector entry with:

- `collect: true`
- terminal execution outcome `{ status: "ok" }`
- collector completion `{ status: "failed", schemaError: "structured_output was not called" }`

Then record a valid structured state for the same run. Current behavior rejects the update; expected behavior reconciles it to a done completion.

A companion test should prove that an execution outcome such as `{ status: "error", error: "completed" }` remains failed.

## Proposed fix

Allow the structured-output state callback to reconcile only this narrow late-success case, persist atomically with rollback on persistence failure, and consume the process-local structured-output cache only after durable reconciliation succeeds.

I have a tested patch with focused collector/registry coverage ready for a PR.

issues.body:
### Summary

Render compact Slack progress instead of a native task card when a turn has no authored multi-step plan and the card would contain only one generated work-summary row.


### Problem to solve

A native task card implies structured multi-step work. For ordinary tool-backed turns without an authored plan, the current card can contain only one generated work-summary row that duplicates nearby narration. The heavier task UI adds visual noise without communicating additional structure or status.


### Proposed solution

In Slack `progress` mode, choose compact presentation when all of the following are true:

- no authored plan exists;
- no approval or actionable attention state is active; and
- the native card would otherwise contain only the generated work-summary row.

Promote to a native task card when an authored multi-step plan, approval, or actionable failure exists. Keep an explicit configuration override for operators who always want native cards.


### Alternatives considered

- Set `progress.style: "compact"` globally. This removes one-row cards but also removes native cards from turns where an actual multi-step plan would benefit from them.
- Set `nativeTaskCards: false`. This changes the card implementation to Block Kit but does not remove the one-row card surface.
- Switch to `streaming.mode: "partial"`. This removes structured progress entirely, including useful progress for genuinely long or planned work.


### Impact

- **Affected:** Slack users using default or card-style progress.
- **Severity:** Low-to-medium UX friction.
- **Frequency:** Common on ordinary tool-backed turns without authored plans.
- **Consequence:** Repetitive one-row cards consume channel space and make routine operations look like formal task plans.


### Evidence/examples

- [#133479](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/133479) documents the current intentional behavior: Slack cards show authored milestones or one stable work summary.
- A sanitized before screenshot should show a native card containing only one generated work-summary row alongside equivalent narration.
- The Slack channel documentation describes compact style as the card-free alternative: https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/slack#text-streaming


### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only

### Additional information

This request does not propose removing native task cards. It proposes reserving them for turns that have meaningful task structure or actionable state. It should remain separate from the recovered-error reconciliation bug above.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A config commit that changes one agent's entry, or an auth publish for one agent, ends with `refreshCommittedProviderCatalogs(owners.values())`. That starts `loadFullModelCatalog({ changedOnly: true })` on every configured owner on the gateway. So adding or removing one agent opens every agent's database, and turns on unrelated agents stall.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run a gateway on 2026.10.10 with a few hundred configured agents. Ours have about 470 each and use the gateway's default static catalog mode.
2. After startup publication finishes, add or remove one agent. The hot reload logs `agents.entries.<id>`.
3. Watch the log after `[reload] config hot reload applied (agents.entries.<id>)`.

### Expected behavior

Only the owners the publication rebuilt refresh their provider catalog. In this case, that is the one changed agent.

The same commit keeps every other owner's snapshot unchanged (`isPreparedModelRuntimeOwnerInRefreshScope`), so they have nothing new to refresh. On 2026.7.35, the same per-agent config changes on the same gateways were routine and did not stall turns.

### Actual behavior

Within a second of `applied`, the gateway starts opening agent databases across the whole roster, and the main thread stalls over and over.

Here is one gateway with about 470 agents in the 24 minutes after the first `applied`. Two more single-agent reloads landed in that window.

| Log line | Count | Worst case |
|---|---|---|
| `[state/agent-db] slow OpenClaw agent database open` | 132 | 4.3 s |
| `[event-loop] main-thread stall` | 155 | 4.5 s |
| `[state/agent-db] agent database clean-close receipt: written` | 1,084 | |

Turns on unrelated agents stalled for the duration. Each episode we saw lasted 30 to 60 minutes. The gateway had already logged the reload as applied, so it looked healthy while chat stalled.

Code path, on `main` at 94d45c8d51:

- After a commit: [`prepared-model-runtime.ts#L583`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/94d45c8d5144dacde3e76ef1bab8046e9523b66b/src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.ts#L583) calls `refreshCommittedProviderCatalogs(owners.values())`. The auth-mutation publish does the same at [`#L710`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/94d45c8d5144dacde3e76ef1bab8046e9523b66b/src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.ts#L710).
- [`refreshCommittedProviderCatalogs`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/94d45c8d5144dacde3e76ef1bab8046e9523b66b/src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.refresh-scope.ts#L37-L54) loops over every owner. It skips only pending, needs-refresh and non-configured owners, and starts each `loadFullModelCatalog({ changedOnly: true })` without awaiting it.
- In [`prepared-model-runtime.catalog-access.ts#L618`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/94d45c8d5144dacde3e76ef1bab8046e9523b66b/src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.catalog-access.ts#L618), an owner whose published inventory is empty does a full provider discovery even with `changedOnly`.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.10 (npm). The same code is on `main` at 94d45c8d51.

### Operating system

Amazon Linux 2023 (x86_64), Node v24.22.1

### Install method

Global npm install. Three gateway profiles on one host, each a systemd user service.

### Model

Not model-specific.

### Provider / routing chain

Not provider-specific. The gateways have OpenRouter, Anthropic and OpenAI providers configured.

### Additional provider/model setup details

All owners use the gateway's static catalog mode: startup, hot reload, and per-agent preparation. Each agent has its own agent directory and database (the default layout).

### Logs

```shell
2026-11-07T21:05:38.250Z [reload] config change detected; evaluating reload (agents.entries.<agent>)
2026-11-07T21:16:44.691Z [reload] config hot reload applied (agents.entries.<agent>)
2026-11-07T21:16:46.366Z [event-loop] main-thread stall: elapsedMs=2177 task=unattributed
[state/agent-db] slow OpenClaw agent database open agentId=<other agent> elapsedMs=4295 ... isMainThread=false admissionMode=sync
2026-11-07T21:16:56.619Z [event-loop] main-thread stall: elapsedMs=4467 task=unattributed
2026-11-07T21:17:04.582Z [event-loop] main-thread stall: elapsedMs=2628 task=unattributed
[state/agent-db] slow OpenClaw agent database open agentId=<other agent> elapsedMs=3241 ... isMainThread=false admissionMode=sync
```

Agent database open lines per minute after `applied`: 18 (21:16), then 73, 85, 46, 82, 82, 84, 71 ... and about 85 a minute through 21:29.

### Impact and severity

- **Affected:** every agent on a gateway with hundreds of configured agents.
- **Severity:** blocks chat. Turns stall gateway-wide.
- **Frequency:** every single-agent add or remove, and every auth publish. Removing a legacy auth file from an agent directory also triggers an auth publish.
- **Consequence:** 30 to 60 minutes of stalled turns per change at about 470 agents. Memory rises during the walk.

### Additional information

- Last known good: 2026.7.35. First known bad: 2026.10.10. We did not run the versions in between.
- In the logged window, this gateway was also running 10.10's session cost usage backfill, which also opens agent databases. So not every count above is the catalog walk. We attribute the walk to the commit for two reasons: the code path above, and the opens starting within a second of `applied`.
- **Suggested fix:** keep the post-commit refresh to the owners in scope.
  - For a scoped commit: the owners the publication rebuilt (`isPreparedModelRuntimeOwnerInRefreshScope` with the publication's agent ids), plus any owners that an adopted auth transaction invalidated.
  - For an auth publish: only the invalidated owners.
  - A full publication keeps refreshing every owner.
- We run this as a local patch on 2026.10.10: five small edits to the built `prepared-model-runtime` chunk. We can share the diff.

issues.body:
## Summary

On OpenClaw 2026.10.8 (dc2523e), a NAS/Docker install spends **58.1 s of every startup** in `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync` — **96 % of `workspaceFactsMs` (60.2 s)**, inside `sidecars.model-runtime` (60.6 s). Startup already takes 157–245 s on this host, so this single stage is **24–39%** of total startup.

The cost is filesystem metadata operations (`stat` / manifest reads) over the whole plugin tree — 101 MB / 6 495 files / 603 directories, of which one plugin's `node_modules` holds 4 553 files. It re-runs on **every** startup, not once per install.

Cross-host comparison pins the mechanism: same build, same concurrency setting, only file count and filesystem differ — and the slowdown decomposes as **48× ≈ 7.3× (file count) × 6.5× (per-file cost)**. It is an I/O-count problem, not an algorithmic one.

## Minimal repro

1. Install a plugin with a large `node_modules` (the `feishu` plugin here contributes 4 553 files).
2. Apply the patch in [How to reproduce the instrumentation](#how-to-reproduce-the-instrumentation) and start the Gateway once. Record `runtimePluginMs`.
3. Disable that plugin, restart, record `runtimePluginMs` again.

The delta is that plugin's scan cost. On this host removing 6 small stock plugins (18 → 12 loaded, confirmed in the log) changed `model-runtime` by −1.6 % — the bulk is one plugin's dependency tree, not plugin count.

## Measured breakdown (via instrumentation patch)

The `onBuildStats` callback already computes 20 metrics, but routes them to `startupTrace.detail("sidecars.model-runtime-build", …)` → the diagnostic events channel, **not** the log file. That is why this was hard to see. Patching that one line to also `console.error(JSON.stringify(stats))` produced:

```
workspaceFactsMs               60247.4 ms   ← the whole phase
runtimePluginMs                58123.9 ms   ← 96 %, nested inside
agentFactsMs                    1316.7 ms
registryMs                       593.6 ms
staticProviderCatalogMs           28.4 ms
configuredProjectionMs            14.7 ms
ambientCredentialsMs               8.0 ms
pluginMetadataMs                   0.1 ms
catalogSourceMs                    0.0 ms
```

Total phase wall time `sidecars.model-runtime` = **60.6 s**, so `workspaceFactsMs` accounts for essentially all of it.

Scale metrics from the same payload:

```
agentCount=3  workspaceGroupCount=3  configuredFactsGroupCount=3
catalogSourceCount=0  credentialGroupCount=1  catalogGroupCount=0
runtimeRegistryCount=3  configuredRuntimeModelCount=21
generatedCatalogPluginCount=2  generatedCatalogReadCount=6
sourceConcurrencyLimit=2  fullCatalogConcurrencyLimit=1
```

## Where the time goes

Inside `prepareWorkspaceBuildGroup`, the `reportStage` labels map 1:1 onto those metrics:

| stage | metric | value |
|---|---|---:|
| `workspace plugins` | `runtimePluginMs` | 58 124 ms |
| `static provider catalog` | `staticProviderCatalogMs` | 28 ms |
| `ambient credentials` | `ambientCredentialsMs` | 8 ms |
| `agent facts` | `agentFactsMs` | 1 317 ms |
| `configured model projection` | `configuredProjectionMs` | 15 ms |

The `workspace plugins` stage's only `await` is `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync`, which goes through `createPluginCache` / `retainPluginCache` / `selectPluginMetadataSnapshot`.

> Scope caveat: `plugin-metadata-snapshot-*.mjs` itself contains only
> one `scan` call (with 14 `stat` and 45 `manifest` references). The
> 6,495-entry filesystem walk therefore happens **beneath** that call —
> inside `createPluginCache` / `selectPluginMetadataSnapshot` and their
> transitive helpers — not in this module. The 58 s is attributed to
> this stage by the `onBuildStats` instrumentation, which measures the
> whole `runtimePluginMs` span around the single `await`.

### Code locations

| what | path | line |
|---|---|---:|
| `prepareWorkspaceBuildGroup` | `dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs` | 400 |
| the `await` that owns the 58 s | `dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs` | 413 |
| `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync` | `dist/plugin-metadata-snapshot-*.mjs` | 550 |

```js
// dist/prepared-model-runtime.facts-*.mjs:413
await resolvePluginMetadataSnapshotAsync(prepareOwnedPluginMetadataSnapshotParams(input, env));
```

## The tree being walked

```
~/.openclaw/npm/projects/    6495 files / 603 dirs / 101 MB
└─ feishu plugin              4553 files in node_modules (2 files are its own)
   @larksuiteoapi/node-sdk     7 files, 28.83 MB
   typebox                  1409 files
   zod                       840 files
   @openclaw/fs-safe          672 files
   protobufjs                 108 files
   @openclaw/fs-safe-*        8 platform variants, ~24 MB
```

## The two instances are a natural A/B

Same OpenClaw version (2026.10.8 / dc2523e), same code path, same
`fullCatalogConcurrencyLimit` (= 1), same `MAX_CONCURRENT_MODEL_RUNTIME_AGENT_SOURCE_BUILDS`.
Only two variables differ: plugin-tree size and filesystem.

| | Comparison host (bare metal, local SSD) | This host (Docker on Synology NAS) |
|---|---|---|
| `runtimePluginMs` | **1,209 ms** | **58,124 ms** (48×) |
| plugin-tree files | **885** = `extensions/` 849 + `npm/projects/` 36 | **6,495** = `npm/projects/` only |
| plugin-tree size | 7.2 MB | 101 MB |
| per-file cost | **1.37 ms** | **8.95 ms** (6.5×) |

Scope note: the two columns are **not** counted identically. The 885
figure includes `extensions/`; the 6,495 figure does not. This host's
`extensions/` tree was not counted, so both the 7.3× file-count ratio
and the 6.5× per-file ratio are **lower bounds** for the true gap.

Decomposition (conservative, given the scope note above):

    48× total ≈ 7.3× more files × 6.5× higher per-file cost

The first factor is ordinary data volume. The second is filesystem:
Docker overlay2 + NAS spindle/network storage makes each `stat`
substantially more expensive. This also explains why the host's ~100%
SQLite page cache does not help — `stat` does not go through it.

Note the fix target is *operation count*, not *operation scheduling*.

## What does not explain it (ruled out)

Single-variable experiments, each verified with a restart. Format: *hypothesis → how it was tested → result*.

1. Hollow `node-llama-cpp` install / provider pointing at a dead host → removed plugin + provider + aliases + install dir + install record → **−2 %** (62.9 s vs 64.4 s)
2. Plugin *count* → disabled 6 unused plugins, 18 → 12 loaded (confirmed in log) → **−1.6 %**
3. DB size → checked what the phase reads → `memory_embedding_cache` / `memory_index_chunks` / `embedding` referenced **0 times**
4. Memory / CPU → `mem_limit` 3 g→5 g, `cpu_shares` 512→4096 → `eventLoopUtilization` 0.997→0.999, **unchanged**
5. Disk I/O on the DB → page cache 100 % resident, `diskBytes=0` → **only covers SQLite**, not the plugin tree
6. External-service probe timeouts → 72 × 5 s `generativelanguage.googleapis.com` timeouts/day → **zero** fall inside the `model-runtime` window (first is 11 s after it ends)

Disabling 6 plugins changed nothing because those were small stock plugins; the bulk is one plugin's `node_modules`.

## Why this matters

- The scan runs on **every** startup, not once per install.
- On containers and NAS/NFS hosts the per-`stat` cost is amplified, so the effect is far larger than the tree-size ratio suggests.
- The metrics that reveal it already exist but never reach the log (see last section).

## Suggested directions (in priority order)

1. **Bounded, manifest-first lookup (largest win).** Check for `openclaw.plugin.json` at the known layouts — the package root, and `node_modules/<pkg>/` directly under each plugin root — and fall back to a full walk only when nothing is found. This preserves support for arbitrary-depth installs while removing the walk from the common case.
2. **Cache the metadata snapshot**, keyed on `pluginGeneration` or directory mtime, so startup does not re-scan an unchanged tree. Pushes steady-state operation count toward 0. A cold install or upgrade would still scan once.
3. **Parallelism — consider last, and probably not at all on network filesystems.** Little's law predicts it will not help:

   ```
   throughput = concurrency / latency_per_operation
   ```

   On NAS / overlay2 the per-operation latency **already includes queueing**. Raise concurrency → queue deepens → latency rises with it → throughput stays flat → total time does not drop. The bottleneck is the metadata path, not the workers feeding it.

   **A measurable guard for anyone tempted to try it:** after raising concurrency, if `runtimePluginMs / fileCount` (cost per file) **rises instead of falling**, the metadata path is saturated and concurrency is a negative optimization. This holds for NAS, containers, and network filesystems generally.

The fix target is *operation count*, not *operation scheduling* — see the per-file cost table above.

## How to reproduce the instrumentation

Patch `onBuildStats` in `dist/server-startup-post-attach-*.mjs` to also print (comma operator, one line, original trace unchanged):

```js
onBuildStats: (stats) => (console.error("MODELRUNTIME_BUILD_STATS " + JSON.stringify(stats)), params.startupTrace?.detail("sidecars.model-runtime-build", [ /* unchanged */ ]))
```

One startup then prints all 20 values to stderr.

## Observability gap (this cost is currently invisible)

`onBuildStats` computes all 20 metrics and then discards them into `startupTrace.detail`, which reaches the diagnostic events channel and never the log file. So a phase can burn 58 s of every startup and leave no trace in any log the operator can read.

**Suggestion:** emit these at debug level by default, or behind a verbose flag. They already exist — surfacing them would make the next occurrence diagnosable without patching the bundle. This issue took a plugin-tree audit and a bundle patch to attribute; with the numbers in the log it would have been one `grep`.

## Environment

- Gateway 2026.10.8 (dc2523e), Linux x64, Node 24.22.1, **Docker on Synology NAS**
- Plugin tree `~/.openclaw/npm/projects/`: 101 MB / 6 495 files / 603 dirs
- 3 agents, 12 plugins enabled, 21 configured runtime models
- Container: 5 GiB memory, 4 cores, no cgroup CPU limit
- Comparison instance (different host, same version): 885-file / 7.2 MB tree, `runtimePluginMs` 1 209 ms

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

With only official plugins loaded, an existing Slack conversation emits a no-final-summary fallback with "Codex settled-turn finalization context is unavailable", then delivers the successful native sessions_send peer completion.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Use official OpenClaw/Codex/Slack 2026.10.8 with only codex, openai and slack plugins loaded, as detailed below. Retain existing Executive and Commitment Assistant sessions.
2. Send a top-level Slack request asking the Executive to delegate using sessions_send mode followup, timeoutSeconds 0.
3. Instruct the specialist to return exactly COMMIT_R10_OK with no tool calls, service access, file or memory writes.
4. Ask the Executive to allow native delayed completion without polling, sleeping or sessions_yield, and give the final answer only after the actual result.
5. Observe accepted/pending admission, the harness finalization error and fallback, then the successful Executive answer.

The exact tested user request: "Synthetic finalization isolation test R10-20261028: ask the existing Commitment Assistant, using sessions_send mode followup and timeoutSeconds 0, to return exactly COMMIT_R10_OK without accessing any services, files, memory or Ninety. You may give brief progress, but do not give a final answer until its actual result returns. After acceptance finish the initiating turn without polling, sleeping or yielding; let native delayed completion continue the task. Then report R10_COMPLETE COMMIT_R10_OK exactly once."

### Expected behavior

An accepted peer request should receive an appropriate pending acknowledgement while outstanding, then its correlated final answer when the result is available, without a missing-summary failure intervening. A successful peer result awaiting dispatch should produce the final answer. Pending acknowledgements worked in official-only R11/R12 and native finalization produced a pending status in an earlier fresh-requester control. Preserve terminal errors for actual failures.

### Actual behavior

Official-only R10 timeline relative to accepted/pending admission:

+0.000s: sessions_send accepted; targetDisposition queued; delivery pending.
+3.054s: specialist COMMIT_R10_OK mirrored to the requester.
+5.768s: host fallback: "The tool run finished, but no final summary was produced. I did not repeat any completed actions."
+13.056s: Executive final R10_COMPLETE COMMIT_R10_OK delivered.

Here the fallback followed the peer result but preceded the final answer; it did not precede specialist completion. The final answer also encountered a separate Slack routing failure.

R9 reproduced both symptoms with only official plugins: fallback +3.391s, peer result +5.168s, final +9.951s after acceptance. R9 initially retried while a pre-existing local Codex server was down; it is excluded from clean latency comparisons. R10 was sent after model connectivity recovered.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.8 (openclaw, @openclaw/slack, @openclaw/codex; official npm packages, unmodified)

### Operating system

macOS arm64 (current host: 26.6.2, build 25G83); Node 24.22.1

### Install method

npm, exact pinned official packages; local development gateway

### Model

openai/gpt-6-sol; medium thinking

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw -> official @openclaw/codex harness -> configured local Unix Codex app-server 0.158.0 -> OpenAI

### Additional provider/model setup details

Isolation run on 2026-10-28: only official codex, openai and slack plugins loaded, confirmed by the running gateway configuration and plugin registry. All custom plugins, other channels, heartbeats and cron were disabled. Host tools were limited to sessions_send and message. Existing persistent peer sessions and workspaces were retained; these are not sessions_spawn children. Slack Socket Mode; replyToMode off globally and per channel, followup queue. Core, Slack and managed Codex package files matched integrity-pinned official npm tarballs; only the installation marker .openclaw-lifecycle-pending was absent. No package code was patched.

### Logs

```shell
[agent/embedded] settled post-tool turn lacked a final answer ... running isolated finalization
[agents/harness] Codex agent harness failed; not falling back to embedded OpenClaw backend ... error="Codex settled-turn finalization context is unavailable"
[agent/embedded] settled-turn finalization failed ... using terminal fallback reply
[agent:nested] session=agent:commitment-assistant:main ... COMMIT_R6_OK
[agents/agent-command] ... ended with stopReason=stop
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Executed official-only R10 delegation:

{"agentId":"commitment-assistant","mode":"followup","timeoutSeconds":0,"message":"Synthetic finalization isolation test R10-20261028. Return exactly COMMIT_R10_OK. Do not access any services, files, memory, or Ninety. Do not perform any other operations."}

The specialist retained its existing session ID and made zero tool calls. Exactly one R10 final marker was observed in captured Slack replies. Official-only controls R11 (deliberate thread) and R12 (main channel) produced initial pending acknowledgements and no missing-summary fallback; R12 still had the separate routing failure.

Earlier integration-enabled R6 reproduced the fallback before specialist completion. In R7 the executed timeoutSeconds 120 returned accepted/pending in about 0.1s and the fallback followed. This is not evidence that every positive wait fails.

### Impact and severity

Affected: our Slack Executive/specialist workflow. The error reproduced in two official-only existing-conversation requests, including R10 after model connectivity recovered. It was absent in official-only pending-acknowledgement controls R11/R12 and one earlier fresh Slack requester control. Users receive a missing-summary error before a successful final answer. This blocks acceptance of native deferred completion; no data loss is established.

### Additional information

Custom plugin execution has been ruled out as necessary for this reproduction. All custom plugins were disabled and the gateway/plugin registry confirmed only official codex, openai and slack loaded. Existing workspace instructions and conversation history were retained; the exact internal reason finalization context is missing remains unproven. No known-good release was established.

Fixes #181779 and #183077 are present in the tested 2026.10.8 packages. Fresh isolated internal-chat profiles with only official OpenAI/Codex completed a zero-wait peer exchange without fallback on both external Codex 0.158.0 and explicitly pinned local 0.160.0. Those controls omit Slack and historical conversation state; they do not establish a server upgrade as a fix. An earlier fresh Slack requester produced a proper native pending status once, although its delayed answer still misrouted. We are not claiming every zero-wait peer request fails.

All examples are synthetic; private messages, workspace/channel/user IDs, tokens and credentials are omitted. Reduced trace fields can be supplied on request.

issues.body:
### Summary

`docs/gateway/config-agents/models.md` states that nucleus sampling is a general per-model `params` contract:

> Nucleus sampling accepts `params.topP` or `params.top_p`. If both are present after config merging, `topP` wins; a per-request `topP` overrides either spelling. Provider-specific sampling restrictions still apply.

`temperature` from the same `params` block reaches every provider. `topP` does not: on `anthropic`, `anthropic-vertex`, and `bedrock` a configured value is silently dropped and the request runs with the provider default, with no warning and no error.

### Repro shape

These three request builders each assemble their sampling fields from an explicit list that omits nucleus sampling:

| Route | Builder | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic-messages` | `packages/ai/src/transports/anthropic-messages.ts` builds `params` from an explicit `Pick<MessageCreateParamsStreaming, "temperature" \| "stop_sequences" \| "tools" \| "output_config" \| "metadata" \| "tool_choice">` | `top_p` is never written |
| `anthropic-vertex` | `extensions/anthropic-vertex/stream-runtime.ts` copies `temperature`, `maxTokens`, `signal`, `cacheRetention`, `sessionId`, `headers`, `onPayload`, `onResponse`, `maxRetryDelayMs`, `metadata` into the shared Anthropic transport | `topP` is not copied, and the shared transport does not read it either |
| `bedrock-converse-stream` | `extensions/amazon-bedrock/stream.runtime.ts` builds `inferenceConfig` with only `maxTokens` and `temperature` | `inferenceConfig.topP` is never set, although the Bedrock SDK supports it (`InferenceConfiguration.topP`) |

For comparison, the routes that do forward it: `openai-completions` (`transports/openai-completions-params.ts`), `openai-responses` (`transports/openai-responses-params-internal.ts`), and Google after #190695.

### Root cause

`topP` is not part of the shared base projection. `SimpleStreamOptions` in `packages/llm-core/src/types.ts` has no `topP` field, and `buildBaseOptions` (`packages/ai/src/providers/simple-options.ts`) does not carry it. The only place it is normalized from config is `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/extra-params.ts`, which maps `top_p` -> `topP` onto the stream options record.

Each provider therefore has to read it back out itself, and #190695 documents that intent in code:

> // Nucleus sampling is a Google call option, not part of the shared base projection.

So this is arguably by design per-route rather than a single dropped field — which is why it is filed for a scope decision rather than sent as a patch.

### Two candidate directions

1. **Complete the contract**: forward `topP` from the three missing routes. For `anthropic`/`anthropic-vertex` this needs to respect the existing model restriction: the SDK marks `top_p` deprecated for models after Claude Opus 4.6 ("A value >= 0.99 will be accepted for backwards compatibility, all other values will be rejected with a 400 error"), and `applyClaudeRequestContract` already has a `delete params.top_p` branch for those models that currently never fires because nothing writes the field. A naive fix would forward a value that the API rejects with 400 for current Claude models, so the route needs the same suppression predicate that already strips `temperature`.
2. **Narrow the contract**: state in `models.md` which routes honor `params.topP` and which accept it silently, so operators are not led to believe a configured value is applied on Anthropic or Bedrock.

### Impact

Operators who set `agents.defaults.models["anthropic/claude-*"].params.topP` or the `top_p` spelling, or the Bedrock equivalent, get no effect and no signal. `temperature` from the identical block is applied, so the two settings behave inconsistently for what the docs present as one contract.

### Not investigated

- Whether any Bedrock model family rejects `topP` in `inferenceConfig` (the field is in the shared inference config, and model-specific acceptance was not exercised).
- Behavior on Bedrock Mantle, which has a separate credential path.
- No request-capture proof was run for these three routes; the findings above come from reading the request builders and comparing them with the routes that do forward the field.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

With the default group mention requirement, the WhatsApp self-number fallback in `isBotMentionedFromTargets` strips every non-digit character from the whole message body and then checks whether the bot's E.164 digits appear anywhere in that digit string. Digits from unrelated numbers (times, room numbers, extensions, order and invoice ids, numeric ids in URLs) are concatenated before the check, so a message that never contains the bot's number is treated as a mention and the bot replies in the group without being addressed.

Reproduces on v2026.8.2 and on `main` at cf59ce40 (2026-09-02); `extensions/whatsapp/src/auto-reply/mentions.ts` lines 92-105 are byte-identical in both. 

Code (`extensions/whatsapp/src/auto-reply/mentions.ts:94-99`):

```ts
const selfDigits = targets.self.e164.replace(/\D/g, "");
if (selfDigits) {
  const bodyDigits = bodyClean.replace(/[^\d]/g, "");
  if (bodyDigits.includes(selfDigits)) {
    return true;
  }
```

The narrower check two lines later (strip whitespace and hyphens, then match `\+?<digits>`) expresses the intended semantics, but the loose check runs first and returns before it is reached.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure a WhatsApp account whose number is +1 555 123 4567 in a group with the default `requireMention` (no `mentionPatterns`, no `groups.*.requireMention: false`).
2. As an admitted group member, send a plain text message with no @-mention: `Meeting at 15:55, room 123, ext 4567`.
3. Observe the bot reply.

Deterministic unit-level reproduction against the production function (add next to `web-auto-reply-utils.test.ts` and run with `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`):

```ts
const msg = makeMsg({
  body: "Meeting at 15:55, room 123, ext 4567",
  selfE164: "+15551234567",
  selfJid: "15551234567@s.whatsapp.net",
});
expect(debugMention(msg, { mentionRegexes: [] }).wasMentioned).toBe(false); // actual: true
```

The same happens end to end through `applyGroupGating` (`extensions/whatsapp/src/auto-reply/monitor/group-gating.ts:217`): `shouldProcess=true`, `groupMention={wasMentioned:true, requireMention:true}` for that body, while `Meeting at 10:30, room 42, ext 9999` is correctly held back.

### Expected behavior

Only a contiguous rendering of the bot's number should count as a mention: `15551234567`, `+1 555 123 4567`, `+1-555-123-4567`, `+1 (555) 123-4567`, `1.555.123.4567`. Digits scattered across unrelated numbers should not, and the number appearing inside a longer number (`invoice 9915551234567001`) should not either.

### Actual behavior

Any message whose concatenated digit stream contains the bot's digits is treated as a mention. The bot replies uninvited, consuming a model turn and revealing its presence in the group.

### OpenClaw version

v2026.8.2 (release commit 0965053f) and `main` at cf59ce40 (2026-09-02). Introduced with the fallback itself in 7ea43b014 (2025-12-03); the code has never changed since.

### Operating system

Any

### Install method

N/A

### Model

N/A

### Provider / routing chain

N/A

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell

```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Over-triggering only. The sender must already pass the group allowlist before mention gating runs, so this is not an access bypass. Accidental hits on ordinary chatter are rare because the full 11-13 digit sequence must appear in order; realistic triggers are long numeric identifiers and pasted URLs. Low severity, but the fix is small, fully tested, and removes a class of surprise replies.

### Additional information

- `docs/channels/group-messages.md` describes the fallback as "the bot's E.164 digits anywhere in the text", which reads as the number appearing in the text, not digits assembled from unrelated numbers.
- Fix PR: replaces the two checks with a single boundary-anchored match over a body with phone punctuation stripped; adds three regression tests; all 12 mention tests pass.

issues.body:
## Describe the bug

With `tools.toolSearch: true` enabled, when a configured MCP server (e.g. `memos`, streamable-http) becomes unreachable and its tools disappear from the tool-search catalog, the agent repeatedly searches the catalog for those tools and never finds them. Instead of failing fast (or reporting that the tool is unavailable), it keeps re-issuing tool-search queries and stalls the whole turn.

## To Reproduce

1. Enable `tools.toolSearch: true`.
2. Have a configured MCP server that exposes several tools (e.g. `memos` over streamable-http).
3. Stop that MCP server so its tools drop out of the tool-search catalog.
4. Ask the agent to do something that requires one of those tools.

## Expected behavior

The agent should get a clear "tool not found / MCP server disconnected" signal (or otherwise fall back gracefully), so it can surface the outage and stop instead of looping.

## Actual behavior

The agent repeatedly runs tool-search queries for the missing tool, gets no matching results, and keeps retrying — a live-loop that burns turns/tokens and blocks the task. No error or "server disconnected" hint is surfaced to the model.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.8.1 (ea80657)
- OS: Linux (WSL2), node v24.15.0
- MCP server involved: `memos` (streamable-http), was down during the incident

## Additional context

Turning `tools.toolSearch` off immediately restores normal direct tool invocation. The same outage *without* `toolSearch` enabled just surfaces as an unavailable tool rather than a loop. So the loop behavior is specific to the tool-search bridge when a tool disappears mid-session.

issues.body:
## Environment

OpenClaw 2026.8.2 (0965053), updated from 2026.8.1 (ea80657) on 2026-09-02 with a byte-identical config
macOS on Mac mini M4 (arm64), Node v26.3.1, npm -g install
10 agents, ~100 cron jobs, Telegram channels, local model servers (OpenAI-compatible) + OpenRouter
Gateway bind loopback, Tailscale serve, token auth

## Summary

After updating 2026.8.1 (ea80657) to 2026.8.2 (0965053) with a byte-identical config, every heartbeat job on 10 agents ends with `cron: job execution timed out` (600 s). Under 2026.8.1 the same jobs completed with `ok` receipts.

What the gateway logs every 30 s while a heartbeat is running:

```
stalled session: sessionKey=agent:<id>:main state=processing age=5xx s queueDepth=0
reason=active_work_without_progress classification=stalled_agent_run activeWorkKind=model_call
lastProgress=model_call:stream_progress lastProgressAge=5xx s lastAssistant="<complete final answer>" recovery=none
```

The heartbeat's work is done (`lastAssistant` holds a complete final message such as "HEARTBEAT.md updated. All checks within policy"), but the model call is never marked complete, so the run waits until the cron timeout kills it.

## Reproduction across providers

Reproduced on three providers: a local OpenAI-compatible server (mtplx), a local proxy (morpheus-node / deepseek-v4-flash), and OpenRouter (openai/gpt-oss-20b). The OpenRouter model completes agentTurn cron runs on the same gateway in 5-12 s, and a probe that moved one agent's heartbeat to it stalled for the full 600 s as well. A few runs eventually finished on their own at 119-562 s. Regular agentTurn and command cron jobs are unaffected throughout.

Heartbeat config shape on all agents: `target: "none"`, `lightContext: true`, a custom prompt that asks the model to read HEARTBEAT.md and reply through `heartbeat_respond`.

## Evidence

Stalled-session log blocks for two agents (2026-09-02, gateway log):

```
stalled session: sessionId=91d91075-... sessionKey=agent:nexus:main state=processing age=1139s queueDepth=0
reason=active_work_without_progress classification=stalled_agent_run activeWorkKind=model_call
lastProgress=model_call:stream_progress lastProgressAge=381s
lastAssistant="HEARTBEAT.md updated. No new cliff (disk 95%→94%, favorable dip within the already-alerted band;" [complete final answer]

stalled session: sessionId=988dccd6-... sessionKey=agent:intern:main state=processing age=380s queueDepth=0
reason=active_work_without_progress classification=stalled_agent_run activeWorkKind=model_call
lastProgress=model_call:stream_progress lastProgressAge=379s
lastAssistant="HEARTBEAT.md contains only comments and no configured periodic tasks — nothing to check, nothing [complete final answer]"
```

Heartbeat cron receipts from the store (all 10 agents; excerpt):

```
agent  status      error                             started (local)
dev    error       cron: job execution timed out     2026-09-02 10:38:09
pro    error       cron: job execution timed out     2026-09-02 10:38:14
intern error       cron: job execution timed out     2026-09-02 10:38:20
butler error       cron: job execution timed out     2026-09-02 10:38:24
ira    error       cron: job execution timed out     2026-09-02 10:38:30
rexy   error       cron: job execution timed out     2026-09-02 10:38:34
spine  error       cron: job execution timed out     2026-09-02 10:38:34
main   error       cron: job execution timed out     2026-09-02 10:49:05
... (mass timeouts on every agent from 10:38 onward; a handful of earlier ok receipts at 10:01-10:08)
```

OpenRouter probe receipt (heartbeat.model moved to openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-20b; the same model completed agentTurn crons on this gateway in 5-12 s):

```
status=error  error="cron: job execution timed out"  started=2026-09-02 14:58:24  finished=2026-09-02 15:08:24
```

Same job under 2026.8.1 (before the update, byte-identical config):

```
intern  ok  2026-09-02 09:56:09
coo     ok  2026-09-02 09:52:22
main    ok  2026-09-02 09:50:34
```

Side effect — each stalled run pins a local model server for up to 900 s:

```
lane task error: lane=session:agent:intern:main durationMs=904489 error="⚠️ mtplx/qwen3.8-27b-abliterated-mtplx request failed."
```

With 6-10 of them in flight this drove a machine-wide memory-pressure and swap loop (swap 8 GB to 22 GB, free disk 43 GB to 19 GB) until heartbeats were disabled with `every: "0m"`.

## Two smaller observations

1. An agent whose HEARTBEAT.md contains only comments no longer skips the model call (one agent ran 562 s on a comments-only file); 2026.8.1 documented that case as a skip.
2. The new fallback text "The tool run finished, but no final summary was produced. I did not repeat any completed actions." is delivered to the cron's announce target; small models trigger it on nearly every run, which turns an announce-mode job into a notification flood.

## Expected behavior

A heartbeat run completes when the model's final message arrives, as agentTurn runs do; a comments-only HEARTBEAT.md still skips.

**Ask:** is there a heartbeat "settle" condition in 2026.8.2 that `target: "none"` together with a `heartbeat_respond` reply never satisfies? If so, what shape is expected, and can the run be closed on the final assistant message regardless?
