labels.name: issue-rating: 🦞 diamond lobster
labels.description: Very strong issue quality with high-confidence source-level or clear reproduction.

issues.body:
### What happened

When a WhatsApp send is interrupted after the platform attempt has started — a listener drop, a
gateway restart, or an event-loop stall — the delivery entry lands in `send_attempt_started` and
is then **permanently unrecoverable**. Recovery refuses to replay it, no reconciliation can
resolve it, and the user-visible reply is silently lost.

Log line, repeated on every drain cycle:

```
Delivery entry <id> delivery state is send_attempt_started;
  refusing blind replay without adapter reconciliation
WhatsApp periodic drain: retry failed for entry <id>: delivery state is
  send_attempt_started; refusing blind replay without adapter reconciliation
```

Observed over two days on a gateway hosting six WhatsApp accounts:

- **6 distinct delivery entries** wedged, every one in `send_attempt_started`
- one entry refused repeatedly across roughly **4 hours** (first refusal 05:56:55, still being
  refused at 09:53:40) before ageing out
- another accumulated **16 refusals in 22 minutes**
- **39 occurrences** of `No active WhatsApp Web listener (account: <id>)` in the same window —
  sends attempted while the listener was down

### Why

This is not a missing queue. `src/infra/outbound/delivery-queue-recovery.ts` is careful and has
the right shape already — it replays when reconciliation proves the send did not happen:

```ts
const reconciliationProvedPreSendFailure =
  reconciliation?.status === "not_sent" && entry.recoveryState === "send_attempt_started";
if (reconciliationProvedPreSendFailure) {
  opts.log.info(
    `Delivery entry ${entry.id} reconciled ${entry.recoveryState} as not sent; replaying`,
  );
} else {
  let errMsg = `delivery state is ${entry.recoveryState}; refusing blind replay without adapter reconciliation`;
  ...
}
```

It also has an unresolved-but-retryable branch and a `not_sent` post-send-evidence branch. All
three depend on the channel adapter supplying a reconciliation result.

**The WhatsApp adapter does not implement that hook.** `reconcileUnknownSend` is implemented by:

- `extensions/matrix/src/channel-message-adapter.ts`
- `extensions/slack/src/channel.ts`
- `extensions/clickclack/src/channel.ts`

and there is no WhatsApp equivalent. Because `reconciliation` is absent rather than
`not_sent` / `unresolved`, control always falls to the bare `refusing blind replay without
adapter reconciliation` branch — the error string in our logs is exactly that variant, never the
`not_sent` or `unresolved` wording. The entry is marked durably failed and the message is
dropped.

The refusal itself is correct behaviour: replaying blindly risks duplicate delivery. The gap is
that WhatsApp can never provide the evidence needed to make the safe decision, so the
conservative path is the *only* path.

### Impact

Silent loss of user-visible replies, precisely when the system is already degraded. The
triggering conditions are common rather than exotic:

- an event-loop stall long enough to drop the socket mid-send (we separately measured multi-second
  stalls from synchronous corpus enumeration — see #130014)
- `openclaw channels login` restarting the gateway, which bounces every account's listener
- any transient 408/428 closure landing between attempt-start and receipt

There is no operator-visible signal that a reply was lost. The only trace is a `warn` line that
repeats on each drain cycle, and there is no dead-letter surface to inspect or replay from.

### Version

`OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)`, Node 24.15.0, Windows 11.

### Reproduction

1. Send an outbound WhatsApp message and interrupt the process (or drop the listener) after the
   platform attempt has started but before the receipt is recorded.
2. Restart and let the periodic drain run.
3. The entry logs `refusing blind replay without adapter reconciliation` on every cycle and is
   never delivered.

Easiest natural trigger: run `openclaw channels login --channel whatsapp --account <id>` while
another account has a send in flight. The login restarts the gateway and bounces all listeners.

### Suggested direction

1. **Implement `reconcileUnknownSend` for the WhatsApp channel.** Baileys exposes message
   receipts and the send key, so an attempt-scoped lookup should be able to answer sent /
   not_sent / unresolved for a recent attempt, which is all the recovery path needs.
2. **Failing that, give unreconcilable entries a terminal, visible state** — a dead-letter
   surface with a count, so an operator can see that N replies were dropped rather than only a
   repeating `warn`. Related: `delivery-queue-recovery.ts` already comments that recovery "must
   not leave a dead-lettered delivery permanently replayable", so the concept exists.
3. **Consider suppressing the send attempt entirely when the listener is known inactive**, so the
   entry never reaches `send_attempt_started` and stays cleanly replayable. The 39
   `No active WhatsApp Web listener` occurrences suggest sends are being attempted against a
   listener the runtime already knows is down.

Happy to test a patch and report whether the wedged-entry count goes to zero.

labels.description: Very strong issue quality with high-confidence source-level or clear reproduction.

issues.body:
## Environment

- Originally hit on openclaw 2026.6.33 (extended-stable) with `@openclaw/matrix`
  2026.6.33 (version-matched). Still current on **2026.6.34 / matrix 2026.6.34**:
  I diffed the 6.33→6.34 delta (38 commits, 446 files) and **nothing touches crypto
  locks, snapshots or E2EE outside the QA harness**, so the mechanism below is
  unchanged. 6.34's channel-health work (`channel-health-monitor.ts` finishing a
  timed-out recovery, `channel-health-policy.ts` adding `activeRunStartedAt`) improves
  post-timeout RESTART, but does not address the leaked lock and does not help the
  "reports healthy while unable to decrypt" symptom — that new policy branch keys on
  `snapshot.connected === false`, and an affected account reports connected.
- Node in the official gateway image; Synology DSM host, 4 Matrix accounts
  (1 default + 3 named), all E2EE, all on matrix.org
- Crypto state at `~/.openclaw/matrix/accounts/<account>/<hs>__<user>/<hash>/`

## Summary

When a Matrix channel exceeds its 5s stop abort window, it is force-killed while
holding the lock on `crypto-idb-snapshot.json`. The lock file is left behind with
**no snapshot file beside it**. Every subsequent start then fails to restore the
Rust crypto store for that account:

```
[IdbPersistence] Failed to restore IndexedDB snapshot .../crypto-idb-snapshot.json:
  Error: file lock timeout for .../crypto-idb-snapshot.json.lock
```

The account still connects, still syncs, still sends. It simply cannot decrypt
inbound messages:

```
DecryptionError[msg: The sender's device has not sent us the keys for this message.]
```

**Nothing surfaces this.** `openclaw channels status` reports the account
`connected, healthy` throughout. The one diagnostic line appears once, unflagged,
among thousands of routine log lines. From the user's side the bot is simply mute.

## Impact

Three of four bots stopped answering DMs for ~2 hours. Silent to senders and to
every health check; the only detector was a human noticing. Recovery required
reading container logs closely enough to spot a single `file lock timeout` line.

Worse, the failure is **latched**: it persists across restarts, because each new
start hits the same orphaned lock. A clean `docker compose stop -t 90` + cold start
does not clear it (the 5s abort is internal to the plugin, so Docker's grace period
never applies).

## Reproduction

1. Run a gateway with several Matrix accounts, E2EE enabled.
2. Trigger a channel restart — a config hot-reload of any `channels.matrix.*` key
   is enough. Ours was `channels.matrix.accounts.<id>.dm.allowFrom`.
3. Observe on the affected accounts:
   ```
   [matrix] [<account>] channel stop exceeded 5000ms after abort; continuing shutdown
   ```
4. Inspect the account state dirs:
   ```sh
   find ~/.openclaw/matrix/accounts -name 'crypto-idb-snapshot.json.lock'
   ```
   A `.lock` with no `crypto-idb-snapshot.json` beside it is orphaned.
5. DM the bot. It never replies; the gateway logs the DecryptionError above while
   `channels status` still shows the account healthy.

## The account split is the useful clue

In our fleet the **default** account stops cleanly and was never affected. All three
**named** accounts logged the 5s abort and all three orphaned a lock, at the same
timestamp to the nanosecond:

```
17:52:05.6551513310  0 bytes  accounts/darcy/.../crypto-idb-snapshot.json.lock
17:52:05.6551513310  0 bytes  accounts/hal/.../crypto-idb-snapshot.json.lock
17:52:05.6551513310  0 bytes  accounts/demerzel/.../crypto-idb-snapshot.json.lock
```

"Only the default account works" was the fingerprint that eventually identified this.
Why named accounts fail to stop in time and `default` does not is the part we could
not determine from outside the plugin.

Store size does not explain it — the unaffected default account has the **largest**
crypto store (1.68 MB vs 1.15–1.44 MB).

## Fix applied locally

Stop the fleet, move the orphaned locks aside, start it. Two of three accounts
recovered fully and immediately.

## Suggested fixes, in preference order

1. **Clear stale locks at startup.** A `.lock` with no snapshot beside it cannot be
   held by a live process across a start; treat it as stale and remove it.
2. **Make the lock self-describing** — write pid/boot-id/timestamp into it, so
   staleness is decidable rather than inferred. It is currently zero bytes.
3. **Release the lock on the abort path**, so a force-killed channel doesn't leak it.
4. **Fail loudly.** An account that cannot restore its crypto store must not report
   `connected, healthy`. This is the part that turned a small bug into a 2-hour
   outage and four wrong diagnoses.

(1) and (4) would each independently have prevented this.

## Note on a near miss

We first suspected #90455 (fake-indexeddb retaining transactions, explicitly worse
with multiple accounts) as the reason stop exceeds 5s. That fix is in v2026.6.11 and
we run 2026.6.33, so it is ruled out here — but a similar store-bloat mechanism
remains a plausible cause of the slow stop, and may be worth checking on the
multi-account path specifically.

issues.body:
Contributor proposal. Maintainer alignment is **pending**. This issue describes
a capability map and possible landing sequence; it is not an accepted OpenClaw
roadmap or release commitment.

Canonical-issue check (2026-08-25): the focused searches recorded under
Evidence returned no matching OpenClaw issue or PR for room-scoped Buzz sender
policy, passive unmentioned context, Buzz DMs, Buzz bot loop protection, or
Buzz reactions/media. This is an observation, not proof of permanent absence;
repeat the searches immediately before publication. Related threading and
multi-account issues are listed below and remain separate.

## Summary

Bring the OpenClaw Buzz channel closer to the capabilities users expect from a first-class team assistant: room-scoped activation policy, direct messages, reactions and attachments, passive bounded context for unmentioned room traffic, and explicit protection against bot-to-bot reply loops.

## Problem to solve

The current Buzz channel is already strong at identity, relay authentication, room membership, native mentions, threads, replay/catch-up, presence, typing, directory publication, and room-based OpenClaw routing. Its remaining gaps become visible when the same personal agent participates in several rooms or collaborates with other agents:

1. `groupPolicy` and `groupAllowFrom` apply to the whole Buzz account. Individual room entries can only set `enabled` and `requireMention`, so one room cannot be restricted to the owner while another also permits a named collaborator or bot.
2. The plugin advertises group chat only. OpenClaw's own Buzz documentation already lists direct messages as planned work, but the current adapter does not discover, route, or expose them as direct conversations.
3. The same official roadmap already lists reactions and media. The current OpenClaw adapter still exposes text and typing only.
4. Messages rejected by the mention gate are not retained as bounded room context. The agent must either process every message or remain unaware of the conversation until explicitly called.
5. Membership exposes human/bot roles, but the inbound policy does not use them. Two bots can create an unbounded sequence of fresh replies even though OpenClaw already has reusable `allowBots` and pair-loop-guard contracts in other channels.

This is not a request to replace the Buzz channel with a Buzz-managed ACP agent. The desired architecture keeps the main OpenClaw identity and lifecycle in OpenClaw while using Buzz as a channel.

## Proposed direction for maintainer feedback

This contributor proposal asks maintainers to decide four ownership and product
boundaries. It is not an accepted roadmap, implementation checklist, or
commitment to land every capability. A capability receives a separate issue
only after its boundary and owner are accepted.

Possible independent slices after those decisions include:

- **Room-scoped sender policy**
   - Extend `channels.buzz.groups.<room UUID>` with partial overrides for sender policy and sender allowlist.
   - Resolve each field as exact-room override → existing account value.
   - Preserve all existing configurations and defaults.

- **Bot-aware activation and bounded loops**
   - Reuse the public Plugin SDK `allowBots` and `botLoopProtection` contracts already used by ClickClack.
   - Resolve bot or human role only from a validated room-membership record
     whose trusted issuer, signature verification, room binding, freshness,
     and revocation semantics are established by Buzz.
   - Treat role only as classification. Evaluate sender authorization
     separately; a valid bot role never grants permission to activate an agent.
   - Preserve legacy behavior when the new fields are absent; only an explicit policy changes bot-authored admission.

- **Stable inbound-turn lifecycle**
   - If channel-framework maintainers request it, move Buzz inbound processing onto the current channel-turn runner without changing observable behavior.
   - Keep native mention, command authorization, session routing, reply/thread routing, typing, and session recording unchanged.

- **Passive bounded context**
   - Add an explicit per-room option such as `observeUnmentioned`.
   - Authorized, unmentioned messages are recorded into bounded room/thread history without invoking the model or producing a reply.
   - Do not map this directly to the current `observeOnly` lifecycle result: current source uses that result for inference without a visible reply. Reuse an existing no-inference dropped-history path if maintainers identify one; otherwise this remains a channel-framework contract decision.
   - Mentioned messages continue to dispatch normally and receive the bounded prior context.

- **Direct messages**
   - Discover Buzz channels marked `t=dm` for the current identity.
   - Route them as `peer.kind=direct`, expose `chatTypes: ["direct", "group"]`, and apply explicit DM authorization semantics.
   - Reuse protocol edge cases already exercised by the Hermes Buzz adapter, including DM discovery when `dms list` is incomplete, while retaining OpenClaw's own direct-peer routing and authorization owners.
   - Preserve reply/session routing without applying group-only overrides to DMs.

- **Reactions**
   - Parse inbound NIP-25 kind-7 reactions as non-turn events or bounded system context.
   - Add guarded outbound reaction actions scoped to the authorized Buzz conversation and target event. Removal may affect only a reaction authored by the same agent identity, matched by author, target, and emoji.
   - Follow the existing OpenClaw channel-action contract; use Hermes only as evidence that Buzz kind-7 transport works, not as the owner of OpenClaw action semantics.

- **Attachments/media**
   - Parse and expose Buzz `imeta` attachment metadata on inbound messages.
   - Add bounded outbound upload support through the authenticated Buzz upload endpoint and emit NIP-92-compatible `imeta` tags.
   - Reuse the existing safe media-fetch/upload owner and enforce type, size, MIME sniffing, redirects, private-address/DNS-rebinding, credential-leakage, URL, and conversation-boundary checks.
   - Hermes' tested local-file upload and URL delivery are useful Buzz interoperability evidence, but OpenClaw should retain its own media security and credential boundaries rather than copying the Hermes transport architecture.

## Alternatives considered

- **Run the main OpenClaw agent as a Buzz-managed ACP runtime.** This loses the chosen architecture: the agent identity and lifecycle would belong to Buzz Desktop rather than the existing OpenClaw main agent.
- **Use prompt instructions to prevent ping-pong.** Helpful as a behavioral hint, but not a hard runtime bound and not sufficient for collaborating autonomous agents.
- **Make all rooms open and rely only on mentions.** A mention identifies the target; it does not authorize the sender. This cannot express private-assistant policy.
- **Put everything in one PR.** It would mix config migration, ingress lifecycle, protocol coverage, media security, and product semantics, making review and rollback unnecessarily risky.
- **Create a new Buzz-only core API.** Reuse the current public ingress, dropped-history, bot-policy, and loop-guard seams wherever they satisfy the exact contract. Request a new core surface only if the no-inference history requirement cannot be expressed safely with those public seams.

## Impact

- **Affected users:** OpenClaw users connecting a persistent personal/team agent to Buzz, especially multi-room and multi-agent setups.
- **Severity:** medium for basic chat; high for private-assistant and agent-coordination workflows because current global policy either over-authorizes callers or prevents legitimate collaboration.
- **Frequency:** every inbound Buzz message in a configured room; loop risk appears whenever agents can mention one another.
- **Consequence:** duplicated configurations, missing context, unavailable DMs/rich messages, and the possibility of unnecessary model/tool work from bot reply loops.

## Evidence/examples

Source-inspection status: `code_proven` for the bounded claims below at OpenClaw
`888c8422013e13023164c62d734f31ebb54ff572` and Buzz
`f24971033178926153b49d320bd876d15d9cb2bf`.

- `extensions/buzz/src/config-schema.ts`: room entries contain only `enabled` and `requireMention`; sender policy is account-wide.
- `extensions/buzz/src/channel.ts`: Buzz advertises `chatTypes: ["group"]`.
- `extensions/buzz/src/buzz-bus.ts`: the transport surface exposes text and typing, not reactions or media.
- `extensions/buzz/src/inbound.ts`: a non-dispatch ingress result returns before any bounded history is recorded.
- `extensions/buzz/src/directory-state.ts`: relay-signed room membership roles are already available and can distinguish `bot` from human roles.
- `src/channels/turn/execution.ts` and `src/channels/turn/lifecycle.ts`: current `observeOnly` performs inference without a visible reply, so it is not proof of a no-inference passive-history path.
- ClickClack already provides a public-SDK precedent for per-room `allowBots` and `botLoopProtection` resolution.
- Buzz protocol source defines DM channels through `t=dm`, reactions as NIP-25 kind 7, and attachments as NIP-92 `imeta` tags.
- `docs/channels/buzz.md`: DMs, reactions, and media are already listed as planned work; this proposal requests owner alignment and prioritization rather than claiming a new roadmap.
- Hermes Agent `0.20.5` at `b0cf2597c2dbb9dacd5c4f063ae7e71587f02c2e`
  provides an independent Buzz adapter precedent for DM discovery, threaded
  replies, reactions, images, NIP-42 WebSocket ingress with polling fallback,
  and a relay+pubkey scoped identity lock. Its adapter/tests are protocol and
  interoperability evidence, not OpenClaw product authority or code to copy.

Duplicate-search provenance on 2026-08-25, repository
`openclaw/openclaw`, best-match, top 20:

- Issues: `Buzz room policy sender allowlist`; `Buzz observe unmentioned
  passive context`; `Buzz direct messages DM channel`; `Buzz bot loop
  protection allowBots`; `Buzz reactions media attachments`.
- PRs: `buzz room policy allowlist`; `buzz observe unmentioned`; `buzz direct
  message`; `buzz allowBots loop protection`; `buzz reactions media
  attachment`.
- Publication gate: repeat all searches and record the observation timestamp
  and current repository heads.

Related existing issues, deliberately not duplicated by this proposal:

- [#120339 — no way to disable reply threading](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/120339)
- [#124873 — replies nest progressively inside existing threads](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/124873)
- [#123200 — no multi-account support](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/123200)

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance. I can implement the first accepted narrow
slice and provide focused tests plus a redacted Buzz relay smoke. I do not plan
to open all child issues or PRs until maintainers confirm the ownership and
product semantics below.

## Additional information

### Non-goals

- Replacing the OpenClaw main agent with a Buzz-managed ACP agent.
- Solving Buzz multi-account support, reply mode, or progressive nesting in this issue.
- Publishing a fake Buzz managed-agent policy or Desktop-owned record for an external OpenClaw identity.
- Weakening relay membership, sender authorization, media validation, or conversation-boundary checks.
- Adding a new Plugin SDK contract unless implementation proves the existing public seams insufficient.

### Compatibility constraints

- Existing `channels.buzz` configurations must remain valid and preserve behavior.
- Group-only settings must never affect direct messages.
- Bot/human classification must use a validated room-membership record with
  proven issuer authority, signature, room binding, freshness, and revocation
  semantics. Mutable profile data is never role authority.
- Role classification and sender authorization remain separate decisions.
- Passive bounded context must not invoke the model, execute tools, send typing, or emit a reply. The current `observeOnly` result does not satisfy that contract.
- Media and reaction actions must be bound to the authorized conversation and target event.

### Maintainer decisions requested

1. Is a room-level partial override of the existing account sender policy the
   preferred compatibility shape?
2. Which Buzz issuer and validation path authoritatively establishes room roles,
   and should an undefined `allowBots` preserve current Buzz behavior?
3. Is there an existing public no-inference dropped-history path for passive
   Buzz context, and do maintainers explicitly want the stable channel-turn
   refactor required to reach it?
4. Should DMs, reactions, and media remain separate capability issues after the
   policy/lifecycle work, or is there an existing owner/roadmap they should join?

### Possible independent slices after maintainer decisions

These are candidate slices, not accepted backlog items. Create only the next
maintainer-approved issue. DMs, reactions, and media remain independent
capability proposals and are not implied deliverables of this issue.

- Buzz: room-scoped sender policy overrides.
- Buzz: bot-aware activation and pair loop protection.
- Buzz: migrate inbound processing to the stable channel-turn lifecycle.
- Buzz: observe unmentioned room messages as bounded context without dispatch.
- Buzz: direct-message support.
- Buzz: native reactions.
- Buzz: media and attachment support.

### Ownership map

- `extensions/buzz/**` config, ingress, directory, and transport changes:
  OpenClaw Buzz channel owners/reviewers.
- shared channel-turn, bot policy, and action contracts: OpenClaw channel
  framework owners; reuse public Plugin SDK contracts before requesting core
  changes.
- Membership authority is shared: Buzz owns issuer, signature, room binding,
  freshness, and revocation semantics; OpenClaw owns fail-closed validation,
  cache/replay behavior, and enforcement in the adapter.
- `t=dm`, NIP-25 kind 7, NIP-92 `imeta`, and authenticated upload protocol:
  existing Buzz protocol owned by `block/buzz`; OpenClaw channel owners own the
  safe adapter and action boundaries.
- Operator-specific agent names, pubkeys, room names, and personal allowlists:
  local configuration, inappropriate for upstream.

Close this umbrella only when the requested boundary decisions are recorded or
rejected. Child PRs do not close it.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Summary

Gateway on macOS (LaunchDaemon-supervised, single stable process) stopped servicing `accept()` on its main port for ~19 hours while remaining otherwise fully alive (crons firing, model-fetch calls completing 200, RPC on a co-located sidecar port unaffected). This reproduces the failure class in #56215 / #101540 with a full evidence chain and a confirmed root cause: the never-merged keepalive fix in #91466.

### Steps to reproduce

Not yet a clean minimal repro — this is a production incident writeup with full forensic evidence. Reproduction hypothesis (matches #101540's original report and the #91466 PR description):

1. Run the gateway with `gateway.keepalive` unset (its default state on any release that predates #91466 — the config key does not exist at all pre-merge).
2. Let a long-lived local client hold a websocket connection to the gateway's client port and then go half-open (process suspend, network partition, or a slow/blocked consumer that stops reading) without a clean close handshake.
3. Because there is no server-side ping/pong keepalive with a close-on-timeout, the socket is never closed by the gateway. It (and its accept-queue slot) linger until the OS-level TCP timeout, which on macOS can be many hours.
4. Repeat/accumulate until the listen backlog (`kern.ipc.somaxconn`, default 128) is fully occupied by dead half-open sockets that were never drained — new connections then queue forever and time out, while the process itself remains fully responsive on every other code path.

### Actual behavior (production incident, full forensics)

- **Onset:** 2026-08-23 22:23:06.994 local (03:23:06.994Z) — first `GatewayTransportError: gateway closed (1006 abnormal closure (no close frame))` from a local loopback client dialing `ws://127.0.0.1:18789`.
- **Immediately preceding onset:** a model-fetch response to the upstream LLM provider took `elapsedMs=8578` (vs. a steady ~1.3-1.8s baseline in the same log window) — consistent with, though not proven to cause, whatever event-loop/socket-table disruption tipped the gateway into this state.
- **During the outage (confirmed by direct inspection, not by the affected process's own self-report):**
  - Kernel accept queue pinned at exactly `kern.ipc.somaxconn = 128` — 115 `CLOSE_WAIT` + 13 `ESTABLISHED`, frozen across a 60-second sample, not one socket draining.
  - `lsof` showed the gateway holding only the `LISTEN` fd and none of the 128 queued sockets — they were never accepted.
  - 8/8 fresh TCP connects to the loopback port timed out; a co-located sidecar bridge on a different port answered normally (401, 1.2ms) on the same loopback in the same window — ruling out host-level network/socket-table exhaustion.
  - The process itself was fully alive throughout: scheduled jobs kept firing, model-fetch calls kept completing with 200s, fd count was ~84/256 (no `EMFILE`).
  - All 128 queued connections originated from a single peer (our own polling client), consistent with one client retrying every ~12s against a port that had stopped accepting, not a flood.
  - The `1006` error repeated at ~5/minute for the full ~19h window (2,982+ entries, matching a retrying local client's own reconnect cadence, not gateway-side batching).
- **Resolution:** `sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/ai.openclaw.gateway` (2026-08-24 16:14:16 local / 21:14:16Z). New pid came up, `/health` returned 200 within seconds (first successful loopback connect in ~19h), accept queue drained immediately to normal churn (1-2 `CLOSE_WAIT`, 10 `TIME_WAIT`), and the `1006` rate went from steady 5/min to exactly zero, 1 second after the new listener bound.
- **No internal diagnostic fired.** `~/.openclaw/logs/stability/` has zero stability bundles for the entire incident window — this failure mode produced no `gateway.*` reason code and no self-detected pressure/health event. The only detection was an operator noticing an unrelated sidecar's polling logs.

### Expected behavior

Either (a) the gateway should never let a client's dead socket occupy an accept-queue/backlog slot indefinitely, or (b) if that is architecturally unavoidable without a keepalive, the gateway's own health/readiness diagnostics should detect and report "listener socket accepting connections" as a distinct, testable condition from "process alive" / "RPC on sidecar port working" — the current health surface make an accept()-level stall invisible from both inside (`openclaw doctor`, stability bundles) and outside (dependent services that only check a sidecar or the process table).

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (`0790d9f`)

### Operating system

macOS 26.3.1, arm64 (Apple Silicon), LaunchDaemon-supervised (`system` domain, not a user LaunchAgent), single confirmed gateway process throughout (no dual-supervisor/EADDRINUSE condition — ruled out directly).

### Node version

v22.23.2

### Related issues (root cause, high confidence)

This looks like the same underlying defect already reported and never actually fixed, just administratively closed twice:

- **#56215** — "Gateway WebSocket connections leak - CLOSE_WAIT/FIN_WAIT_2 zombie connections cause crashes" (closed as stale 2026-07-27, never fixed, reporter never got a chance to confirm/deny on a later release before auto-close).
- **#101540** — "WebSocket connection and timer leak due to silent TCP drop missing `close` handling" (closed as duplicate of #56215, pointing at the exact file/lines: `src/gateway/server/ws-connection.ts`, `pingTimer` only cleared inside `close()`, which is never invoked on a silent TCP drop).
- **#91466** — "Gateway: server-side WebSocket keepalive + close-on-timeout" — the candidate fix for exactly this. **Confirmed CLOSED, never merged** (`state=CLOSED`, `mergedAt=null`). Confirmed on our installed 2026.7.1-2: `gateway.keepalive` does not exist as a config path at all (`openclaw config get gateway.keepalive` → "Config path not found"). The PR's own description states the pre-fix behavior is "a previous unconditional 25s ping that never closed anything" — exactly consistent with our observed accumulation to exactly `somaxconn` over ~19h with zero draining.

Given a Sev1-adjacent production gateway incident with full forensic reproduction of the exact symptom class #91466 was written to fix, I'd ask that #91466 (or an equivalent close-on-timeout mechanism) be reconsidered for merge, or that the maintainers explain why it was closed without landing so we can evaluate whether we should carry it as a local patch under our own dist-patch process in the meantime.

### Workaround (in place on our fleet)

We added a direct TCP-level `curl` health probe against the gateway's client port to our existing daemon-pid/listener-pid watchdog (which was blind to this exact failure mode, since pid-match stayed healthy the entire outage). 3 consecutive failed direct probes now trigger `launchctl kickstart -k`. This detects and recovers from the symptom; it does not fix the underlying leak.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: any long-running gateway install where a client (dashboard, sidecar bridge, internal polling process, etc.) can go half-open without a clean WS close handshake — likely common on any host that sleeps, has flaky local IPC, or runs long-lived local pollers.
- Severity: High. A fully "healthy-looking" gateway (process alive, sidecar/dependent services fine) can be completely unreachable on its primary port for many hours with zero internal alerting.
- Frequency: at least once confirmed on our fleet over multiple weeks of uptime; likely underreported elsewhere given #56215's original reporter also saw it recur over hours and was auto-closed for going stale rather than the defect being resolved.

issues.body:
On an iPhone running iOS 27, opening the Control UI from its Home Screen icon requested `/chat/main?homescreen=1` and returned HTTP 404 with the body `Not found`. The same route without the parameter, `/chat/main`, returns HTTP 200. Both responses were reproduced without cookies or a session.

The chat return-path parser rejects any query parameter that is not in its allowlist. This is still present on main at `fd83c2d59181`: [query validation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fd83c2d59181b0021ba5b63423f5f0e05c80e483/src/gateway/control-ui-session-entry-path.ts#L31-L41). The [chat request handler](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/fd83c2d59181b0021ba5b63423f5f0e05c80e483/src/gateway/control-ui-public-session.runtime.ts#L158-L184) turns that rejection into a 404.

To reproduce the server behavior, request `/chat/main`, then request `/chat/main?homescreen=1`. The extra parameter alone changes the response from 200 to 404.

The same iPhone also added `?homescreen=1` when opening another site whose manifest has no `start_url`. This did not happen in the iOS 27 Simulator: Add to Home Screen saved the page URL unchanged. We do not know what on the physical phone adds the parameter, and are not attributing it to Apple. Searches of the installed OpenClaw distribution and current main's UI found no code that generates `homescreen=1`.

Could unknown query parameters be ignored instead of making an otherwise valid chat URL return 404? Recognized parameters should still be validated, and session authorization should remain unchanged.

issues.body:
### Environment

- openclaw `2026.8.1-beta.2` (also reproduced on `2026.7.2-beta.7`), `@openclaw/slack` version-locked to core
- Gateway on GKE (linux/amd64), Slack channel in `socket` mode, `dmPolicy: disabled`, single agent
- Three production incidents on our side: Aug 11, Aug 13, Aug 24 — each ended with the bot deaf in Slack while the gateway reported healthy

### Incident flavor 1 — reconnect flapping leaks sockets until `too_many_websockets` (Aug 11, Aug 13; 2026.7.2-beta.7)

Network blips (edge 503s on the primary wss host) caused socket-mode to flap. Each reconnect opened a new WebSocket **without closing the previous one**. The pod accumulated exactly 10 established TCP connections to Slack's wss endpoints — Slack's per-app-token connection cap — after which every new connect was answered with `{"type":"disconnect","reason":"too_many_websockets"}`, producing a permanent retry loop (`SMWebsocketError cause: TypeError`).

Notes:
- The health-monitor's provider restart does **not** close the zombie sockets, so the retry loop survives it. Only a full pod restart recovers.
- Verified via `/proc/net/tcp` in the pod: 10 ESTABLISHED to Slack wss IPs; `apps.connections.open` and tokens were healthy.

### Incident flavor 2 — half-open death, zero reconnects, zero logs (Aug 24; 2026.8.1-beta.2)

A single logged `socket-mode:socket-mode WebSocket error! SMWebsocketError` at 07:00 UTC; after that, the remaining connections died half-open (no FIN/RST observed by the client). Inbound events stopped entirely at 12:09 UTC. For the following hours there was **not one reconnect/disconnect/ping line in the gateway log** — the gateway's `/readyz` stayed green the whole time, so orchestrator probes see a healthy pod while the bot is deaf.

### Contributing factors (from reading `extensions/slack`)

1. `clientPingTimeout` is hardcoded to `15000` in `src/monitor/provider-support.ts` and passed to `SocketModeReceiver`; there is no channel-config exposure for ping/reconnect behavior, so operators can neither tune nor verify the watchdog.
2. Socket-mode lifecycle events (ping/pong timeouts, reconnect attempts, disconnect reasons) go to the plugin's custom `socketModeLogger` and are **not forwarded to the gateway's main log**. Both incident flavors were invisible in pod logs — that observability gap is what turned them into multi-hour outages (one lasted ~2 days before a human noticed).
3. `reconnect-policy.ts` already parses `num_connections` from the `hello` frame for the shared-connection warning — the signal needed to detect the leak exists, it just doesn't gate anything.

### Asks, in order of impact

1. **Close the superseded socket on reconnect** (or track and cap client-side): the leak is what converts a transient network blip into a permanent `too_many_websockets` lock that survives provider restarts.
2. **Forward socket-mode lifecycle events to the main gateway log** at warn level (connect, disconnect + reason, ping timeout, reconnect attempt/backoff). A deaf channel should be loud in logs.
3. Expose ping/reconnect knobs (`clientPingTimeout`, backoff policy) in channel config.
4. Consider a health signal channels can degrade `/readyz` with (or a per-channel health endpoint) — today a dead Slack receive path is indistinguishable from healthy at the orchestrator level.

Happy to provide fuller logs/timelines for any of the three episodes.

<!-- Title: harden native-hook relay cleanup at Gateway lifecycle rotation -->

## Summary

Gateway lifecycle rotation revokes retained native-hook recovery authority but does not itself retire the corresponding relay registration and bridge resources.

The stale relay fails closed, and the current Gateway restart path normally unregisters it before rotation by closing Codex clients and releasing direct-child claims. The lower-level lifecycle contract nevertheless permits an old-generation relay, localhost bridge, SQLite locator row, timer, and retained closures to remain installed until another cleanup path runs.

## Current behavior

A successfully yielded direct child can keep its relay after foreground closure. The retained policy callback captures the agent-run lifecycle generation and checks it on every invocation.

When the process-wide owner calls `rotateAgentEventLifecycleGeneration()`:

- the retained callback begins throwing `admitted run native hook recovery is no longer active`;
- the relay remains in the process-global registration map;
- its localhost bridge and SQLite bridge record remain published;
- its expiry timer and captured recovery lease remain installed.

Physical cleanup happens later through last-child release, attempt abort, same-ID replacement, explicit teardown, or TTL expiry.

The sole current production rotation path closes the Gateway and Codex harness first, so this is lifecycle hardening rather than a demonstrated normal restart leak.

## Reproduction and proof

At OpenClaw `323a0efdd078d6599cf5c95aace1dacddcacd3ba`:

1. Create a retained native-hook relay with one claimed direct child.
2. Authorize successful-yield retention and close foreground ownership.
3. Rotate through `rotateAgentEventLifecycleGeneration()` without first releasing the child claim.
4. Invoke the retained `PreToolUse` path and observe that authority rejects as stale.
5. Observe that the relay registration and bridge resources remain installed until a separate cleanup path runs.

## Expected behavior

Lifecycle invalidation should revoke authority and retire its process-local relay resources at the same owner boundary. Old-generation registrations should not remain discoverable after they can no longer authorize any invocation.

Cleanup must compare against the exact old registration so a reentrant or same-ID successor cannot be removed accidentally.

## Impact

If a future or exceptional path rotates lifecycle generation before client and claim cleanup:

- affected child tools fail closed on every protected invocation;
- each stale relay retains a registration, listening bridge, locator row, timer, and captured closures;
- multiple distinct retained sessions could accumulate these resources until replacement or expiry.

No authorization bypass is present. The current normal restart sequence prevents this state, which keeps urgency low.

## Proposed direction

Make the generic relay registry participate in the existing lifecycle-rotation cleanup:

- Register the native-hook relay registry with the existing agent-event lifecycle rotation owner.
- At rotation, snapshot the exact relay registrations present when cleanup begins.
- Compare-unregister each snapshot entry through canonical relay cleanup.
- Reuse canonical relay unregistration so it removes the relay map entry, bridge server and row, retained lease, invocation state, approvals, permission state, and timers together.
- Preserve a current-generation same-ID successor created reentrantly by an old registration's cleanup callback.

Do not wait for the next invocation to discover stale authority, weaken the generation assertion, or depend solely on TTL.

## Acceptance criteria

- `rotateAgentEventLifecycleGeneration()` physically removes the exact relay registrations and bridge resources present when rotation begins.
- The retained recovery lease is released at the same boundary.
- Later calls receive normal not-found/structured-deny behavior without invoking stale policy.
- A same-ID current-generation successor created reentrantly by an old registration's `onDispose` remains registered and callable.
- Ordinary and retained relay registrations are both retired by the registry-level cleanup.
- Normal last-claim, abort, replacement, and TTL cleanup continue to be idempotent.
- Current Gateway restart ordering remains valid and covered.
- A focused regression combines retained relay, foreground close, live child claim, lifecycle rotation, and resource assertions.

## Relevant code

- `src/infra/agent-run-registry.ts:85-112`
- `src/infra/agent-events.ts:150-193`
- `src/agents/admitted-run-context.ts:105-135`
- `src/agents/harness/host-capability.ts:271-290`
- `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.ts:157-240`
- `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.ts:307-388`
- `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.ts:390-452`
- `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay-bridge.ts:130-203`
- `extensions/codex/src/app-server/native-hook-relay.ts:218-224`
- `extensions/codex/src/app-server/native-hook-relay.ts:263-310`
- `src/cli/gateway-cli/run-loop.ts:751-1032`
- `src/gateway/server-close.ts:913-1098`

## Dependency contract

Codex has no OpenClaw lifecycle-generation concept. It continues invoking its configured command hook until OpenClaw removes or replaces the relay locator. A structured unavailable `PreToolUse` response remains fail-closed:

- `../codex/codex-rs/core/src/hook_runtime.rs:162-223`
- `../codex/codex-rs/hooks/src/events/pre_tool_use.rs:193-249`

## Non-goals

- Changing Gateway restart order without evidence it is wrong.
- Weakening lifecycle-generation fencing.
- Preserving stale relay discovery as a compatibility behavior.
- Adding a user-facing configuration option.

issues.body:
### Summary

Make the length at which Tool Search cuts a network-content result configurable, with three choices: the current 20,000 characters, a length that scales with the model's context window, or a fixed number.

### Problem to solve

`renderToolSearchControlText` in `src/agents/tool-search-control-result.ts` cuts any Tool Search result marked as network content at 20,000 characters (19,988 plus `\n[truncated]`). That covers every MCP tool and OpenClaw's own `web_fetch` when they're called through `dispatch_action`. The count covers the whole `{ tool, result }` envelope written as indented JSON, before the external-content wrapper is added. No config key changes it, on 2026.11.1 or on main.

OpenClaw's live tool-result cap already scales with the model: 16,000 characters below 100K tokens, 32,000 at 100K+, 64,000 at 200K+, and never more than 30% of the window. On a 200K+ model, a tool the model calls directly can return 64,000 characters, and the same tool behind Tool Search stops at 20,000. Tool Search is on by default when `tools.toolSearch` is unset, so most MCP and `web_fetch` calls get the lower limit.

Two cases where the model loses text:

- `web_fetch` returns up to 20,000 characters of page text by default (`maxChars` and `maxCharsCap`). With its other fields and the envelope, a long page always runs past the cut, and the end of the text is dropped.
- A paged read reports where its window ended (`next_start_line`, an offset or a cursor). When the cut falls inside the window, the model continues from that point and never sees the lines between the cut and the cursor.

### Proposed solution

One setting under `tools.toolSearch` that takes:

1. Unset: 20,000, as now.
2. Scale with context: the live tool-result cap for the active model, less room for the wrapper, so a result through `dispatch_action` can be as long as the same tool's result called directly.
3. A number: a fixed limit, at or under the live tool-result cap so that cap never has to cut a wrapped result.

### Alternatives considered

- Keeping tool output under the limit. Our own MCP server's default read size for this agent is 15,000, and its replies put paging fields before long text so they survive a cut. The model still asks for more when it wants a whole document (`max_chars` of 20,000 and 40,000 in the recent cuts), and `web_fetch`'s own default is 20,000.
- `tools.toolSearch: false`. It removes the cut, but every MCP schema goes back into every request.
- Patching the two numbers in `dist`. It works (we run 60,000 now) but has to be redone after every update.

### Impact

- Affected: agents on large-context models that call MCP tools or `web_fetch` through Tool Search, which is the default.
- Severity: medium. The model gets part of a result and can't get the rest from the same call, and a paged read can skip text without any sign.
- Frequency: one agent (local model, 320,000-token window) had 78 of 3,062 `tool_call`/`dispatch_action` results cut between 2026-10-14 and 2026-11-07, and 9 of 757 since 2026-11-03 (7 `web_fetch`, 2 from a paged read tool).
- Consequence: answers from partial pages, extra calls to re-read in smaller pieces, and skipped lines.

### Evidence/examples

Every cut result in that agent's transcripts was 19,615 to 20,307 characters long and ended in `\n[truncated]` inside the wrapper.

A skipped range: a paged read tool returned lines 1 to 49 of a 78-line file with `next_start_line: 50`. The cut left about 46 lines. The model's next call started at line 50, so lines 47 to 49 never reached it.

The code, on 2026.11.1 and main:

```ts
const bounded =
  text.length <= 20_000 ? truncateSanitizedExternalContent(text, 20_000) : undefined;
const truncated = bounded?.truncated ?? true;
const modelText =
  !bounded || bounded.truncated
    ? `${truncateSanitizedExternalContent(text, 19_988).text}\n[truncated]`
    : bounded.text;
```

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only

### Additional information

Nothing changes for anyone who leaves the setting unset.

issues.body:
## Summary

`buildCodexNativeHookRelayId` hashes `agentId`, `sessionKey || sessionId`, and `runId`:

```js
hash.update(params.runId?.trim() || "");
// T5780_NATIVE_HOOK_RELAY_ATTEMPT_SCOPED_ID: overlapping attempts must not replace each other's relay.
```

The comment states the invariant, but the `|| ""` fallback silently breaks it: when `runId` is absent or blank, two overlapping attempts on the same agent + session collapse to the **same relay id**.

`registerNativeHookRelayBridge` then calls `unregisterNativeHookRelayBridge(registration.relayId, ...)` before creating the new bridge — so the second attempt **evicts the first attempt's live bridge**. The first attempt keeps running and every subsequent tool call fails with `Native hook relay unavailable`.

## Observed

Dispatching successive Codex-native subagents for the same session produced exactly this: a subagent completed early tool calls (clone succeeded), then every later call — including `pwd` — was rejected with `Native hook relay unavailable`, immediately after a sibling subagent was started.

## Expected

Either derive a guaranteed-unique attempt component when `runId` is missing (e.g. a per-registration UUID), or fail registration loudly rather than silently degrading to a colliding id. Eviction of a *live* bridge should never be silent — the evicted run should receive a typed terminal error instead of per-call denials.

## Environment

OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f), Node v25.9.0, macOS 26.3 (arm64).

issues.body:
## Problem

In the native **Android OpenClaw app**, the chat composer never auto-capitalizes sentence starts, even when the user has Gboard's "Auto-capitalization" enabled (Gboard > Corrections & suggestions). Typing `why don't you auto capitalize?!` produces exactly that — all lowercase — unlike every mainstream messaging app.

## Root cause

The composer `BasicTextField` in `apps/android/app/src/main/java/ai/openclaw/app/ui/chat/ChatScreen.kt` sets no `keyboardOptions`, and Compose's `KeyboardOptions` default is `capitalization = KeyboardCapitalization.Unspecified` — so the IME receives no `textCapSentences` hint. The same applies to the free-text "Other answer" field in `ChatQuestionCard.kt`, which uses `KeyboardOptions.Default`.

## Reproduction

1. Pixel 10, Android 17, Gboard with Auto-capitalization ON (see recording attached in a follow-up comment).
2. Open the OpenClaw app (2026.10.90), tap the chat composer.
3. Type `why don't you auto capitalize?!` — no capitalization is offered or applied at sentence starts.

## Expected

Sentence-start capitalization like Signal/Telegram/WhatsApp, i.e. `KeyboardOptions(capitalization = KeyboardCapitalization.Sentences)` on chat prose inputs.

## Suggested fix

One line on each of the two prose inputs; emoji/secret/URI/search fields intentionally untouched.

issues.title: backup create fails on large state trees: SQLite header probe hard 10s timeout cannot handle ~250k paths

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Normal backlog priority with limited blast radius.

labels.name: impact:other
labels.description: This issue has meaningful maintainer-visible impact outside the owned taxonomy.

issues.body:
### Description

`openclaw backup create` fails on large state trees with:
`Could not determine whether backup files are SQLite databases. Check that the backup worker can run and the source files are readable, then retry the backup.`

The SQLite header probe (`infra/sqlite-header-probe.worker`) is spawned via `spawnSync` with a **hard-coded 10-second timeout** (`timeout: 1e4` in `dist/backup-sqlite-snapshot-*.mjs`). The probe receives a JSON array of **every candidate file in `~/.openclaw`** as stdin. On a mature state tree this array was **26.2 million characters (~250k file paths)** — the probe cannot classify that many files in 10 seconds, so `result.error` = ETIMEDOUT and backup creation aborts.

The worker itself is fast (single-file probe completes in ~0.2s standalone on both Node 26.4.0 and 26.13.0), and the failure reproduces identically:
- from a CLI inside the gateway process tree
- from a standalone user terminal with the gateway **stopped**
- on Node 26.4.0 and Node 26.13.0

So it is not environment, lock contention, or I/O load — the 10s budget simply does not scale with tree size.

### Environment
- OpenClaw 2026.11.1 (4ffdd20), Ubuntu 26.04 x64, Node 26.4.0 and 26.13.0 (fails on both)
- State tree: ~250k files under `~/.openclaw` (agents, sessions archives, workspace, skills archives)

### Reproduction
1. Accumulate a large `~/.openclaw` tree (~100k+ files)
2. Run `openclaw backup create`
3. After ~2 minutes of discovery, the header probe spawnSync hits its 10s timeout → error above

`NODE_DEBUG=child_process` shows the spawnSync: 26,249,772-character stdin payload, `timeout: 10000`.

### Impact
- `openclaw backup create` is unusable on large installs
- Doctor's "newest successful backup is more than 14 days old → Create one now with openclaw backup create" advice cannot be followed
- Doctor's own update state-capture hits the same worker and fails the same way

### Suggested fix
- Scale or batch the probe (e.g., chunk the path list across multiple worker spawns), or
- Classify by extension/size heuristics first and probe only candidates, or
- Make the timeout proportional to input size / configurable

### Local workaround (verified)
Patching the dist `timeout: 1e4` → `120e4` lets `openclaw backup create` proceed past the probe and complete. (Patch is overwritten by updates — hence this report.)

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Summary

After moving core from a beta install to stable (`update.channel=stable`, core `2026.11.1`), tracked official plugins (`codex`, `whatsapp`, `acpx`) kept install specs like `@openclaw/codex@beta`. `openclaw plugins update --all` then continued resolving the **beta** dist-tag, picked an incompatible newer beta, fell back to the newest *compatible* beta (`2026.10.10-beta.5`), and even reported a **downgrade** of Codex off the matching stable line (`2026.11.1 -> 2026.10.10-beta.5`).

Doctor had already flagged drift expecting `2026.11.1`. Manual `openclaw plugins install @openclaw/<name>@2026.11.1 --force` fixed it.

This is the reverse of the closed beta-blocker [#115081](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/115081) (bulk update on beta selected stable when channel was unset). Here channel *is* stable, but sticky `@beta` installSpecs keep plugins on the beta channel.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run an npm global OpenClaw install that has been on beta long enough that official plugins were installed as `@openclaw/<plugin>@beta` (observed: `codex`, `whatsapp`, `acpx` with `trust.installSpec` / installSpec `@openclaw/…@beta`).
2. Move core to stable, e.g. after a manual core install:
   ```bash
   npm install -g openclaw@2026.11.1 --allow-scripts=openclaw
   openclaw config set update.channel stable
   openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive --yes
   ```
3. With Gateway stopped (for exclusive ownership), run:
   ```bash
   openclaw plugins update --all --accept-capabilities
   ```

## Expected behavior

With `update.channel=stable` and core on `2026.11.1`, bulk plugin update should retarget tracked official plugin install specs to the stable/`latest` line (or the version matching core), and install `@openclaw/<plugin>@2026.11.1` (or `latest`), not keep resolving `@beta`.

## Actual behavior

```text
Resolved @openclaw/acpx@beta to @openclaw/acpx@2026.11.5-beta.1, but that version is incompatible with this OpenClaw runtime; using newest compatible @openclaw/acpx@2026.10.10-beta.5.
…
Resolved @openclaw/codex@beta to @openclaw/codex@2026.11.5-beta.1, but that version is incompatible with this OpenClaw runtime; using newest compatible @openclaw/codex@2026.10.10-beta.5.
…
Downgraded codex: 2026.11.1 -> 2026.10.10-beta.5.
whatsapp already at 2026.10.10-beta.5.
acpx already at 2026.10.10-beta.5.
```

Doctor before that had reported drift:

```text
- acpx: 2026.10.10-beta.5 (npm) -> expected 2026.11.1
- whatsapp: 2026.10.10-beta.5 (npm) -> expected 2026.11.1
```

Workaround:

```bash
openclaw plugins install @openclaw/codex@2026.11.1 --force --accept-capabilities
openclaw plugins install @openclaw/whatsapp@2026.11.1 --force --accept-capabilities
openclaw plugins install @openclaw/acpx@2026.11.1 --force --accept-capabilities
```

After that, `plugins list` showed `spec=@openclaw/codex@2026.11.1` (etc.) and status `loaded`.

## OpenClaw version

Core: `2026.11.1 (4ffdd20)` after recovery  
Prior stuck core: `2026.10.10-beta.5`  
Plugins before workaround: `@openclaw/*@beta` resolving to `2026.10.10-beta.5`

## Operating system

Linux (Debian-based), systemd user gateway

## Install method

npm global (nvm Node `v24.22.1`)

## Additional context

Hit while recovering from the SQLite header-probe update block in [#193962](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/193962) (manual `npm i -g openclaw@2026.11.1` path). Channel config correctly showed `stable`; only the plugin installSpecs remained on `@beta`.

Related but different: [#161921](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/161921) (plugins stuck after `state-migrated-no-rollback`), closed [#115081](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/115081) (beta→stable selection without explicit channel).

issues.body:
# Codex native thread is replaced on MCP OAuth access-token renewal

No private credentials or transcripts included.

## Versions and scope

Observed on OpenClaw 2026.9.3 with the native Codex runtime and an OAuth-authenticated
vidIQ MCP integration. Latest npm `openclaw` and `@openclaw/codex` tags were both
2026.9.4 on September 14, 2026. The published 9.4 artifacts retain the affected path;
9.4 was inspected offline, not installed or tested live.

## Expected / actual

Renewing a token within the same verified OAuth grant should refresh authentication
without discarding the conversation binding and re-injecting history. Genuine
account, endpoint, scope, policy or other identity changes must remain effective.

Instead, a token renewal can log `user MCP config changed; starting a new thread`.
One observed replacement injected 246,144 characters of context. Its first request
reported 92,884 input tokens, 13,184 cached; the following request cached most input.
This demonstrates avoidable cold context, not a conversion to subscription cost.

## Published 9.4 code evidence

- `bundle-mcp-codex-BkWFngr8.mjs:181`: `tokenProjection: "literal"`.
- `thread-lifecycle-DXl1-I6b.js:1149–1162`: Authorization is hashed into the MCP
  configuration fingerprint; changing only a synthetic token changes that input.
- Same file around line 4475: fingerprint incompatibility clears the binding and
  starts a new thread.

Local reproducible check: `node probe-token-change.mjs` uses the extracted published
redaction functions with synthetic tokens and no external calls. It confirms token
sensitivity, not a complete live 9.4 reproduction.

## Observed correlation and limitations

On 9.3 the OAuth store refresh was followed 6 ms later by the thread-replacement log.
Other recorded tool/runtime fingerprints remained stable. Earlier samples retained
configuration hashes rather than full before/after values, so exact field-level proof
is unavailable for every rotation. The installation also contains local history fixes;
the 9.4 published-code check helps distinguish this path from those modifications.

## Repair research

Ignoring Authorization changes alone is unsafe: reloading config or resuming an
already-loaded thread retained the old bearer in local simulated MCP calls.
Unsubscribing an idle persisted thread, observing authoritative unload, then resuming
that same thread with current config refreshed actual MCP authentication and preserved
thread ID, history and cache key in local synthetic tests. Production use still needs
trustworthy same-grant classification, concurrency guards, and policy/account invalidation.

Please confirm the supported renewal route and whether an upstream fix already exists.

## Reproduction procedure

1. Run a persistent native Codex conversation with an OAuth-authenticated remote MCP server.
2. Record native thread identity and first-request input/cached-input counters without logging tokens.
3. Allow that server access token to refresh within the same OAuth grant; do not change account, server, tool policy, or scopes.
4. On the next naturally occurring turn, compare native thread identity and inspect the configuration-change reason.
5. Compare with a control turn without renewal. The observed installation replaced the thread after renewal and then returned to high cache reuse on the following call.

### Offline published-code check (synthetic credentials only)

The following reproduces the relevant published fingerprint transformation, not a complete Gateway reproduction. Run as a Node .mjs file:

```js
import crypto$1 from 'node:crypto';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
function redactUserMcpServersFingerprintSecrets(value) {
	if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.map(redactUserMcpServersFingerprintSecrets);
	if (!value || typeof value !== "object") return value;
	return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(value).map(([key, entry]) => {
		if (key === "http_headers" && entry && typeof entry === "object" && !Array.isArray(entry)) return [key, Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(entry).map(([header, headerValue]) => [header, header.toLowerCase() === "authorization" ? fingerprintUserMcpServersAuthorizationHeader(headerValue) : headerValue]))];
		return [key, redactUserMcpServersFingerprintSecrets(entry)];
	}));
}
function fingerprintUserMcpServersAuthorizationHeader(value) {
	return typeof value === "string" && value.length > 0 ? `<redacted:sha256:${crypto$1.createHash("sha256").update(value).digest("hex")}>` : "<redacted>";
}

const cfg=t=>({mcp_servers:{test:{url:'http://127.0.0.1:1/mcp',http_headers:{Authorization:'Bearer '+t}}}});
assert.notDeepEqual(redactUserMcpServersFingerprintSecrets(cfg('synthetic-A')),redactUserMcpServersFingerprintSecrets(cfg('synthetic-B')));
console.log('PASS: published 9.4 token-only renewal changes fingerprint input');
```

## Local mitigation implemented; not an upstream patch claim

A local coordinated distribution repair is installed on 2026.9.3. It adds a host-minted grant identity, retains it only for verified same-grant renewal, and fingerprints structure/policy separately. Verified renewals use the existing ownership-checked, unload-attested saved-thread resume path. Unknown identity, interactive login/account replacement, logout, and policy/configuration changes remain invalidating.

All OAuth writers must participate, including the independent bundled `dist/worker/worker.mjs` writer. An initial candidate missed that writer; a synthetic account-change regression demonstrated why partial deployment is unsafe. The final local candidate includes that writer. Local component/branch/syntax and synthetic protocol tests passed; installation readiness passed. Full isolated Gateway integration and post-install natural-renewal cache savings are NOT established by those tests. This is repair evidence, not a claim that the local patch is ready for upstream merging unchanged.

Please investigate an official supported solution; merely removing Authorization from the fingerprint would risk stale authentication. Separate handoff-continuity context: #143386.

issues.body:
**Version:** OpenClaw 2026.8.1-beta.2 (8f382a2), @openclaw/discord 2026.8.1-beta.2

**Two independent bugs; each alone makes the Activity iframe hang with no error in gateway logs.**

### 1. `vendor/embedded-app-sdk.mjs` 404s — asset path resolved against package root, shipped under `dist/`

`activities-api-*.js` registers:
```js
vendorAssetPath: api.resolvePath("assets/embedded-app-sdk.mjs")
```
`api.resolvePath` → `resolvePluginPath(input, record.rootDir)` resolves relative input against the plugin **package root** (`extensions/discord/src/activities/register.ts:28`, still so on `main`). The published package's `files` is `["dist/**", …]` and the `openclaw.build.staticAssets` copy emits `dist/assets/embedded-app-sdk.mjs`, so in every npm install `readVendorAsset` fails and the route returns 404. The monorepo checkout is unaffected only because `scripts/build-discord-activity-sdk.mts` writes to `extensions/discord/assets/` there — which is presumably why #108725 ("Activities open correctly from packaged builds") did not catch it. The shell HTML's `import('./vendor/embedded-app-sdk.mjs')` rejects inside the iframe; nothing is logged server-side.

Workaround: `ln -s dist/assets <plugin>/assets` (takes effect without restart since the failure is not cached).
Fix: `api.resolvePath("dist/assets/embedded-app-sdk.mjs")`, or resolve relative to `import.meta.url`.

### 2. `reconcileGlobalCommands` deletes the Entry Point command Activities require

Discord refuses the Embedded App SDK RPC handshake unless the application has a PRIMARY_ENTRY_POINT command (`type: 4`, `handler: 2`). `reconcileGlobalCommands` (`extensions/discord/src/internal/command-deploy.ts`) deletes every existing command whose `stableCommandKey` (`${type}:${name}`) is not in the desired set — the Entry Point keys as `4:launch` and is never desired, so it is removed on the next hash change (e.g. any plugin update). Result: `sdk.ready()` never resolves, silently.

Fix: either register a `type: 4` command when `activities` is configured (`activities/discord-api.ts` currently never does), or exclude `type === 4` from the deletion loop.

Introduced with #107442; neither bug is mentioned in any existing issue or PR.

### Repro
Enable `channels.discord.activities`, open the widget's Launch button in a Discord client, observe the iframe spinner forever. Attach to the OOPIF over CDP and run the shell's bootstrap step-by-step: step 1 fails with the 404, and after fixing that, `sdk.ready()` times out until a `type: 4` command exists.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Summary

A Codex-backed agent on current stable OpenClaw can still silently end a multi-step turn immediately after sending an intermediate message(action=send) progress update.

The observed failure is:

Agent is executing a multi-step task normally.
Agent calls message(action=send) to provide an intermediate Telegram update.
The message call succeeds.
The message call does not specify final:true; final is omitted.

The Codex transcript records the assistant item with:

stopReason: "toolUse"

indicating the model was at a tool-use boundary and expected continuation.

No subsequent tool calls occur.

OpenClaw records:

model.completed ... done

followed by:

session.ended ... success

The user must send another prompt such as update? or keep going to create a new turn and resume the work.

This appears to be a residual/regression of the progress-message termination family described in #100175 / #106961, despite the installed Codex plugin containing the #108487 continuation fix.

Importantly, I do not see the explicit terminal-release evidence associated with #109490: there is no terminate:true, turn.dynamic_tool_terminal_release, turn/interrupt, or terminal dynamic tool result marker in either the gateway log or session JSONL.

### Steps to reproduce

1) Configure a Telegram-connected OpenClaw agent using the native Codex runtime.

Reproduced environment:

OpenClaw: 2026.7.1-2
@openclaw/codex: 2026.7.1-1
Model: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
Runtime: codex
Channel: Telegram group

2) Send the agent a development task that requires several sequential actions and is likely to take long enough for the agent to send an intermediate progress update.

For example:

Inspect the current repository changes, review the implementation,
make any required corrections, run the relevant tests, fix any
failures you find, retest, and report back when the work is complete.

3) Allow the agent to begin working normally.

The agent should perform one or more development tools such as:

bash
apply_patch

4) Wait until the agent sends an intermediate Telegram message using the message tool, for example:

I'm checking the implementation now and will run the tests next.

5) Do not send another message to the agent.
6) Observe that after the progress message is delivered, the agent performs no further development work even though the original task is not complete.

7) Check the session trajectory:

openclaw sessions --agent <agent-id> --active 30 --json

Obtain the active/recent session key, then run:

openclaw sessions --agent <agent-id> tail \
  --session-key "<session-key>" \
  --tail 100

8) Observe a sequence similar to:

tool.call        message
tool.result      message ok
model.completed  openai/gpt-5.6-sol done
session.ended    success

There are no subsequent development tool calls after the successful message result.

9) Inspect the corresponding message tool invocation in the session JSONL and confirm that final was not explicitly supplied.

For example:

jq -c '
  .. | objects
  | select(
      (.name? == "message" or .toolName? == "message")
      and (
        ((.arguments? // null) | type) == "object"
        or ((.input? // null) | type) == "object"
        or ((.args? // null) | type) == "object"
      )
    )
  | (.arguments // .input // .args) as $a
  | {
      action: $a.action,
      final_present: ($a | has("final")),
      final: ($a.final // null)
    }
' <session.jsonl>

Observed result:

{
  "action":"send",
  "final_present":false,
  "final":null
}
10) Inspect the assistant transcript metadata:
jq -c '
  select(.type == "message" and .message.role == "assistant")
  | {
      timestamp: .timestamp,
      provider: (.message.provider // null),
      model: (.message.model // null),
      stopReason: (.message.stopReason // null),
      tools: [
        .message.content[]?
        | select(.type == "toolCall")
        | .name
      ]
    }
' <session.jsonl>
11) Observe that the Codex assistant record corresponding to the progress message contains:
{
  "provider":"openai",
  "model":"gpt-5.6-sol",
  "stopReason":"toolUse",
  "tools":["message"]
}
12) Send the agent a new Telegram message such as:
Keep going please
13) Observe that a new OpenClaw/Codex turn starts and the agent resumes the work it had previously stopped performing.

### Expected behavior

After an intermediate message(action=send) where final is omitted:

message tool call
→ message delivered
→ tool result returned to Codex
→ same Codex turn continues
→ further bash/apply_patch/etc. calls
→ task completed
→ authoritative final response
→ session ends

### Actual behavior

Actual result
message tool call
→ message delivered
→ stopReason: "toolUse"
→ no further development tools execute
→ model.completed
→ session.ended success

The original task remains incomplete until the user sends another Telegram prompt, which creates a new turn.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04.3

### Install method

NPM

### Model

openai/gpt-5.6-sol

### Provider / routing chain

Native

### Additional provider/model setup details

This is reproducible on an otherwise stock/current stable OpenClaw installation. No OpenClaw source patches, Codex patches, custom runtime modifications, or workaround configuration changes have been made.

Environment:

OpenClaw: 2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)
@openclaw/codex: 2026.7.1-1
Model: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
Runtime: native Codex agent harness
Node: 22.23.2
Kernel: 6.8.0-136-generic
Channel: Telegram group
Telegram channel/account health reports OK

The behavior has occurred repeatedly across multiple turns, rather than as a one-off.

The key forensic observations are:

message(action=send) succeeds normally.
The message calls inspected in the session JSONL all omit the final field (final_present:false).
The corresponding OpenAI assistant record has stopReason:"toolUse" and tools:["message"].
Immediately afterwards OpenClaw records model.completed ... done and session.ended ... success.
No further development tool calls execute in that turn.
Sending a subsequent user message such as keep going please starts a new turn and the agent resumes the unfinished work.
Searches of both gateway logs and session JSONL found no terminate:true, turn.dynamic_tool_terminal_release, terminal dynamic tool result, turn/interrupt, or interruptCodexTurn markers.

This therefore appears closer to a residual/regression of the progress-message continuation behavior addressed by #108487 / the #100175 and #106961 issue family than to the explicit terminal-release path described in #109490.

The particularly confusing part from a user perspective is that OpenClaw records the prematurely-ended turn as successful (status: done, abortedLastRun:false, session.ended: success) even though the original requested workflow has not completed.

### Logs

```shell
Searches for:

Result:

```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Suggested is high (P1)

Breaks autonomous multi-step Codex workflows over Telegram. An intermediate progress message(action=send) can cause the active Codex turn to end successfully even though the model records stopReason:"toolUse" and the requested work is incomplete. The agent then remains idle until the user sends another message to start a new turn.

This makes long-running development agents unreliable because normal progress communication can interrupt implementation, testing, diagnosis, or remediation mid-task. OpenClaw additionally records the premature termination as session.ended success, so there is no visible failure state to distinguish incomplete work from genuine completion.

The issue is repeatedly reproducible and requires manual user intervention to continue each affected workflow. It can leave repositories in partially-completed states or prevent planned validation/tests from running, although no data loss or corruption has been observed.

_No response_

issues.body:
Denying a tool via `tools.deny` can disable memory persistence, and nothing
tells anyone — not the operator at startup, not `doctor`, and not the agent,
which then reports success for saves that never happened.

### What happened

Trimming the tool surface to shrink prompts (an assistant deployment, not a
coding one), I denied a list that included `write` and `edit`. Everything kept
working. Then:

> **me:** Remember this for later: … Save it to memory.
> **agent:** Guardado, che. …

Nothing was written. `workspace/memory/` had not changed since the previous
day. Removing `write` from the deny list and repeating the request produced
the file immediately.

### Why the agent claims success

A denied tool is removed from the schema the model sees, so from the model's
point of view the capability never existed. It has no signal that it was asked
to do something it cannot do — so it answers as if it complied. That is a
worse outcome than an error, because the operator has positive confirmation of
something that did not occur.

### Why nothing else catches it

- Startup logs the removal by name and count, which reads like intended
  policy: `tool policy removed 13 tool(s) via tools.deny: apply_patch, edit,
  …, write`. Nothing connects `write` to memory persistence.
- `openclaw doctor` does not flag it.
- `memorySearch` stays "enabled" and search keeps working — retrieval is
  unaffected; only writing is gone. So the feature looks healthy.
- The daily session reset then discards the conversation that was never
  written down. The loss is silent and permanent.

### Suggested handling

Any of these; they are independent:

1. **`doctor` check**: if `agents.defaults.memorySearch.enabled` (or the
   session-memory hook) is on while `write` is denied for that agent, warn —
   memory cannot be persisted.
2. **Startup warning** when a tool the runtime itself depends on is denied,
   distinct from the ordinary policy-removal line.
3. **Tell the model.** When policy removes tools, inject a short system note
   naming the removed capabilities so the agent can say "I can't save that"
   instead of inventing a confirmation. This is the one that generalises: it
   fixes the whole class rather than the memory instance.

(3) would also cover the other cases — an agent asked to send a message with
`message` denied, or to schedule with `cron` denied, has the same shape.

### Environment

openclaw 2026.7.1-2, linux arm64, gateway as a systemd system service, WhatsApp
channel, `tools.profile: "coding"` plus `tools.deny`, local vLLM provider,
`memorySearch.provider: "local"`.
