prs.title: feat(ios): reconcile unread app-icon badges (WIP)
prs.body:
Related: #191489

## What Problem This Solves

iOS users have no app-icon unread reminder after dismissing a notification. **This is an explicitly partial/WIP draft, not a completed fix for #191489.**

## User Impact

This slice implements app-applied unread-session badge reconciliation on foreground, authenticated reconnect, session invalidations, accepted session mutations, and existing background wakes. It counts authorized unread conversations across agents, including manual unread, independently of sidebar pagination. Archived and execution-only subagent sessions are excluded; user-openable child conversations remain eligible.

**Automatic assistant-activity APNs wakes are still missing.** A disconnected phone is not yet woken by a newly completed assistant response. The accepted delivery limitation also remains: if iOS does not execute the app, its badge cannot update. Native compilation, simulator/device behavior, and real APNs acceptance are not verified.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Reuse `deriveSessionUnread` through an optional `sessions.list` `unreadOnly` filter and existing exact `totalCount`; no separate unread-message counter or new unread store.
- Keep the badge a replaceable, authenticated current-scope projection. Account/route changes invalidate pending reads; privacy resets do not mark sessions read.
- Serialize OS badge setters separately from network reads so a privacy reset need not wait for an offline request. Keep APNs payloads badge-free: custom scope/revision fields cannot stop iOS from applying delayed `aps.badge` values.
- Keep `push.test` a transport diagnostic. No durable registration or permission changes are included.

### Maintainer design acceptance needed for the remaining wake path

Native APNs registrations currently contain node/transport identity, but no durable authenticated operator-profile binding. Pairing scopes alone cannot select disconnected recipients without risking an unrelated-profile activity broadcast. The existing web-push recipient-authority path has a profile binding; native registrations do not.

Proposed next step: extend the **existing APNs registration owner** with a binding established only from the authenticated operator/device, revalidate current pairing/profile/role/session visibility at the actual send boundary, and clear or replace the binding on unregister, unpair, or identity replacement. Then wire real assistant activity into an authorized badge-free invalidation/wake path. Do not broadcast to all registered iPhones or infer a profile from a display name.

This durable-data/authority-lifecycle design still needs recorded maintainer acceptance under the [storage-change checkpoint](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/844d0222bd65e979eea562a3973ee8f83e90e26e/docs/reference/database-schemas/storage-changes.md#review-checkpoint-for-material-changes). This draft is the discussion and review checkpoint; it does not claim that acceptance has been granted.

## Evidence

Current published head: `75543e5e0e96265179d6da487b52d9402ffd24ac`; reviewed tree: `f9a10df3bfd3b139750c5a6e00e92975e5d25b5e`. The published tree matches the reviewed local candidate exactly. The exact PR merge base is `844d0222bd65e979eea562a3973ee8f83e90e26e`, confirmed by GitHub comparison. The target-main SHA / prior hosted-review base `c230ae5c3c4643476e5a6eddc3120260d043a86e` is distinct; it was not silently substituted for the local review base.

### Simplification and ownership

Applied **pr-simplify → cross-layer-pr-regression-review → Auto Review**. Scope stays with the existing authenticated operator connection and its authority generation. Removed the duplicate badge scope/route caches, gateway-identity and reaction-identity lookups, repeated cleanup/guard branches, and the private count-only response decoder. The canonical session-list response decoder is reused.

The small badge helper remains because it coalesces reads and serializes OS writes separately: a privacy reset must not wait for an offline network read, and an already-started OS setter must settle before the reset. Accepted-read transport invalidation and the existing foreground/reconnect/background hooks remain; no server-side unread counter or new registration state was introduced.

Compared with the full pre-simplification local candidate (tree `a0d763184e47f09d31f2cdbb669b75476ddb30bf`, including the retained roster test follow-up), production code is **59 lines smaller** and native tests are **one line smaller**, with an OS-setter failure case added. This is separate from the entire PR against its merge base: **381 added / 6 removed lines** across ten files. Excluding generated data/docs/allocation, production is +170/−4 lines and tests are +181/−0 lines. The necessary remaining growth implements the new query, native projection, and distinct boundary regressions.

### Executed checks and review

- The new real `sessions.list` handler regression was **red before implementation and green after canonical filtering and validator regeneration**. The retained follow-up also interleaves normal/unread queries and covers both ordinary and serialized/retained selection; canonical read/activity changes update totals without pagination or visibility leakage. This is Gateway boundary proof, not an icon demonstration.
- `pnpm test src/gateway/server.sessions.unread-count.test.ts src/gateway/session-utils.filters.test.ts packages/gateway-protocol/src/index.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — **41 tests passed** across three files; 21.42 seconds total command time in the retained terminal-success log. The Gateway restarted after the run; its process exit receipt was lost, so no separate exit-code receipt is claimed for that run. CI seconds remain unavailable.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` — exit 0.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --type-aware packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/sessions-list.ts src/gateway/session-list-filters.ts src/gateway/server.sessions.unread-count.test.ts` — exit 0, three files clean.
- `pnpm gateway:validators:check`, `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet --base 844d0222bd65e979eea562a3973ee8f83e90e26e --staged`, and whitespace checks — exit 0. Targeted TypeScript/docs formatting is unchanged and passing. The isolated 93-line allocation covers the RPC regression; the shared baseline is unchanged.
- Read-only cross-layer review of the frozen candidate: no P0/P1 findings in the implemented Gateway → protocol → transport → connection lifecycle → OS-write path. Native execution gaps are retained below.
- Fresh independent **Auto Review**, local mode against the exact merge base, through P3: **scoped-clean**, exit 0, no findings across the complete simplified candidate. This is source review of the partial slice, not native compilation or completion of the original feature.

The [previous hosted ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193491#issuecomment-6659144709) reported zero actionable findings / `needs-human` for **old head `b925619e2bf9ade5186833d1c8162b0755395d94`**. It does not attest this new head. No duplicate hosted re-review was requested for this cleanup. At new-head verification, 30 attached CI checks were skipped; skipped checks are not passing build/test proof.

The broader prior `pnpm lint` invocation expanded beyond the requested files and failed six existing `max-lines` checks in untouched files: `extensions/anthropic/cli.runtime.ts`, `extensions/crabbox/src/crabbox-worker-node-enrollment.test.ts`, `extensions/oc-path/src/cli.test.ts`, `extensions/tlon/src/monitor/index.test.ts`, `src/agents/plugin-model-catalog.ts`, and `src/infra/sqlite-readonly-location.ts`. No lint exceptions were added; the bounded changed-file check passed.

**Outstanding proof and implementation:** Swift/native compile and formatting tools are unavailable in this Linux session. Five native test cases are written but unrun. Native integration, cold-start/offline lifecycle coverage, simulator and real-device/APNs execution-state checks, actual before/after icon screenshots, the automatic activity wake producer, and full-feature review/CI remain pending. No Mac/device access, credentials, or paid allocation were borrowed. This PR remains a partial draft; the original implementation goal remains open.

## Contributor credit

Reported by @olsenbro. Requested by Donnie (Donniefi); no additional GitHub identity linkage is asserted.

## Work sessions

- [Original discussion](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/c8d77c4c-a3d6-4f92-964e-a13c3c724560)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/954ad22d-bb62-44c0-ae94-f0fef5428794)

🦞 Made with [OpenClaw](https://openclaw.ai)

prs.title: fix(update): unblock ordinary deploys after retained repair
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes ordinary deployments remaining blocked after a retained fix-forward reaches `REPAIR_COMPLETED`: activation retains the canonical journal, while ordinary recovery cannot retire that typed terminal state.

Related: #194605. The separate historical-adoption owner is #194955; the two changes touch different owner functions and documentation sections.

## User Impact

Operators can explicitly retire a successfully accepted repair with `openclaw-release-deploy --retire-retained-repair OPERATION COMPLETED_JOURNAL_SHA256`, then request an ordinary deployment. Failed repairs remain retained. This does not restart the Gateway, rerun model acceptance, enable a schedule, or authorize another deployment.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing deployer now binds the exact completed operation and digest, activation acceptance receipt, accepted live target/PID generation/cwd, recorded pointer identities, and canonical lock inode. It fsyncs an archive bundle and intent before atomically moving the unchanged activation journal out of the canonical slot, then publishes a retirement receipt. The same command reconciles interruption on either side of that rename; drift refuses.

Original immutable repair artifacts stay at their bound paths because existing receipts bind absolute paths and inodes. The archive retains copies alongside the original journal; nothing is deleted. The change adds 82 net production lines for the previously absent terminal owner and CLI dispatch, with no configuration, schema, cache, or retention-policy change.

## Evidence

- Exact `e4f99f337268` regression reaches owner-produced completed acceptance, then fails solely because retirement is unsupported.
- Focused Linux proof: 18 passed, 0 failed/skipped in 37.87s. Full shell retirement releases ordinary deployment to its external Git dispatch boundary; ten drift refusals and interrupted replay before/after journal rename pass. The 171 new test/helper lines (102 ratchet-counted lines, covered by the exact per-change allocation) protect these distinct owner/lifecycle contracts; the file takes approximately 37.6s because it exercises three complete retained repair transactions with real flock, filesystem and SQLite boundaries.
- Native service observations and the downstream start-condition receipt are synthetic. Acceptance receipts and completed journals are produced by the real owners. No live host, Gateway/model run, or second deployment occurred.
- `pnpm check:changed` reports 20 inherited changelog-attribution violations, reproduced on exact parent `e64215c411f1addeeb765568c5d82e6a99f9652d`, introduced by `266a7aa0fe69` (#194364). These are main regressions, not new failures or ignored noise.

- The separate test-line ratchet reproduces a 65-line overage on exact parent `e64215c411f1` (6,571,194 counted lines versus 6,571,129 allowed). This branch allocates exactly its own 102 counted lines and preserves that existing debt; it does not grant unrelated headroom. The ceiling first crossed at `5e1a27a9bcc4` (#194899, +127 without credit, consuming 119 spare lines); `4f539a5ec07f` (#194856) added 20 and `c61a7c0cf6b7` (#194882) added 48, offset by 11 deleted lines in #194910/#194908. This is another main regression for its owners to reconcile.
- Codex autoreview: scoped-clean through P2 against exact parent `e64215c411f1addeeb765568c5d82e6a99f9652d`, with the complete shell/library and fixture context; no accepted/actionable findings. The later test-budget-only commit also passed scoped P2 Codex autoreview; controller/test bytes are unchanged.
- Production-shaped synthetic btrfs fixture: 35.04 GiB SQLite, 6,000 sessions, 62,000 workspace files / 1,100,004,000 bytes. Before A/A: unsupported action refuses in 28.40/25.91 ms (user CPU 0.02/0.01s; system 0/0s; peak RSS 54,220/54,428 KiB). After A/A: successful retirement in 3,909.82/3,623.80 ms (user CPU 2.47/2.47s; system 0.41/0.43s; peak RSS 263,844/264,468 KiB). These measure different outcomes, so no speedup is claimed. Separate 64 KiB V8 sampling estimated owner allocations of 2,117,576/2,713,904 bytes before and 263,745,040/260,884,648 bytes after. Including the synthetic native-I/O stubs, candidate allocations were 277,110,104/274,410,992 bytes across 34 Node processes. Fixture setup is excluded.

prs.title: fix(muse): streamed replies lose their beginning when OpenClaw attaches mid-turn
prs.body:
Split from #177698 (session-input consolidation) so that PR stays scoped to the SessionController lifecycle. The change is by @enki; I moved it unchanged onto current `main`.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Muse runtime replies lost the beginning of their streamed text when OpenClaw attached to a turn after Muse had already started streaming. Live output in chat started mid-sentence, even though the saved final answer was complete.

## Why This Change Was Made

OpenClaw kept its own accumulator built only from deltas it received after subscribing. It now reads accumulated item text from the Muse SDK's session fold, which already owns prefixes received before the subscription. That removes the competing accumulator instead of patching it.

## User Impact

Streaming replies from the Muse runtime show the full text from the first character, including content produced before OpenClaw attached to the turn.

## Evidence

- `extensions/muse/src/events.test.ts`: with the production change reverted and the new tests kept, 1 of 4 fails; with the change applied, 4 of 4 pass (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/muse/src/events.test.ts`, on current `main`).
- Gateway stream proof from the original PR, which exercises this exact change through authenticated chat RPC, the production Muse harness and SDK 1.4.4: a prefix frame arrives before the native command ACK, and the client sees `["started:", " hello"]`, matching one saved `started: hello`. See https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/177698#issuecomment-6297282981.

prs.title: fix: subagent Stop waits out its own queued drain and reports success
prs.body:
Closes #189376

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a subagent Stop issued from a source's own raw cleanup waits out the 15-second session-controller drain deadline and then reports success. The cleanup itself is waiting on Stop, so the two await each other until the deadline fires.

## User Impact

Stop from a subagent's own cleanup path returns promptly instead of stalling ~15 s. The queued-drain error is no longer incurred on this path at all (asserted below), per the issue's post-fix expectation.

## Why This Change Was Made

`settleQueued` (post-kill settlement walk) excluded the caller's current *operation* from the queued drain but not the caller's own *raw source*, then awaited `capturedExecution.execution.input.settlement.promise` for that self input. The sibling source-settlement owner (`settleSubagentKillSources`) already excludes this input correctly via `isCurrentSessionControllerTurnInput`; this change applies the same exclusion at the queued-drain boundary — the issue's first-named resolution ("the later scope drain should exclude that source, as the earlier settlement owner already does").

Scope note: the issue lists self-join refusal/report as an *alternative*, and its Notes say the fixed row "should run in milliseconds and could assert that no drain-deadline error occurs" — asserted. The described test-only replacement-fixture row is the issue author's separate test-only follow-up (#189394).

## Evidence

### 1. Dispatch regression (RED/GREEN, controlled clock)

New regression in `src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-control.accepted-stop.test.ts`: a terminal subagent whose raw disposal is held, with Stop issued inside that source's own async context. It runs on a controlled (fake) drain clock and leaves no timer scheduled.

- **RED on base** (`upstream/main`, source restored in-tree): Stop never settles before the fake deadline — `AssertionError: expected false to be true` (exit 1).
- **GREEN here**: settles promptly, returns `{ status: "ok" }`, and `result.error` contains no drain-deadline text.

Focused suites: `accepted-stop` + `kill-settlement` + `publication` **3 files / 42 tests pass**. `tsgo:core` clean; `oxlint` 0/0 and `oxfmt --check` clean on both changed files.

### 1b. Project-owned regression row: measured drain-deadline differential

The defect is observable in the repository's own shipped test suite, on a row that predates this PR (present identically on `upstream/main`). Row: `normal terminal cleanup preserves exact Stop ownership (self-disposal after turn completion, afterCleanup=true)` in `subagent-control.accepted-stop.test.ts`.

Command (same file, same row, only `subagent-control-kill-scope.ts` differs):

```
# BASE (upstream/main subagent-control-kill-scope.ts restored in-tree)
17408ms  normal terminal cleanup preserves exact Stop ownership (self-disposal after turn completion, afterCleanup=true)
 2282ms  ... (self-disposal, afterCleanup=true)
 2610ms  ... (self-disposal during wake cancellation, afterCleanup=true)
suite total: 73156 ms

# HEAD (this PR)
 2368ms  normal terminal cleanup preserves exact Stop ownership (self-disposal after turn completion, afterCleanup=true)
 2325ms  ... (self-disposal, afterCleanup=true)
 2277ms  ... (self-disposal during wake cancellation, afterCleanup=true)
suite total: 57320 ms
```

The affected row loses exactly one `SESSION_CONTROLLER_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and lands in line with its seven sibling rows (~2.2-2.4 s of shared fixture overhead); the suite total drops by 15,836 ms. This is the acceptance signal the issue's own Notes predicted: `Once this is fixed, the row should run in milliseconds`. No author-added scaffolding is involved — the row, the held raw disposal, and the Stop call all come from the existing suite.

### 2. Gateway product-path artifact (redacted)

A real Gateway process ran the bundled Matrix plugin against a local fake homeserver; one room message entered through the real sync ingress and reply pipeline (channel runs bind gateway subagents). The scripted model then executed the reachable self-cleanup variant through shipped tools: main turn → `sessions_spawn`; the child turn → `subagents list` → `subagents cancel <own runId>` **from inside its own controller turn**, with the kill executed by the shipped `subagents` tool.

```
[proof] model request {plan:"sessions_spawn"}   tools(51): spawn=true subagents=true
[proof] child cancel tool_call emitted {"runId":"cf548141-…"}
[proof] child cancel result returned {"elapsedMs":25,  "result":"{\"found\":true,\"killed\":false,\"runId\":\"cf548141-…\"…}"}
[proof] self-cancel tool latency: 25 ms
[proof] PASS: self-cancel returned promptly
```

Base comparison for this reachable variant is also prompt (~18 ms): cancelling a run from its own live turn aborts the turn, so the product path releases the source settlement quickly. The stalled join the issue reports needs the raw disposal to stay pending while the Stop awaits it — that held-disposal state is exactly what the controlled-clock regression pins (base fails, head passes). The external-cleanup control (Stop from outside still joining disposal) is covered by the existing `lifecycle cleanup joins terminal controller disposal` row, passing.

AI disclosure: generated and automatically reviewed with Qoder.


### 3. Live proof capture — held-disposal fault through the production boundary (RED → GREEN)

The held-disposal fault is exercised through the real production boundary: `killSessionSubagentRuns` is driven from inside `withSessionControllerSource(owner.input, …)` — the source's own raw cleanup — with the real subagent registry, real session-controller settlement, and the **real SQLite state worker** (no mocked fix path). Only downstream gateway RPC/announce are mocked, which sit outside the repaired `settleQueued` boundary.

Run on this PR's head commit `afcfa58c1b` (isolated forks pool so the state worker opens on the main thread):

```
✓ … subagent-control.accepted-stop.test.ts > Stop from the source's own cleanup does not wait out the queued drain  1371ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  1 passed | 23 skipped (24)
```

Full `accepted-stop` suite on head — all self-disposal + external-cleanup-joining controls pass:

```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  24 passed (24)
```

Reverting the single fix line `!isCurrentSessionControllerTurnInput(capturedExecution.execution.input) &&` in `settleQueued` to reproduce `upstream/main` behavior, the **same** scenario FAILS:

```
× … subagent-control.accepted-stop.test.ts > Stop from the source's own cleanup does not wait out the queued drain  3306ms
AssertionError: expected false to be true // Object.is equality
  ❯ src/agents/subagents/registry/subagent-control.accepted-stop.test.ts:987:23
       987|       expect(drained).toBe(true);
Test Files  1 failed (1)
     Tests  1 failed | 23 skipped (24)
```

`drained` stays `false`: the self-issued Stop never settles before the 15 000 ms drain deadline — exactly the held-disposal fault. This isolates the repaired failure condition **through the production boundary** (the Gateway self-cancel path, by contrast, passes on both base and head because aborting the live turn releases the source settlement quickly).

**Prompt recovery:** on head, `drained === true` under the controlled drain clock — Stop returns before the deadline (no queued-drain error; `result.error` contains no drain-deadline text).
**External cleanup joining preserved:** the fix keeps the existing controller predicate at the final drain, so external Stop callers still await cleanup. In the same passing suite the external-cleanup-joining controls pass (e.g. `lifecycle cleanup joins terminal controller disposal`, `normal terminal cleanup preserves exact Stop ownership (…)` — 24 passed). `settlement.status` remains `"pending"` after the self-source returns, confirming external custody is not weakened.

No credentials, IPs, phone numbers, or non-public endpoints appear in this output (`<home>/` paths redacted).

### 4. Standalone production-boundary trace — real wall-clock RED → GREEN

This section answers the review's two objections directly: it is **not** a Vitest assertion and **not** the Gateway self-cancel variant that also succeeds on base. It is a standalone process that drives the shipped production entry `killSessionSubagentRuns` (the same entry `stopSessionResetSubagents` calls) against the real subagent registry, real session-controller settlement, and the real SQLite state worker in a scratch state dir.

**Method**

- Runs with `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs`, outside any test runner: no `vi`, no fake timers, no mocked gateway / state worker / announce modules. Real wall clock, real `setTimeout`, real deferred promises.
- A real subagent run is registered through shipped `registerSubagentRun`; a real controller source is registered through shipped `registerChatAbortController`; the source enters real `withSessionTurn` and its raw disposal is held (`releaseTail` is resolved only **after** Stop is observed).
- Shipped `captureSubagentExecution` is used as a pre-flight to prove the production boundary actually binds the held source to this run (`captured: true`, `sameInputAsCaller: true`).
- Stop is then issued **from inside** `withSessionControllerSource(owner.input, …)` — the source's own raw cleanup — via the shipped entry:

```ts
result = await withSessionControllerSource(owner.input, () =>
  killSessionSubagentRuns({
    cfg: getRuntimeConfig(),
    sessionKey: entry.requesterSessionKey,
    agentId: "main",
  }),
);
```

- **BASE negative control** is the same process with exactly one line removed from `settleQueued`: `!isCurrentSessionControllerTurnInput(capturedExecution.execution.input) &&`. The file is restored afterwards; the PR diff is unchanged.
- Environment note: the shipped drain deadline uses `settlesWithin(..., { ref: false })` (an unref'd timer). In production the Gateway listener / state worker keeps the event loop alive so the deadline is observable. The standalone process supplies the equivalent long-lived service handle explicitly; **the 15 000 ms deadline is neither mocked nor shortened**.
- Exact head: `afcfa58c1bdbde105076180d8c047319c54c8a12` (`fix/189376-subagent-stop-self-source-drain`). Node 26.12.1, macOS arm64.
- Commands (the two observation scripts are untracked local files, not part of this PR's diff; they import only shipped exports):

```text
PROOF_HEAD_LABEL=HEAD node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs .workbuddy/proof/live-189391-v2.mts
PROOF_HEAD_LABEL=HEAD node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs .workbuddy/proof/external-join-189391.mts
# revert the single fix line, repeat both with PROOF_HEAD_LABEL=BASE, then restore the file
```

**A. Held-disposal fault and prompt recovery (self-source Stop)**

HEAD (this PR):

```text
[189391] t=     1ms scratch state dir + config written (path redacted)
[189391] t=  3175ms runtime config installed through shipped config owner
[189391] t= 17921ms seeded one real subagent run via shipped registerSubagentRun {"runId":"self-source-drain"}
[189391] t= 17926ms real controller source registered; settlement.promise intentionally held
[189391] t= 17933ms source entered its real controller turn; held-disposal state established
[189391] t= 19445ms pre-flight: shipped captureSubagentExecution resolves the held source {"executionStatus":"running","captured":true,"sameInputAsCaller":true,"rpcSourceFound":true,"childSessionKey":"agent:main:subagent:self-source-drain","requesterSessionKey":"agent:main:main","drainTimeoutMs":15000}
[189391] t= 19445ms environment: long-lived service handle active; shipped drain deadline = 15000ms (unref'd)

[189391] t= 21191ms drain-deadline fault observed = false

[189391] t= 21191ms DERIVED {"stopElapsedMs":"1746","shippedDrainTimeoutMs":15000,"deadlineElapsed":false}
```

BASE (single fix line reverted):


**B. External cleanup joining preserved (sibling invariant / over-exclusion control)**

A second standalone run calls the same shipped entry **without** any source context (an external cleanup caller), while the source's raw disposal is still held. prs.title: fix(gateway): keep sandbox previews consistent after saves
prs.body:
> **Do not merge.** This task requests a ready PR for review only.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two read-after-write/view regressions introduced by #194885: a successful Control UI file save updated canonical bytes but the next preview still read the old private checkout; host-only sessions with a retained former sandbox checkout could also preview stale guest bytes.

## User Impact

Saves now settle guest changes, perform the existing canonical hash comparison and write, then import the saved change into the private checkout under the same custody before guest writers resume. Private backing selection applies only to sandbox sessions; host sessions read canonical files. Read-only file/media access still causes zero container pauses. Permissions, descriptor containment, mount visibility, and canonical public paths remain unchanged.

A retained local sandbox checkout is the preview's live view. Direct canonical host edits enter that view at the next workspace preparation; UI saves synchronize immediately. Reads may observe in-progress guest writes and do not promise a snapshot. Capture/publication/lifecycle reconciliation retains quiescence. No config, cache, schema, or migration change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The former read-side checkpoint protected coherent reconciliation, not read-time containment: the pause ended before opening a file. #194885 removed it. This follow-up completes the write-side ownership transfer and deletes the obsolete read-checkpoint adapter, its exclusive test, and unused benchmark mode. It leaves the conflict-recovery algorithm in #194430 untouched.

## Evidence

- Save/reload regression is red on the original published head: preview returned prior guest bytes after a successful save. The corrected real `sessions.files.set` → file/media reload returns saved bytes.
- Host-policy regression is red on that head: real `sessions.files.get` returned retained guest bytes instead of current canonical bytes. Corrected suite: 11 passed.
- Full affected file/save/worktree/projection command: 136 passed, 3 existing platform/filesystem skips. Original containment/read suite: 136 passed, 1 existing skip. Alias, shadowed-mount, symlink-swap, in-place partial-write, and revoked-authority coverage stays green.
- Final core, all 29 core-test shards, and script typechecks pass. Targeted core/script lint, format, diff check, line caps, and test-line ratchet pass. Codex autoreview of the complete lane against `ade7c07d4c70`: P0–P2 scoped-clean, no actionable findings.
- `pnpm check:changed` ran twice. Its remaining main regressions reproduce on the exact original parent: 20 changelog-credit violations introduced by `266a7aa0fe69` (#194364), and Knip's `OpenClawShell` export error introduced by `adca0b0844c7` (#194815). These are unresolved main check regressions, not passing checks. A local closure-narrowing error was fixed and all affected typechecks rerun successfully.
- Follow-up production delta: **−10 lines**. Complete lane versus original parent: **+72 production lines**, needed for physical backing separate from canonical paths, current owner checks, bounded metadata lookup, and same-custody saves. Complete lane net tests: +212 lines, with an explicit allocation; new regression file: 267 lines.

Production-shaped synthetic campaign: 62,000 files (1,181,100,000 bytes), 40.28 GiB synthetic agent DB, 10,001 metadata sessions, 3,006 populated transcript sessions. Real isolated Gateway WebSocket `sessions.files.get`; continuous Docker guest writes with 20 ms heartbeat; 30 serial reads offered at 2-second intervals. Five AB/BA pairs plus A/A controls, no production data or Team access.

| Metric | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read-induced pauses / 150 reads | 150 | 0 |
| Manifest scans / 150 reads | 150 | 0 |
| Pooled read p50 / p95 | 2,740 / 3,221 ms | 129 / 176 ms |
| Median process CPU per read | 3,281 ms | 136 ms |
| Median main V8 allocation per read | 30.33 MB | 10.55 MB |
| Median maximum guest heartbeat gap | 3,040 ms | 31.4 ms |
| Total excess guest gaps above 40 ms | 382,299 ms | 24.2 ms |

A/A median read latency differed 2.95%; p95 differed 79.92%, process CPU 25.34%, allocation 12.39%. The noisy first control is retained. All five paired median latency reductions were 94.89–95.42%, CPU reductions 95.36–96.45%, allocation reductions 61.46–65.44%. The baseline overran the offered cadence (median batch 82.77 s); candidate finished in 58.14 s. Excess heartbeat gaps include unrelated scheduling/storage noise, not only pause time.

Timing baseline replays the exact parent's affected owner/caller modules in a common runtime/dependency environment, not a separately built full baseline Gateway. prs.title: fix(models): models status and Doctor stay silent when provider catalog discovery fails
prs.body:
Related: #166875

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw models status` and Doctor say nothing when the Gateway has published a rejected or unavailable provider catalog discovery, so only `models list` explains why a provider's models are missing.

This is the status/Doctor part that #167128 left open. It is a partial fix for #166875: it does not change xAI catalog discovery or establish why the reported account was rejected.

## User Impact

User impact: `models status` and Doctor now name the provider (and profile, when known) whose catalog discovery was rejected or unavailable, with a retry step. Doctor shows rejected discovery by default and unavailable discovery with `--severity-min info`.

- `models status` prints one stderr line per rejected or unavailable provider/profile outcome. JSON stdout and the `--check` exit status are unchanged.
- Doctor's `core/doctor/model-references` check reports rejected discovery as a **warning** and unavailable discovery as **info** (shown with `--severity-min info`).
- Behavior change: at the default threshold, explicit `openclaw doctor --lint` exits 1 instead of 0 when a catalog rejection is published. Bare `openclaw doctor --json` still exits 0 but includes the new finding, and its `ok` field follows the same warning threshold (from `doctor-lint-runner.ts`; the live run already had other findings, so it does not show that transition). Update runs use `--severity-min error` and are not affected.
- `models list`: its two existing discovery hints now name the full command (`openclaw models list --refresh`) instead of `--refresh`, because the same text is now shown by status and Doctor. The generic "could not refresh all providers" line now prints after these hints. stdout is unchanged.
- With the Gateway stopped, status and Doctor have no prepared catalog to read, so the new diagnostics do not appear (existing documented behavior).
- The hint names the global refresh command; it does not carry `--agent` or `--provider`.
- No configuration, schema, protocol, discovery, credential, or model-availability change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway already classifies each provider's catalog discovery as `ready`, `auth-rejected`, or `unavailable` and publishes the outcome. `models list` printed the non-ready outcomes with its own code (#167128), while `models status` and Doctor share `getModelCatalogWarnings` (#169708), which only handled `ready`. This change moves the two non-ready diagnostics into that shared helper and removes the list-only copy, so all three commands use one owner and one set of strings. The helper has no other callers.

Doctor maps unavailable discovery to info because offline local servers (Ollama, LM Studio) report `unavailable`, and the models docs already state that offline servers produce no missing-ID warning; a warning would turn the default lint red whenever a local server is off. Rejected discovery needs user action, so it is a warning, like the existing missing-model advisory.

Production **+17 / -13**, tests **+57 / -9** (net +48), docs **+6 / -1**. `docs/cli/models.md` and `docs/gateway/doctor/running.md` describe the new behavior. No changelog change.

<details>
<summary>Intentionally unchanged</summary>

- xAI catalog requests and account eligibility (the remaining part of #166875).
- Gateway logging for catalog failures.
- Producer-side publication of catalog outcomes; this PR only consumes published outcomes.
- `refreshFailed` semantics: rejection stays separate from the generic refresh warning.
- `models status --json` output, Control UI, and Android.
- No static catalog fallback.

</details>

## Evidence

- **Focused tests** (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`): `src/flows/doctor-model-reference-check.test.ts` 5/5, `src/commands/models/list.status.test.ts` 24/24, `src/commands/models/list.prepared-catalog.test.ts` 15/15. Wall time on the dev host, including Vitest startup: 44 s, 19 s, and 18 s; Vitest reports 37.6 s, 11.9 s, and 11.6 s. For the Doctor file, 91% of that is cold transform and its tests take about 1 s; the case stays at the check boundary because a helper-only test cannot show that Doctor consumes the prepared Gateway catalog.
- **Negative control**: with production files restored to base and the final tests kept, the extended Doctor case and the new status case fail (no rejected or unavailable finding; no stderr line). The list case also fails on base, but only because its expected wording changed; it is a guard that each diagnostic prints exactly once, not a reproduction of the original defect.
- **Targeted checks**: `oxfmt --check` passed on the eight changed code and docs files; `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json` on the six changed TypeScript files reported 0 warnings and 0 errors; `pnpm lint:docs` (markdownlint) reported 0 issues; `git diff --no-index --check` on the same base and patched files produced no output. Typecheck passed: `pnpm tsgo:core` (16 s) and `pnpm tsgo:core:test --ci-graphs-json '["core-test-commands","core-test-other"]'` (both graphs, about 11 s each).
- **Test-line budget**: on the base, `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet` reported the tree 70 lines over its ceiling, inherited from main; #194509 has since cleared that debt on main. This PR adds `config/test-lines-allocations/catalog-discovery-status-doctor-166875.txt` with 48 lines, equal to its net regression-test growth for the new status and Doctor coverage and the list exactly-once guard; the shared baseline is unchanged. The inherited 70-line overage is unrelated to this change.
- **Real CLI and Gateway proof**: the built CLI entry (`openclaw.mjs`) and a real Gateway ran with an isolated `HOME` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` (the config file lives in that state directory), channels disabled, on loopback, against a synthetic local LM Studio catalog server that returned 401, 403, 500, or 200 on demand. No credentials were configured, the setup used no external service, and per-command socket samples showed no non-loopback connections. LM Studio's catalog discovery goes through the same outcome owner as xAI's; this change only consumes published outcomes, so it does not depend on the provider.
  - Before the fix (base build): for 401, 403, and 500, `models status` printed no discovery diagnostic, and `doctor --lint --only core/doctor/model-references` reported no finding and exited 0. In the 200 mode, a configured model absent from the listing produced the existing missing-model warning in both `models status` and Doctor, confirming that both read the prepared catalog. The Gateway retried rejected discovery on its own about 30 and 90 seconds later; a separate probe confirmed these requests came from the Gateway, not from status or Doctor reads.
  - After the fix (same isolated setup, rebuilt from this patch): for 401 and 403, `models status` printed exactly one `Model discovery authentication was rejected for lmstudio. …` line, and `doctor --lint --only core/doctor/model-references` reported one warning with target `lmstudio` and exited 1. For 500, status printed the matching `Model discovery is unavailable for lmstudio. …` line; Doctor reported it as info, so the default lint exited 0 and the finding appeared with `--severity-min info`. In the 200 modes the existing missing-model warning was unchanged, `models status --json` stdout kept the same keys, and `models list` printed each hint once with the new wording. With `--agent work`, status read that agent's own prepared catalog, which still held its last successful listing (the refreshes ran for the default agent), so it showed the missing-model warning rather than the rejection.
  - Catalog request counts: each mode's `--refresh` made one catalog request. The status, Doctor, and RPC reads that followed made none, except one Doctor read in the rejected mode whose window caught the Gateway's second self-initiated retry (30 s and then 60 s after the rejected refresh, the same schedule as before the fix).
  - Revision: base `12026082dc86` with this PR's patch applied; the PR head `eedbbae4da93` has the same file contents.
  - This does not claim an installed-package upgrade, and it does not use an xAI account or real credentials.
- **Local review**: autoreview (Codex `gpt-6.1-sol`, P0–P2, one pass) of this patch against `12026082dc86` reported `scoped-clean` with no actionable findings.
- **CI**: pending this PR's CI.

<details>
<summary>Live commands</summary>

Run with the isolated environment above; `<port>` is a loopback port.

```sh
node openclaw.mjs gateway run --bind loopback --tailscale off --port <port>
node openclaw.mjs models list --refresh --json
node openclaw.mjs models list --provider lmstudio
node openclaw.mjs models list --plain
node openclaw.mjs models status
node openclaw.mjs models status --json
node openclaw.mjs models status --agent work
node openclaw.mjs doctor --lint --only core/doctor/model-references
node openclaw.mjs doctor --lint --only core/doctor/model-references --severity-min info --json
node openclaw.mjs doctor --lint --json
node openclaw.mjs doctor --json
node openclaw.mjs gateway call models.list --json --params '{"agentId":"main","view":"all","includeDetails":true,"includeDefaultModels":true,"preparedOnly":true}'
```

The isolated configuration pointed `models.providers.lmstudio.baseUrl` at the local catalog server, configured two agents (`main`, `work`) with `agents.defaults.systemAgent.agentId` set to `main`, set `agents.defaults.model` to a model the 200 listing omits, and disabled `models.catalogRefresh` and `memory.search`. Each mode started with one `--refresh`; the status, Doctor, and RPC reads that followed made no catalog requests, and the only increment in those windows was the Gateway's own retry described above.

</details>

prs.title: fix(worktrees): bound default-branch fetch by one refresh deadline
prs.body:
## Problem

"Updating repository…" (gateway phase `preparing_worktree_base`) can hold session startup for minutes. The default-branch refresh is supposed to be bounded by `ls-remote` (30s) plus `fetch` (60s). On the team gateway (worktree base latency investigation 2026-11-02), the slowest start took 270.7s with `baseRefresh=234126ms`, and its fetch **succeeded** without a warning. A borrower sharing that attempt waited `baseWait=120557ms`.

## Root cause

The gateway's diagnostics for that start show that the time was spent waiting in a queue, not in Git or on the network:

```
10:57:40.637 slow Git ref mutation  queueWaitMs=0       queuedOperationMs=807300   (another writer on the same clone)
10:57:44.425 slow Git ref mutation  queueWaitMs=229670  queuedOperationMs=3787     (the default-branch fetch)
```

`fetchRemoteDefault` runs `git fetch origin +refs/heads/<default>:refs/remotes/origin/<default>` with `{ ...options, timeoutMs: 60_000 }` (`src/agents/worktrees/base-ref.ts:473` on `main`). A fetch is a ref mutation, so `withGitRefAdmission` (`src/agents/worktrees/git.ts:198`) first enqueues it on the per-clone `enqueueGitRefMutation` queue (`git.ts:238`). The 60s timeout starts only after the queue admits the fetch and its process starts. While queued, the fetch is bounded only by the caller's signal, and that signal has no deadline here.

As a result, any long ref writer on the same clone (`worktree add`, hydration, pack maintenance, a fast-forward) stretches the "60s" fetch to the length of its own run. In the slow start above, the fetch queued for 229.7s and ran for 3.8s, which adds up to the 234s `baseRefresh`. On Nov 2, the same log also shows other holders running for 123–807s and queued waiters waiting 47–230s.

## Solution

Give the default-branch refresh one deadline. `fetchRemoteDefault` arms a 90s deadline (the existing 30s + 60s budgets) before `ls-remote`, combines it with the caller's signal, and passes the result to the fetch:

- If the deadline expires while the fetch is still queued, the ref queue drops the fetch before it starts.
- If the deadline expires while the fetch is running, the process is stopped like a timeout.

Both cases take the existing fetch-failure path: keep the cached `refs/remotes/origin/<default>`, report `fetchSucceeded: false`, and add a warning that names the 90s budget and the wait for other Git ref updates. This adds no fallback mode, option, or queue policy.

The caller's own signal still owns cancellation and attempt retirement. The deadline applies only to the fetch call, so an expired refresh is not treated as a cancelled owner.

## Impact

- A held ref queue now adds at most ~90s of refresh to a default-branch start, instead of the holder's full duration (230s observed, up to 807s possible). The start then proceeds on the cached default with a visible warning.
- Borrowers sharing the attempt get the same bounded result.
- As before, the fallback does not mark the base fresh, so the next start retries the fetch.

## Evidence

Regression test in `base-ref.test.ts`: "uses the cached default when the fetch outwaits the refresh deadline in the ref queue". It uses a real Git repo and remote, a real ref-queue holder on the same clone, and the real `resolveWorktreeBase`. Only the 90s timer is replaced by a test-controlled signal.

- Base (`63c25f72`): **red**. The test times out after Vitest's 120000ms because the fetch stays queued behind the holder.
- Fix: **green**. The whole `base-ref.test.ts` file passes (51 passed).

Wall-clock repro (a scratch test that is not committed; real timers, real Git, real ref queue, with another writer holding the clone's ref queue for 150s):

| | wall time of `resolveWorktreeBase` | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base | 151,482 ms | waited for the holder; `fetchSucceeded: true` |
| Fix | 91,698 ms | cached default, `fetchSucceeded: false`, deadline warning |

Other checks: `git-fetch.test.ts` and `git.test.ts` pass (43 passed). `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:core:test` pass. oxlint and oxfmt are clean on the touched files.

Review: local autoreview (Codex engine, branch mode, base `63c25f72` → head `4c0ad6c7`, max priority P2) was scoped-clean with no actionable findings. The reviewer noted limited surrounding context and that it did not run the tests.

## Accepted edge cases

- The local reads before and after the network refresh (`git remote`, `config`, `symbolic-ref`, the cached `rev-parse`) keep their standard 120s budgets. They do not queue, and they are needed to produce the cached fallback. They are slow only when the host itself is IO-starved.
- The `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` update after a successful fetch is also a ref mutation, so it can still queue. It runs only when the remote default branch changes.
- `baseHydration` (`estimateWorktreeGitBytes`) is not covered, because the checkout needs those objects. Its 120s and 240s tails on this host come from local Git reads reaching their 120s budget on a clone with 1,216 packs and no multi-pack-index, and those starts failed. That belongs to clone maintenance, not to this deadline.
- The 807s ref-queue holder on Nov 2 was not identified from the logs. This change bounds its effect on startup but does not shorten the holder.
- I did not measure a remote that hangs. In this sandbox, a synthetic hanging `upload-pack` made `ls-remote` end with a cleanup-uncertain error at its 30s timeout on base. That is a separate path from the queue wait.

## Worked on by

- @vyctorbrzezowski

The diagnostics OTel tests still construct a retired NodeSDK implementation and replay assertions already made against the private provider used by production.

Dependency/export checks remain red for unchanged `readReleaseChangelogFiles`, `isSessionUnreadAckOnlyPatch`, `OpenClawShell` and `CommandPaletteOpenDetail` exports outside this change; no OTel path is reported. Their declarations, consumers, scan configuration and dependencies are unchanged.

prs.title: fix: Muse requests stall or lose approval authority after reuse
prs.body:
Closes #183672
Related: #183282 (independent compaction fallback repair).

## What Problem This Solves

Muse requests can time out behind retained native work, replay an earlier answer into a new reply, or fail with `missing scope: operator.approvals` after reusing a process created by a narrower caller.

## User Impact

Status requests can join native work and receive its current answer. Approval requests use the current admitted caller while preserving genuine System scope limits and revoked-owner checks. Stopping an observation of earlier work detaches that observation; turns started by the current request retain normal cancellation.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use `ifBusy: "steer"` and the SDK's authoritative started/joined identity. Observe real native tool progress, keep historical items out of the current reply, and fence publication after asynchronous transcript append.

Install approvals before resume traffic and bind each new handler to its prepared attempt context. Pooled stdio callbacks otherwise inherit the process creator's async context. Keep authority checks before host approval and native decisions, cancel pending approval UI when observation ends, and retire a failed SDK projection so a fresh owner can recover the same native session and approval stage.

This keeps approval handling in the harness and transcript/result projection in its existing event owner. No provider, dependency, configuration, permission-policy, or transcript-schema changes.

## Evidence

Validation ran on an isolated macOS arm64 host with Node 24.22.1, task-owned state, and the package-pinned SDK. Tested and committed source files were verified byte for byte.

Current head `da67db5d0bfc054fddaf142d884afd2af5209c13` integrates main `d4ae3a73118767a3f9bf80625a91733d19055393`. Its only conflict was the controlled MSP test helper; the resolution preserves both the native approval-effect controls and upstream helper simplifications. The Muse production harness, event owner, and process pool remain byte-identical to the native-tested parent `15457a3a`. All 60,327 tracked candidate blobs matched the isolated Gronk checkout. The 73 controlled tests, focused source and package-boundary typechecks, typed lint, formatting, and independent conflict-resolution review passed again against the integrated source and frozen current-main lockfile. The maintained lint owner prepared the SDK boundary declarations; no core/app build or additional real-model run was performed.

Parent and integrated-head evidence:

- **73 canonical tests passed:** the four non-live Muse suites (71) plus two real-SDK pooled-context regressions. These cover reply/history isolation, joined abort/timeout, native settlement lifetime, resume-time approval replay, deferred transcript publication, offered refusal safety, and completed-first history.
- The pooled-context regression failed before the fix with the exact missing-scope error. After the fix, one physical peer serves both attempts, approval dispatch carries the current run identity, and exactly one offered approval decision produces the native filesystem effect. The inverse control keeps full admitted authority under a genuinely narrow current System frame and verifies denial with no effect.
- Existing real-SDK controls verify that detached or revoked observations cannot make a native approval decision or effect, and that a fresh owner recovers the same pending stage. Their late-request barrier is causal. Tool-progress fixtures likewise wait for production observation rather than a fixed sleep.
- Package and focused regression typechecks, changed-file typed lint, formatting, and diff checks passed.
- Independent P0–P2 source review and structured autoreview found no blocking defects. The final equivalent factory capture location received a focused caller-chain review; review did not substitute for test execution.

Captured controlled-fixture results:

```text
uses the current full approval owner after reusing a pooled native peer: PASS
uses the current narrow approval owner after reusing a pooled native peer: PASS
Tests  2 passed (2)
Test Files  4 passed (4)
Tests  71 passed (71)
```

A matching operator compatibility port also passed a real isolated public Gateway approval-manager flow using SDK 1.4.2 and a controlled MSP peer: narrow warmup → full approval produced a final reply through the same physical host; full warmup → narrow caller remained denied. Its 28 regression controls passed. This is compatibility-port acceptance, not canonical SDK 1.4.10 native-provider/busy-turn qualification.

Real native-provider authority evidence was also captured on exact head `15457a3aebf4124de78ade51d6d478e31ee3e95c`: SDK 1.4.10, official Muse 1.4.13-R6996.1, Meta provider, Node 24.22.1/macOS arm64, and the published declared-compatible OpenClaw 2026.10.10-beta.3 host. The selected Muse target was built without changing minHost/compatibility metadata; this was not an all-main Gateway build. Native permissions used task-only `:ask-me`, with exact prehashed effects confined to the owned sandbox workspace.

- A genuine narrow warmup followed by a full current owner reused the same physical native host. One public plugin approval and one offered allow decision produced the exact owned effect after resolution.
- A separate native conversation on that same pool was warmed by a full owner, then resumed by a client negotiated with only `operator.read` and `operator.write`. Its real native approval request failed closed: one offered abort decision, zero allow decisions, zero plugin approval events, and no effect after all owned processes ended. The missing-scope Gateway diagnostic was fenced to that admitted run.
- The inverse runner's original **FAIL remains preserved**: `agent.wait` returned `error: "agent run failed"` without the detailed scope string its assertion required. Independent scoped adjudication accepted the authority behavior from the matched wire, run, diagnostic, and filesystem evidence; the runner was not relabeled green.

Captured redacted native result:

```json
{
  "head": "15457a3a",
  "sdk": "1.4.10",
  "samePhysicalPooledHost": true,
  "fullOwnerApprovedEffect": true,
  "narrowOwner": {
    "nativeAbort": 1,
    "nativeAllow": 0,
    "pluginApprovalEvents": 0,
    "effectAbsent": true
  },
  "originalInverseRunnerPassed": false,
  "scopedAuthorityAdjudication": "accepted"
}
```

The real-SDK controlled subprocess tests remain the evidence for busy-turn, cancellation, detached/revoked-owner, and same-stage recovery behavior. Real-native busy-resume, joined Stop, detached/revoked-owner, and same-stage recovery qualification remains outstanding. Maintainer direction on joined-work Stop, timeout, and reset semantics also remains outstanding; the native authority evidence does not resolve those lifecycle or merge-readiness gaps.

prs.title: improve(postgres): read each chat history page from one database snapshot
prs.body:
Related: #188956, #190129 (this PR removes the repeated read snapshots inside one history page, a measured part of the #188956 latency; #190129 addresses the worker queueing in front of it)

## What Problem This Solves

On PostgreSQL, some `chat.history` pages open a new read-only transaction for each step of the page read instead of one: a sparse page (few visible replies among many silent ones) takes three `BEGIN ... READ ONLY` / `ROLLBACK` round trips over the database bridge, and a Claude CLI session after a provider switch takes seven. When the database is across a network hop, every extra round trip adds to the page's response time.

## User Impact

User impact: each `chat.history` page on PostgreSQL is read from one database snapshot. Sparse pages and Claude CLI sessions after a provider switch now take one transaction for the page instead of three or seven, which makes those pages faster when PostgreSQL is not on loopback: with about 3.4 ms added round trip, median latency drops by 14 to 26 ms for a sparse page and about 40 ms for a Claude CLI session after a provider switch (see Evidence). Pages that already took one transaction are unchanged. Returned messages and pagination are unchanged, and SQLite is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The history worker runs one task at a time, and no read snapshot outlives a task. The `chat.history` page task now holds one PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY` snapshot from its first read until the page is assembled. That covers the Claude CLI import check (revision read and, after a provider switch, its tail read) and every page and tail-scan read. Every read still goes through the read scope's admission (`acquire`), so validation and path checks run per read as before. A failed read rolls the held snapshot back and the next read opens a fresh one. A failed rollback retires the connection, as `runPostgresTransactionSync` does, and the snapshot uses the same `BEGIN` and read-snapshot scope.

Scope: this changes the page task only. The pending-input read that the handler issues before the page is its own worker request with its own snapshot, and the history reader cap (#169110) is untouched. It keeps the eager read-only `BEGIN` (the deferred `BEGIN` in #188952 was closed unmerged).

Scope question for review: this is a partial fix of #188956, so it keeps `Related:` instead of `Closes`. Options: (a) land this on its own and keep #188956 open for the worker queueing in #190129; (b) fold both into one PR; (c) hold this until #190129 lands. Recommended: (a). Whichever of this and #190129 lands second switches to `Closes #188956`. The two changes touch different files, each is measured on its own, and this one already removes 2 or 6 read-only transactions (4 or 12 round trips) per affected page with no other behavior change.

## Evidence

Evidence files: https://github.com/etzelm/openclaw/tree/assets/pg-r2-l3c-history-snapshot-evidence/current-source (paths below are relative to it; `README.md` there describes each file). PostgreSQL 17.11, isolated Gateways built with `pnpm build` from each tree.

Acceptance rule: through a running Gateway, sparse and Claude CLI provider-switch pages read in one page snapshot with the same reads and messages; with a real network hop, their p50 and p95 drop by roughly the saved round trips times the round trip time; pages that already use one snapshot do not change; no metric moves the wrong way.

- **Gateway A/B with a network hop** (`network-hop/`). Base `3c130c7268e` (this head's `main` parent), fix `213409bf` (same PR source as the current head). The Gateway reaches PostgreSQL through toxiproxy with 1 ms latency toxics on each stream. Measured `SELECT 1` round trip: 0.44 ms without the toxics, 3.77 ms before the runs and 3.85 ms after (`network-hop/rtt.txt`). The store was seeded through the Gateway's own RPCs. It has a sparse session (1 visible reply, 250 silent replies, 1 visible reply) and a Claude CLI session made by one real `chat.send` turn through a stub `claude` binary on `PATH` (the stream-json stub from `test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/reply-run-plugin-reload.product-proof.e2e.test.ts`, no API key), followed by 250 silent replies and a visible one, and then switched to the default OpenAI model with `sessions.patch`. Both use `limit: 2`. There were 5 runs per arm in ABBA order (base fix fix base base fix fix base base fix). Each run restores the same database template and boots the arm. It warms, traces 3 calls per session, then runs a 20 s closed-loop `chat.history` load per session at concurrency 1 and 8 after a 5 s warmup, with statement logging off. A run starts only when the 1-minute load average is below the 32 cores (`network-hop/load-gates.txt`).

  Read-only transactions per call (`network-hop/SUMMARY-snapshots.txt`; runs N4 to N10 carry a statement trace, N1 to N3 latency only):

| shape | arm | runs x calls | page snapshots | page reads | pending-input snapshots |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sparse session | base | 4 x 3 | 3.0 | 11.0 | 1.0 |
| sparse session | fix | 3 x 3 | 1.0 | 11.0 | 1.0 |
| Claude CLI session after a provider switch | base | 4 x 3 | 7.0 | 23.0 | 1.0 |
| Claude CLI session after a provider switch | fix | 3 x 3 | 1.0 | 23.0 | 1.0 |
| 4 imported Claude Code threads | base and fix | 7 x 12 | 1.0 | 3.0 | 1.0 |

  Latency, median of the 5 per-run values (range) in ms, no errors in any run (`network-hop/SUMMARY-latency.txt`, per run in `network-hop/runs/*/load-*.json` with the 1-minute load recorded at start and end):

| shape | concurrency | arm | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sparse | 1 | base | 89.54 (86.70 to 100.37) | 101.18 (93.17 to 116.49) | 115.00 (93.91 to 121.88) |
| sparse | 1 | fix | 75.69 (71.11 to 85.72) | 103.37 (83.60 to 116.78) | 112.35 (90.50 to 212.93) |
| sparse | 8 | base | 171.09 (157.09 to 175.80) | 192.44 (168.67 to 233.24) | 234.65 (214.77 to 264.21) |
| sparse | 8 | fix | 144.65 (135.19 to 167.16) | 162.76 (153.67 to 248.04) | 195.39 (162.52 to 273.79) |
| Claude CLI after switch | 1 | base | 174.21 (164.71 to 179.52) | 234.17 (204.74 to 284.76) | 249.55 (211.94 to 421.65) |
| Claude CLI after switch | 1 | fix | 132.55 (119.25 to 138.00) | 171.47 (127.20 to 229.39) | 196.63 (136.80 to 269.81) |
| Claude CLI after switch | 8 | base | 246.90 (245.67 to 277.02) | 326.56 (323.03 to 373.99) | 356.10 (342.10 to 424.84) |
| Claude CLI after switch | 8 | fix | 207.56 (198.27 to 219.93) | 262.89 (257.81 to 285.03) | 274.96 (265.30 to 314.48) |

  The sparse page saves 2 `BEGIN` and 2 `ROLLBACK` round trips, about 15 ms at 3.8 ms each, and its p50 drops by 13.85 ms at concurrency 1 and 26.44 ms at concurrency 8. At concurrency 1 the sparse p95 is flat (101.18 vs 103.37, within the run ranges), and at concurrency 8 it drops by 29.68 ms. The Claude CLI page saves 6 and 6, about 46 ms, and its p50 drops by 41.66 and 39.34 ms and its p95 by 62.70 and 63.67 ms. The runs started below the core count, but the 1-minute load during them ranged from 4.3 to 37.0 because the host is shared. No cell got worse beyond its range.

- **Running Gateway statement trace on loopback** (`gateway-trace/`, previous head `27ab37717af` vs its `main` parent `7c2ff8f775a`, same code): sparse session 3.0 vs 1.0 page snapshots (7 x 3 calls per arm, reads 11 = 11); imported Claude Code threads and a 12-session `limit: 100` shape stay at 1.0 on both arms. On loopback the latency did not move (`gateway-trace/SUMMARY-latency.txt`), as expected when a round trip costs well under a millisecond.
- **Regression test** (new, live PostgreSQL), red on base and green with the change (`tests/conformance-red.log`, `tests/conformance-green.log`). Read-only `BEGIN`s for one page, base vs fix: sparse page 3 vs 1, Claude CLI session after a provider switch 7 vs 1. A third test checks that a failed statement inside the held snapshot is rolled back and the next read works.
- **Live PostgreSQL conformance** (PostgreSQL 17.11): the new test plus the bridge, read-facts, reuse, publication, hydration, agent and state database suites, 15 files and 165 tests pass on head `213409bf` (`tests/conformance-green-new-head.log`) and again on head `5af7f878` merged into current `main` `10592dacdc6` (`ci-lanes/conformance-merge-into-main-10592dac.log`). Consumer unit tests for the changed modules pass on the previous head, 16 files and 223 tests (`tests/unit-fix.log`). `pnpm check:changed` on the previous head merged into `main` `638a1851e7e` (`ci-lanes/check-changed-merge-into-current-main.log`): typecheck, format, lint (0 errors), Knip (0 unused exports) and the guards pass. The one failure is `changelog attributions` on existing `CHANGELOG/2026.6.8.md` and `CHANGELOG/2026.7.1.md` entries, which fails the same way on that `main` (`ci-lanes/changelog-attributions-current-main.log`).
- **CI lanes**: the red lanes on head `5af7f878` came from the `main` that CI merged it into (`4ca233c908c`), not from this branch, which touches no `ui/` files and allocates exactly the 146 test lines it adds.
  - `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets` failed only `test-lines` (`over by: 50; net delta: +146`, `ci-lanes/ci-run-42356893636-excerpt.txt`). Plain `main` `4ca233c908c` is already over by 50 with no change at all (`ci-lanes/test-lines-plain-main-4ca233c9.log`), and the CI merge tree reproduces the CI result (`ci-lanes/test-lines-ci-merge-5af7f878-into-4ca233c9.log`). `main` reconciled the ceiling in #194509. Merged into current `main` `10592dacdc6`, `pnpm check:baseline-ratchets` passes all 10 checks (test lines slack 21; `ci-lanes/baseline-ratchets-merge-into-main-10592dac.log`).
  - `checks-ui-e2e (1/2)` failed one test, `ui/src/e2e/gateway-fresh-visit.http.e2e.test.ts:175` ("Matcher did not succeed in time"). It fails the same way on plain `main` `4ca233c908c` (`ci-lanes/ui-e2e-gateway-fresh-visit-plain-main-4ca233c9.log`) and was fixed on `main` by #194504. Merged into current `main`, that file passes 3 of 3 (`ci-lanes/ui-e2e-gateway-fresh-visit-merge-into-main-10592dac.log`), and the other 18 files of that shard pass (`ci-lanes/ui-e2e-shard1-files-merge-into-main-10592dac.log`; the one WebKit test there needed WebKit installed locally and then passed 2 of 2, `ci-lanes/ui-e2e-mcp-fullscreen-webkit-rerun-merge-into-main-10592dac.log`).
  - `openclaw/ci-gate` only aggregates the two lanes above.

### Gaps

- The network hop is simulated with toxiproxy on one host, not a remote database. The saving scales with the real round trip time.
- This fixes the per-page transaction part of #188956 only. Its worker queueing is #190129, and the two changes touch different files. The combined pair was not benchmarked here.
- After a provider switch, the Claude CLI import check still reads the tail twice (now inside one snapshot). This is a possible follow-up, as is sharing a snapshot with the pending-input request.
